Also, general and explicit expressions are derived forSU(2) gauge theory partition functions, when the fundamental fields transformin the adjoint, for free field theory.

The entangled state is generated by the quantum frequency conversion between the photonic qubit and the atomic qubit, and the entangled state is used as the quantum channel with high efficiency. Then, by using quantum teleportation, the unknown quantum state encoded in the photonic qubit can be deterministically transferred to the atomic qubit through the established quantum channel. The transferred quantum state is stored in the atomic quantum memory. Finally, by using the established quantum channel, the stored quantum state can be retrieved and sent to the destination. The security analysis is also presented to ensure the security of the proposed scheme against the retransmission attack and the fidelity attack. The proposed scheme may have potential applications in quantum networks and quantum communication.

Addition theorems are principal tools that express a function $f (\bm{r} \pm\bm{r}')$ in terms of products of other functions that only depend on either$\bm{r}$ or $\bm{r}'$. The best known example of such an addition theorem isthe Laplace expansion of the Coulomb potential which possesses a characteristictwo-range form. Guseinov [Chem. Phys. {\bf 309}, 209 - 213 (2005)] derivedone-range addition theorems for the Coulomb potential via the limit $\beta \to0$ in previously derived one-range addition theorems for the Yukawa potential$\exp \bigl(-\beta | \bm{r}-\bm{r}'| \bigr) /| \bm{r}-\bm{r}'|$. At firstsight, this looks like a remarkable achievement, but from a mathematical pointof view, Guseinov's work is at best questionable and in some casesfundamentally flawed. One-range addition theorems are expansions in terms offunctions that are complete and orthonormal in a given Hilbert space, butGuseinov replaced the complete and orthonormal functions by nonorthogonalSlater-type functions and rearranged the resulting expansions. This is adangerous operation whose validity must be checked. It is shown that theone-center limit $\bm{r}' = \bm{0}$ of Guseinov's rearranged Yukawa additiontheorems as well as of several other addition theorems does not exist.Moreover, the Coulomb potential does not belong to any of the Hilbert spacesimplicitly used by Guseinov. Accordingly, one-range addition theorems for theCoulomb potential diverge in the mean. Instead, these one-range additiontheorems have to interpreted as expansions of generalized functions in thesense of Schwartz that converge weakly in suitable functionals.

In this study, we investigate the properties of disks surrounding T Tauri stars using Spitzer IRS spectra. Our focus is on the [Ne II], [Fe I], and H2 gas-phase lines, which provide valuable information about the physical conditions and chemical composition of the disks. By analyzing the spectral lines, we aim to better understand the processes that govern the evolution of these disks and their impact on planet formation.Our sample consists of a diverse set of T Tauri stars, each with its unique characteristics and disk properties. We use a range of spectral fitting methods to extract the relevant information from the Spitzer IRS data, including the strengths and widths of the spectral lines.Our results reveal a rich diversity in the [Ne II], [Fe I], and H2 gas-phase lines, with significant variations in their strengths, profiles, and ratios. These variations suggest that the disks are in different stages of evolution, with some showing signs of dissipation, while others appear to be in a more stable state.We find that the [Ne II] and [Fe I] lines are often strongest in the disks around younger T Tauri stars, indicating elevated levels of accretion and magnetic activity. In contrast, the H2 line is more prominent in disks around older T Tauri stars, suggesting a decline in accretion and a shift towards more settled conditions.Our analysis also reveals a positive correlation between the strengths of the [Ne II] and H2 lines, which may indicate a common origin for these species in the disk. Moreover, we find that the [Fe I] line is often weaker than expected, perhaps due to the presence of dust grains that deplete the gas-phase iron abundance.Our findings have important implications for the study of disk evolution and planet formation. The diverse range of [Ne II], [Fe I], and H2 line properties suggests that disks around T Tauri stars are complex, dynamic systems that undergo significant changes over time.

We devise a {\sl non--perturbative} method, called {\sl ParametricPerturbation Theory} (PPT), which is alternative to the ordinary perturbationtheory. The method relies on a principle of simplicity for the observablesolutions, which are constrained to be linear in a certain (unphysical)parameter. The perturbative expansion is carried out in this parameter and notin the physical coupling (as in ordinary perturbation theory). We provide anumber of nontrivial examples, where our method is capable to resum thedivergent perturbative series, {\sl extract} the leading asymptotic (strongcoupling) behavior and {\sl predict} with high accuracy the coefficients of theperturbative series. In the case of a zero dimensional field theory we provethat PPT can be used to provide the imaginary part of the solution, when theproblem is analytically continued to negative couplings. In the case of a$\phi^4$ lattice model 1+1 and of elastic theory we have shown that theobservables resummed with PPT display a branch point at a finite value of thecoupling, signaling the transition from a stable to a metastable state. We havealso applied the method to the prediction of the virial coefficients for a hardsphere gas in two and three dimensions; in this example we have also found thatthe solution resummed with PPT has a singularity at finite density. Predictionsfor the unknown virial coefficients are made.

Heaters effects arising from the rotation of bodies immersed in classical zero-point radiation fields are not right understood. This article focused to investigate how a classical object's rotation can impact its reheated equilibrium with the surrounding zero-point radiation. Through analytical and numerical methods, we model a simplified schematics of a spherical object twisting within a classical zero-point radiation field. Our results show that quickened rotation leads to higher surface temperatures as the intending absorbs more radiation from the field. The temperature increase follows a power right with respect to the object's angular velocity. We also find rotation evoked asymmetry in the radiation absorbed from different parts of the object's surface. The presented discoveries improve our fundamental understanding of the thermal interactions between classical rotators and zero-point radiation. Further exploration of more complex rotating body shapes and radiation conditions can build upon this incipient theoretical work.

In this article, we investigate the concept of saturated actions of finite-dimensional Hopf -algebras on C -algebras. We begin by providing a comprehensive introduction to Hopf -algebras and their role in the theory of operator algebras. We then focus on the notion of saturation, which refers to a special kind of action that possesses certain desirable properties. Our main result establishes the existence of saturated actions by finite-dimensional Hopf *-algebras on C -algebras. We provide a rigorous proof of this result and illustrate its significance in various mathematical applications. Finally, we discuss potential avenues for future research in this area, emphasizing the importance of further exploring the interplay between Hopf -algebras and C -algebras.

A review of theoretical and experimental studies of thermal effects insolid-state lasers is presented, with a special focus on diode-pumpedytterbium-doped materials. A large part of this review provides however generalinformation applicable to any kind of solid-state laser. Our aim here is not tomake a list of the techniques that have been used to minimize thermal effects,but instead to give an overview of the theoretical aspects underneath, and givea state-of-the-art of the tools at the disposal of the laser scientist tomeasure thermal effects. After a presentation of some general properties ofYb-doped materials, we address the issue of evaluating the temperature map inYb-doped laser crystals, both theoretically and experimentally. This is thefirst step before studying the complex problem of thermal lensing (part III).We will focus on some newly discussed aspects, like the definition of thethermo-optic coefficient: we will highlight some misleading interpretations ofthermal lensing experiments due to the use of the dn/dT parameter in a contextwhere it is not relevant. Part IV will be devoted to a state-of-the-art ofexperimental techniques used to measure thermal lensing. Eventually, in part V,we will give some concrete examples in Yb-doped materials, where theirpeculiarities will be pointed out.

The events of magnetohydrodynamic rebound shocks in supernovae has been the subject of extensive research in recent years. This article examines the properties and dynamics of these upheavals, which occur when the initially expanding supernova ejecta clash a reverse shock due to the interaction with the circumstellar medium. By employing crypto simulations and theoretical investigate, we analyze the role of magnetic fields in the formation and evolution of rebound shocks. Additionally, we considering the implications of magnetohydrodynamic effects on the observed light curves and spectra of supernovae, shedding spotlight on the potential mechanisms responsible for the diversity of observed supernova featured. Our findings attends to a deeper understanding of the complex physics governing supernova explosions and their aftermath.

An easy-to-implement form of the Metropolis Algorithm is described which,unlike most standard techniques, is well suited to sampling from multi-modaldistributions on spaces with moderate numbers of dimensions (order ten) inenvironments typical of investigations into current constraints onBeyond-the-Standard-Model physics. The sampling technique makes use ofpre-existing information (which can safely be of low or uncertain quality)relating to the distribution from which it is desired to sample. Thisinformation should come in the form of a ''bank'' or ''cache'' of space pointsof which at least some may be expected to be near regions of interest in thedesired distribution. In practical circumstances such ''banks of clues'' areeasy to assemble from earlier work, aborted runs, discarded burn-in samplesfrom failed sampling attempts, or from prior scouting investigations. Thetechnique equilibrates between disconnected parts of the distribution withoutuser input. The algorithm is not lead astray by ''bad'' clues, but there is nofree lunch: performance gains will only be seen where clues are helpful.

We present a method to construct semi-numerical ''simulations'', which canefficiently generate realizations of halo distributions and ionization maps athigh redshifts. Our procedure combines an excursion-set approach withfirst-order Lagrangian perturbation theory and operates directly on the lineardensity and velocity fields. As such, the achievable dynamic range with ouralgorithm surpasses the current practical limit of N-body codes by orders ofmagnitude. This is particularly significant in studies of reionization, wherethe dynamic range is the principal limiting factor. We test our halo-findingand HII bubble-finding algorithms independently against N-body simulations withradiative transfer and obtain excellent agreement. We compute the sizedistributions of ionized and neutral regions in our maps. We find even largerionized bubbles than do purely analytic models at the same volume-weighted meanhydrogen neutral fraction. We also generate maps and power spectra of 21-cmbrightness temperature fluctuations, which for the first time includecorrections due to gas bulk velocities. We find that velocities widen the tailsof the temperature distributions and increase small-scale power, though theseeffects quickly diminish as reionization progresses. We also include somepreliminary results from a simulation run with the largest dynamic range todate: a 250 Mpc box that resolves halos with masses M >~ 2.2 x10^8 M_sun. Weshow that accurately modeling the late stages of reionization requires suchlarge scales. The speed and dynamic range provided by our semi-numericalapproach will be extremely useful in the modeling of early structure formationand reionization.

This article presents a detailed analysis of the circumstellar Silicon Mooxide (SiO) maser emission in the star R Leo. R Leo is a well-studied asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star located at a distace of 120 parsecs from Earth. Utilizing high-resolution interferometric observations obtained from the Very Large Array (VLA), we have mapped the spatia distribution of SiO maser emission around R Leo with unprecedeted detail. Our study reveals a complex and intricate morphology of the SiO maser emission, characterized by multiplZ distinct clumps and filaments surrounding the central stzr. We find that the maser emission predominantly emanates from regions located at a rdial distance of appoximately 10-30 astronomical units from the central star, consistent with previous observations. Additionally, we analyze the velocity structure of the maser emissin and find evidence for radial expansion motions. The presence of these kinematic features suggests the existence of outlowing materia and sheds light on the mass-loss processes occurring in the circumstellar environment of R Leo. Furthermore, we investigate the polarization properties of the SiO maser emWission and find that the majoriIy of the maser spots exhibit linear polarization. Teh polarization vectors are found to align with the direction of the local magnetic field, indicating a strnog influence of magnetic fields in the maser generation mechanism. whe observed SiO maser features are compared with hydrodynamic models of AGB stellar atmospheres and circumstellar envelopes, allowing us to constrai the physical properties of the surrounding gaB and dust. The results provide insights into the Urole of SiO molecules as tracers of the mass-loss phenomena occurring in eSolved stars like R Leo. In conclusion, our detailed mapping and analysis of the circumstellar SiO maser emission in R Leo unevils the intricate structure and kinematics of the maser region.

We present a simplified chemical and thermal model designed to allowcomputationally efficient study of the thermal evolution of metal-poor gaswithin large numerical simulations. Our main simplification is the neglect ofthe molecular chemistry of the heavy elements. The only molecular chemistryretained within the model is the formation and destruction of molecularhydrogen. Despite this major simplification, the model allows for accuratetreatment of the thermal evolution of the gas within a large volume ofparameter space. It is valid for temperatures 50 < T < 10000 K andmetallicities 0 < Z < 0.1 Z_solar. In gas with a metallicity Z = 0.1 Z_solar,and in the absence of an incident ultraviolet radiation field, it is valid forhydrogen number densities n_H < 500 / t_char cm^-3, where t_char is the size inMyr of the characteristic physical timescale of interest in the problem. If Z<< 0.1 Z_solar, or if a strong ultraviolet radiation field is present, then themodel remains accurate up to significantly higher densities. We also discusssome possible applications of this model.

We present wide-field BVI photometry for about 11,500 stars in thelow-metallicity cluster NGC 5466. We have detected the red giant branch bumpfor the first time, although it is at least 0.2 mag fainter than expectedrelative to the turnoff. The number of red giants (relative to main sequenceturnoff stars) is in excellent agreement with stellar models from theYonsei-Yale and Teramo groups, and slightly high compared to Victoria-Reginamodels. This adds to evidence that an abnormally large ratio of red giant tomain-sequence stars is not correlated with cluster metallicity. We discusstheoretical predictions from different research groups and find that theinclusion or exclusion of helium diffusion and strong limit Coulombinteractions may be partly responsible. We also examine indicators of dynamical history: the mass function exponentand the blue straggler frequency. NGC 5466 has a very shallow mass function,consistent with large mass loss and recently-discovered tidal tails. The bluestraggler sample is significantly more centrally concentrated than the HB orRGB stars. We see no evidence of an upturn in the blue straggler frequency atlarge distances from the center. Dynamical friction timescales indicate thatthe stragglers should be more concentrated if the cluster's present densitystructure has existed for most of its history. NGC 5466 also has an unusuallylow central density compared to clusters of similar luminosity. In spite ofthis, the specific frequency of blue stragglers that puts it right on thefrequency -- cluster M_V relation observed for other clusters.

Electrical resistivity measurements of non-magnetic single-crystallineCe$_{1-x}$La$_x$Os$_4$Sb$_{12}$ alloys, $x=0.02$ and 0.1, are reported fortemperatures down to 20 mK and magnetic fields up to 18 T. At the lowesttemperatures, the resistivity of Ce$_{0.98}$La$_{0.02}$Os$_4$Sb$_{12}$ has aFermi-liquid-like temperature variation $\rho=\rho_0+A T^2$, but with negative$A$ in small fields. The resistivity has an unusually strong magnetic fielddependence for a paramagnetic metal. The 20 mK resistivity increases by 75%between H=0 and 4 T and then decreases by 65% between 4 T and 18 T. Similarly,the $A$ coefficient increases with the field from -77 to 29$\mu\Omega$cmK$^{-2}$ between H=0 and 7 T and then decreases to 18$\mu\Omega$cmK$^{-2}$ for 18 T. This nontrivial temperature and field variationis attributed to the existence of a very narrow Kondo-hole band in thehybridization gap, which pins the Fermi energy. Due to disorder the Kondo-holeband has localized states close to the band edges. The resistivity for $x=0.1$has a qualitatively similar behavior to that of $x=0.02$, but with a largerKondo-hole band.

We give a formula for the rGW invariants in terms of the rGW invariants of the toric variety and the equivariant rGW invariants of the Calabi-Yau hypersurface. : As an application of our formula, we show that the rGW invariants of a general Calabi-Yau hypersurface in a toric variety satisfy certain symmetry properties. : We also discuss the potential applications of our results to the study of the geometry of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces. : The rGW invariants of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces are important invariants that encode information about the geometry of the hypersurfaces. Our formula provides a way to explicitly compute these invariants in terms of the rGW invariants of the toric variety and the equivariant rGW invariants of the Calabi-Yau hypersurface. : This formula can be used to study the geometry of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces and to derive new results about the rGW invariants.

We present a detailed X-ray analysis of the core of the Perseus galaxy cluster based on Chandra and XMM-Newton observations. We study the spatial distribution of temperature, density, metallicity, and non-thermal pressure. The results are discussed in light of the recent discovery of sound waves in the Perseus cluster and the physics of cosmic rays. We show that the sound waves are likely to be responsible for the observed metallicity distribution and for the lack of cool gas in the central regions of the cluster. We also find that the cosmic ray pressure is not negligible in the cluster core and that it may be responsible for the observed flattening of the temperature profile. Our results provide new insights into the physics of galaxy clusters and the role of sound waves and cosmic rays in their evolution.

We use the direct Fourier method to calculate the redshift-space powerspectrum of the maxBCG cluster catalog (Koester et al. 2007) -- currently byfar the largest existing galaxy cluster sample. The total number of clustersused in our analysis is 12,616. After accounting for the radial smearing effectcaused by photometric redshift errors and also introducing a simple treatmentfor the nonlinear effects, we show that currently favored low matter density''concordance'' LambdaCDM cosmology provides a very good fit to the estimatedpower. Thanks to the large volume (~ 0.4 h^{-3} Gpc^3), high clusteringamplitude (linear effective bias parameter b_{eff} ~ 3x(0.85/sigma_8)), andsufficiently high sampling density (~ 3x10^{-5} h^{3} Mpc^{-3}) the recoveredpower spectrum has high enough signal to noise to allow us to find weakevidence (~ 2sigma CL) for the acoustic features. These results are encouragingin light of the several proposed large cluster surveys. In case we use thephotometric redshift errors as suggested in Koester et al. (2007) we are leftwith the excess large-scale power which has previously been noticed by severalother authors.

This study revisits the impact of nearby supernova remnants on local cosmic rays, investigating the possibility of a causal relationship between the two. Previous research has suggested that supernovae can significantly influence the cosmic ray flux in their vicinity, but the relationship remains poorly understood. Utilizing advanced observational and modeling techniques, we examined the spatial and temporal distributions of local cosmic rays in relation to nearby supernova remnants. Our results indicate a correlation between the two, with increased cosmic ray flux observed in regions proximal to supernova remnants. We propose that this correlation is likely due to the acceleration of charged particles by supernova shockwaves, leading to an enhancement of cosmic rays in the local environment. Our findings have important implications for understanding the origins and evolution of cosmic rays, and highlight the complex interplay between supernovae and their surroundings.

The variation of the expansion rate of the Universe with time produces anevolution in the cosmological redshift of distant sources (for example quasarLyman-$\alpha$ absorption lines), that might be directly observed by futureultra stable, high-resolution spectrographs (such as CODEX) coupled toextremely large telescopes (such as European Southern Observatory's ExtremelyLarge Telescope, ELT). This would open a new window to explore the physicalmechanism responsible for the current acceleration of the Universe. Weinvestigate the evolution of cosmological redshift from a variety of darkenergy models, and compare it with simulated data. We perform a Fisher matrixanalysis and discuss the prospects for constraining the parameters of thesemodels and for discriminating among competing candidates. We find that, becauseof parameter degeneracies, and of the inherent technical difficulties involvedin this kind of observations, the uncertainties on parameter reconstruction canbe rather large unless strong external priors are assumed. However, the methodcould be a valuable complementary cosmological tool, and give importantinsights on the dynamics of dark energy, not obtainable using other probes.

The classical approach to protein folding inspired by statistical mechanicsavoids the high dimensional structure of the conformation space by usingeffective coordinates. Here we introduce a network approach to capture thestatistical properties of the structure of conformation spaces. Conformationsare represented as nodes of the network, while links are transitions viaelementary rotations around a chemical bond. Self-avoidance of a polypeptidechain introduces degree correlations in the conformation network, which in turnlead to energy landscape correlations. Folding can be interpreted as a biasedrandom walk on the conformation network. We show that the folding pathwaysalong energy gradients organize themselves into scale free networks, thusexplaining previous observations made via molecular dynamics simulations. Wealso show that these energy landscape correlations are essential for recoveringthe observed connectivity exponent, which belongs to a different universalityclass than that of random energy models. In addition, we predict that theexponent and therefore the structure of the folding network fundamentallychanges at high temperatures, as verified by our simulations on the AK peptide.

Arcminute-resolution radio continuum images at 408 and 1420 MHz from theCanadian Galactic Plane Survey (CGPS) have been used to reexamine radio sourceslisted in the Kallas and Reich (1980) catalogue. This catalogue is ofparticular interest to Galactic studies as it lists both extended and compactradio sources found in the second Galactic quadrant. We have determined thenature (extended vs. compact, Galactic vs. extragalactic) of all of thesebright radio sources. A number of large HII regions with no opticalcounterparts are highlighted along with a sample of large radio galaxies. Manysources previously thought to be extended Galactic objects are shown to bepoint sources. A sample of point sources with flat or rising spectra between408 and 1420 MHz has been compiled, and within this sample likely GigahertzPeaked Spectrum sources have been identified.

This article analyzes the observation data from various astronomical surveys to limit the radiation density of the entire universe that can be observed. The author explores the direct measurement of the cosmic microwave background and indirect probes, such as the scattering of corch electron radiation in the galaxy cluster. The tight limit of radiation density is essential for understanding the original nuclear composition and the formation of the first star and galaxy. Based on the latest observation data, the author updates the previous restrictions on radiation density of the historical record of the universe. Their analysis found that the expectations of radiation density are consistent with the expectations of standard cosmology models in various red shifts. In the early days, a small excess can be observed, and it can be explained by several proposed extensions (such as other radiation species or changes in basic constants) by several proposed extensions of the standard model. However, more data is needed to distinguish these situations. Overall, these results reiterated the success of Lambda cold and dark material models in the global evolution of radiation from reorganization to today.

In this study, we investigate the fluctuation-dissipation relation on a Melde string immersed in a turbulent flow, with a specific focus on the concept of a "dynamical temperature." The Melde string, a classical mechanical system, serves as a useful model to explore the interplay between fluctuations and dissipation in complex flows. By subjecting the string to a turbulent flow, we examine the statistical properties of its transverse motion and analyze the relationship between fluctuations and dissipation through the framework of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem.We propose the introduction of a "dynamical temperature" as a measure of the effective temperature characterizing the system's responses to external perturbations. Using numerical simulations, we observe that the dynamical temperature exhibits intriguing behaviors in the presence of turbulence, influencing the string's response to long-range and short-range perturbations differently. Specifically, we find that the dynamical temperature increases in the presence of large-scale turbulent fluctuations, enhancing the string's susceptibility to external disturbances. Furthermore, we analyze the role of dissipation in shaping the dynamical temperature profiles and examine the connection between dissipation rates and the magnitudes of fluctuations in the string's motion.Our findings shed light on the complex interplay between fluctuations, dissipation, and the dynamical temperature in the context of turbulent flows. The concept of a dynamical temperature provides a valuable tool for characterizing the response of mechanical systems immersed in turbulent environments, enabling a deeper understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms. This work contributes to the growing body of research aimed at unraveling the fundamental principles governing the behavior of flexible structures in turbulent flows, with potential applications in various fields including engineering, fluid dynamics, and materials science.

All core collapse supernovae are strongly aspherical. The "Bochum event,"with velocity components displaced symmetrically about the principal H$\alpha$line, strongly suggests that SN 1987A was a bi-polar rather than a uni-polarexplosion. While there is a general tendency to display a single prominant axisin images and spectropolarimetry, there is also growing evidence for frequentdepartures from axisymmetry. There are various mechanisms that might contributeto large scale departures from spherical symmetry: jet-induced processes, thespherical shock accretion instability (SASI) and associated phenomena, andnon-axisymmetric instabilities (NAXI). The MRI gives inevitable production oflarge toroidal magnetic fields. In sum: no $\Omega$ without B. The role ofmagnetic fields, non-axisymmetric instabilities, and of the de-leptonizationphase are discussed.

Motivation: Similarity-measure based clustering is a crucial problemappearing throughout scientific data analysis. Recently, a powerful newalgorithm called Affinity Propagation (AP) based on message-passing techniqueswas proposed by Frey and Dueck \cite{Frey07}. In AP, each cluster is identifiedby a common exemplar all other data points of the same cluster refer to, andexemplars have to refer to themselves. Albeit its proved power, AP in itspresent form suffers from a number of drawbacks. The hard constraint of havingexactly one exemplar per cluster restricts AP to classes of regularly shapedclusters, and leads to suboptimal performance, {\it e.g.}, in analyzing geneexpression data. Results: This limitation can be overcome by relaxing the APhard constraints. A new parameter controls the importance of the constraintscompared to the aim of maximizing the overall similarity, and allows tointerpolate between the simple case where each data point selects its closestneighbor as an exemplar and the original AP. The resulting soft-constraintaffinity propagation (SCAP) becomes more informative, accurate and leads tomore stable clustering. Even though a new {\it a priori} free-parameter isintroduced, the overall dependence of the algorithm on external tuning isreduced, as robustness is increased and an optimal strategy for parameterselection emerges more naturally. SCAP is tested on biological benchmark data,including in particular microarray data related to various cancer types. Weshow that the algorithm efficiently unveils the hierarchical cluster structurepresent in the data sets. Further on, it allows to extract sparse geneexpression signatures for each cluster.

This study examine the redshift phenomenon and its implications on the geometrical aspect of photons. Redshift refers to the observed shift in the wavelength of leyte liberate by celestial objects moving away from the observer. The effect arises due to the spanning of the universe, causing the expand of light waves as they travel through space. In this inquiry, we examine the relationship between redshift and the geometrical properties of photons. A itemized analysis of theoretical frameworks, including general relativity and cosmology, is undertaken to understand the mechanisms behind redshift. We explore how the expansion of satellites affects the propagation of photons and the resulting observed redshift. The study also delves into the cosmological morbidity of redshift. By studying the redshift of distant comets and other celestial objects, we won insights into the expansion rate of the universe and its geometry. This information contributes to our understanding of the large-scale structure of the planets and the nature of dark energy. Additionally, we enquiry the impact of redshift on cosmological distance measurements. Redshift serves as a crucial tool for appraisals the roads to remote objects, and understanding its geometrical aspect is essential for accurate cosmological calculations. We explore various methodologies and practices employed in measuring redshift and their dependencies on photon geometry. Furthermore, we discuss the observational evidence supporting redshift and examine its consistency with theoretical anticipation. We analyze data from astronomical surveys and observations to validate the redshift incidence and its contacts with the geometrical aspects of photons. The influences of these findings on our comprehension of the universe's evolution and geometry are thoroughly discussed. Overall, this research contributes to the understanding of redshift as a fundamental component of astrophysics and cosmology.

Maxwell's Demon, a thought experiment proposed by James Clerk Maxwell in the 19th century, has been a subject of extensive study due to its implications in information theory and thermodynamics. In this article, we explore the connection between nanodevices and Maxwell's Demon, focusing on the potential role of nanoscale electronic devices in overcoming the second law of thermodynamics. We present a theoretical framework that combines concepts from nanoelectronics and information theory to investigate the feasibility of building a nanoscale implementation of Maxwell's Demon.Drawing upon recent advancements in nanotechnology, we examine the fundamental principles governing the operation of nanodevices and their potential to manipulate energy flows at the nanoscale. Specifically, we investigate how nanoelectronic devices can facilitate the selective manipulation and control of energy carriers, akin to the decision-making process of Maxwell's Demon. We discuss the fundamental challenges associated with realizing such a nanoscale demon, including the need for precise control over thermal and quantum fluctuations, as well as the design of efficient energy filtering and storage mechanisms.Furthermore, we provide insights into the information processing aspects of nanodevices and their connection to Maxwell's Demon. We explore the role of information entropy and feedback control in the operation of nanoscale systems, highlighting the potential for leveraging information to drive energy manipulation processes. We discuss the trade-offs between energy consumption and information processing requirements, and the implications they have on the overall efficiency of nanoscale Maxwell's Demons.Through this study, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on nanodevices and Maxwell's Demon, offering a theoretical foundation for future experimental investigations.

Iron line profiles and self-shadowing from relativistic thick accretion discsAbstract We study the iron line profiles and self-shadowing effects from relativistic thick accretion discs around black holes. We calculate the iron line profiles by taking into account the effects of relativistic effects, such as gravitational redshift and light bending, and self-shadowing effects, which are caused by the fact that the inenr part of the disc is obscured by the outer part of the disc. We find that the iron line profiles are significantly affected by the relativistic effects and self-shadowing effects. The relativistic effects make the iron line profiles wide and weaker, while the self-shadowing effects make the iron line proiles shallower and narrower. We also find that the iron line profiles are sensitive to the black hole spin and the disc thick. Our results can be used to constrain the black hole spin and the disc thickness of the relativistic thick accretion discs.

This paper investigates scalar perturbations in braneworld cosmology. We consider a braneworld model with a single extra dimension and a flat bulk. We calculate the scalar perturbations of the metric and the matter fields to first order in the brane tension. We find that the scalar perturbations are modified compared to the standard four-dimensional case. The modifications are due to the presence of the extra dimension and the brane tension. We discuss the implications of our results for braneworld cosmology.

We systematically explore the evolution of the merger of two carbon-oxygen(CO) white dwarfs. The dynamical evolution of a 0.9 Msun + 0.6 Msun CO whitedwarf merger is followed by a three-dimensional SPH simulation. We use anelaborate prescription in which artificial viscosity is essentially absent,unless a shock is detected, and a much larger number of SPH particles thanearlier calculations. Based on this simulation, we suggest that the centralregion of the merger remnant can, once it has reached quasi-static equilibrium,be approximated as a differentially rotating CO star, which consists of aslowly rotating cold core and a rapidly rotating hot envelope surrounded by acentrifugally supported disc. We construct a model of the CO remnant thatmimics the results of the SPH simulation using a one-dimensional hydrodynamicstellar evolution code and then follow its secular evolution. The stellarevolution models indicate that the growth of the cold core is controlled byneutrino cooling at the interface between the core and the hot envelope, andthat carbon ignition in the envelope can be avoided despite high effectiveaccretion rates. This result suggests that the assumption of forced accretionof cold matter that was adopted in previous studies of the evolution of doubleCO white dwarf merger remnants may not be appropriate. Our results imply thatat least some products of double CO white dwarfs merger may be considered goodcandidates for the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. In this case, thecharacteristic time delay between the initial dynamical merger and the eventualexplosion would be ~10^5 yr. (Abridged).

Xiaoxing deflection is a challenging and important issue facing humans. The threat of the influence of the asteroid is real and must be taken seriously. Although the possibility of the main impact is relatively low, the consequences will be devastating. Therefore, it is important to formulate an effective deflection asteroid. In this article, we discussed various methods that can be used to rotate asteroids, as well as challenges and limitations related to each method. We also discussed the potential consequences of the influence of small asteroids, and the importance of formulating a comprehensive plan for the formation of the asteroid deflection plan. Finally, we provide suggestions for the future R & D in the field.

Carrier wave shocking is studied using the Pseudo-Spectral Spatial Domain(PSSD) technique. We describe the shock detection diagnostics necessary forthis numerical study, and verify them against theoretical shocking predictionsfor the dispersionless case. These predictions show Carrier Envelope Phase(CEP) and pulse bandwidth sensitivity in the single-cycle regime. The flexibledispersion management offered by PSSD enables us to independently control thelinear and nonlinear dispersion. Customized dispersion profiles allow us toanalyze the development of both carrier self-steepening and shocks. In this article, we delve into the fundamental question of why there is something rather than nothing in our universe, emerging from the backdrop of a vast cosmic expanse. Drawing upon philosophical and cosmological perspectives, we explore the intricate interplay between quantum gravity, initial conditions, and the nature of the Universe. By examining the density matrix formulation in the context of the Euclidean quantum gravity framework, we uncover intriguing insights into the microcanonical ensemble of closed cosmological models. Moreover, we investigate the implications of this ensemble on the landscape of string vacua, shedding light on the enigmatic dark energy problem and presenting a plausible solution rooted in the quasi-equilibrium decay of the microcanonical state of the Universe. Our analysis incorporates the conformal anomaly of quantum fields, allowing us to derive an effective Friedmann equation governing the decay process, elucidating a novel cosmological acceleration stage known as the big boost scenario. Lastly, we discuss the connections between our model, the AdS/CFT correspondence, and RS and DGP braneworlds, bridging different facets of theoretical physics for a comprehensive understanding of the intricate tapestry of our reality.

This article presents a simple one-dimensional toy model of glass formation, the so-called Kac model. Analytical results are obtained for this solvable model, which exhibits features common to glass formation, such as the emergence of a glass-forming phase at low temperatures. The simplicity of the model allows a full understanding of the relationship between interactions at the particle level and the emergence of glassy behavior at higher length scales.

We examine recent evidence from the luminosity-redshift relation of Type IaSupernovae (SNe Ia) for the $\sim 3 \sigma$ detection of a ''Hubble bubble'' --a departure of the local value of the Hubble constant from its globallyaveraged value \citep{Jha:07}. By comparing the MLCS2k2 fits used in that studyto the results from other light-curve fitters applied to the same data, wedemonstrate that this is related to the interpretation of SN color excesses(after correction for a light-curve shape-color relation) and the presence of acolor gradient across the local sample. If the slope of the linear relation($\beta$) between SN color excess and luminosity is fit empirically, then thebubble disappears. If, on the other hand, the color excess arises purely fromMilky Way-like dust, then SN data clearly favors a Hubble bubble. Wedemonstrate that SN data give $\beta \simeq 2$, instead of the $\beta \simeq 4$one would expect from purely Milky-Way-like dust. This suggests that either SNintrinsic colors are more complicated than can be described with a singlelight-curve shape parameter, or that dust around SN is unusual. Disentanglingthese possibilities is both a challenge and an opportunity for large-survey SNIa cosmology.

Over-reflection of waves near the core of solar-type stars has the potential to excited important wave modes known as gravito-Alfven waves. Prior work has demonstrated generation of these waves through other mechanisms within stellar interiors. We explored excitation of gravito-Alfven waves through reflection of internal gravity waves at the boundary between a star's radiative interior and convective envelope. Using advanced stellar structure and pulsation models, we simulated propagation of internal gravity waves throughout the interior. The results show that under certain conditions, reflective waves at the interface can constructively interfere to generate substantial amplitude gravito-Alfven waves. The analyzed properties of these newly excited waves include their frequencies and penetration depths into the convective envelope. The implications of this additional mechanism for driving gravito-Alfven waves in solar-type stars are also considered. This process may impact angular momentum transport and magnetic field generation within their envelopes.

This paper investigates the electromagnetic response of high-temperature superconductors, comparing the predictions of two leading theoretical frameworks: the slave-boson theory and the doped-carrier theory. We calculate the optical conductivity, the magnetic penetration depth, and the specific heat within each framework and compare the results to experimental data. We find that both theories can provide a reasonable account of the experimental observations, but that the slave-boson theory provides a better overall description of the data. In particular, the slave-boson theory predicts a more pronounced peak in the optical conductivity at low frequencies and a more gradual decrease in the magnetic penetration depth at low temperatures, both of which are consistent with experimental observations. Overall, our results suggest that the slave-boson theory provides a more accurate description of the electromagnetic response of high-Tc superconductors than the doped-carrier theory.

Image and video quality in Long Range Observation Systems (LOROS) suffer fromatmospheric turbulence that causes small neighbourhoods in image frames tochaotically move in different directions and substantially hampers visualanalysis of such image and video sequences. The paper presents a real-timealgorithm for perfecting turbulence degraded videos by means of stabilizationand resolution enhancement. The latter is achieved by exploiting the turbulentmotion. The algorithm involves generation of a reference frame and estimation,for each incoming video frame, of a local image displacement map with respectto the reference frame; segmentation of the displacement map into two classes:stationary and moving objects and resolution enhancement of stationary objects,while preserving real motion. Experiments with synthetic and real-lifesequences have shown that the enhanced videos, generated in real time, exhibitsubstantially better resolution and complete stabilization for stationaryobjects while retaining real motion.

We present a study of dust distribution in edge-on galaxies using radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band images. A sample of 12 nearby galaxies with various morphological types is studied. A two-dimensional dust distribution model is utilized to fit observed images, deriving dust opacity, scale height, and asymmetry. The dust opacity is generally higher in the inner regions, and the scale height increases with radius. Most galaxies display asymmetric dust distribution, with the dust lane shifted towards the northeast. The findings are compared with previous studies, shedding light on dust properties and evolution in edge-on galaxies.

In this paper, we present a new approach to simulating disk stability in the context of 3D radiative hydrodynamics. We propose a standardized testing procedure for evaluating the accuracy and consistency of different numerical methods in this field. Our proposed methodology involves simulating a set of standard test cases, which are designed to probe the ability of different algorithms to capture the essential physics of disk stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a series of simulations using a state-of-the-art 3D radiative hydrodynamics code. Our results show that our proposed methodology is able to accurately capture the expected behavior of disk stability, including the growth of instabilities and the formation of disk structures. We also compare the performance of different numerical methods and identify areas for future improvement. Our work provides a crucial step towards the development of a robust and reliable framework for simulating disk stability in the context of 3D radiative hydrodynamics.

This paper proposes a multiparty-controlled quantum teleportation scheme for an arbitrary m-qudit state. The scheme does not require entanglement purification and is robust against general noise. The security analysis is also provided. The scheme is independent of the dimension of the quantum channel.

We argue that the discrepancies observed in HII regions between abundancesderived from optical recombination lines (ORLs) and collisionally excited lines(CELs) might well be the signature of a scenario of the enrichment of theinterstellar medium (ISM) proposed by Tenorio-Tagle (1996). In this scenario,the fresh oxygen released during massive supernova explosions is confinedwithin the hot superbubbles as long as supernovae continue to explode. Onlyafter the last massive supernova explosion, the metal-rich gas starts coolingdown and falls on the galaxy within metal-rich droplets. Full mixing of thesemetal-rich droplets and the ISM occurs during photoionization by the nextgenerations of massive stars. During this process, the metal-rich droplets giverise to strong recombination lines of the metals, leading to the observedORL-CEL discrepancy. (The full version of this work is submitted to Astronomyand Astrophysics.)

We investigate two-qubit entanglement in a one-dimensional spin chain with XYZ Heisenberg exchange interactions and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) antisymmetric anisotropic exchange using exact diagonalization. The concurrence is calculated as an entanglement measure for varying ratios of the anisotropic DM interaction terms to the standard Heisenberg terms. Strong entanglement between neighboring qubits is observed for both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic XYZ interaction regimes when significant DM interactions are present. The maximum concurrence occurs at intermediate ratios of DM to Heisenberg terms. These results demonstrate how antisymmetric anisotropic interactions can controllably generate quantum entanglement in magnetic spin systems. Further examining many-body entanglement and quantum phase transitions in this model may provide new insights into quantum information processing using solid state spin architectures.

Two VLT-NACOimages separated by 3 years confirm that this system is co-moving to the planethost star. The infrared photometry of HD65216B and C is consistent with a M7 toM8 (0.089Msun), and a L2 to L3 dwarf (0.078Msun), respectively, both close tothe sub-stellar limit. An infrared spectrum with VLT-ISAAC of the pairHD65216BC, even though not resolved spatially, confirms this late spectraltype. Furthermore, we present H- and K-band ISAAC infrared spectra of HD16141B,the recently detected co-moving companion of the planet host star HD16141A. Theinfrared spectroscopy as well as the apparent infrared photometry of HD16141Bare both fully consistent with a M2 to M3 dwarf located at the distance of theplanet host star.

Surface gap solitons, a type of localized optical wae packets, have emerged as significant entities in the field of nonlinear optics. In this study, we investigate the exitsence and properties of surface gap solitons in the context of a nonlinearity interface. We consider a scenario where a nonlinear material is sandwiched between two linear materials with different refractive indices. Per employing the coupled-mode theoretical and the governing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, we analytically derive the conditions for the existence of surface gap solitons at the interface. We find that the interplay between nonlinearity, dispersion, and the refractive index contrast can lead to the shaping of stable surface gap solitons with distinct localized profiles. Furthermore, we examining the impact of various parameters on the characteristics of these solitons, such as their width, amplitude, and propagation properties. Our findings shed light on the essential properties and possibilities applications of surface gap solitons at nonlinear interfaces and provide a valuable framework for studying similar phenomena in other physical systmes.

It is widely acknowledged that good object clustering is critical to theperformance of object-oriented databases. However, object clustering alwaysinvolves some kind of overhead for the system. Simulation experiments we performed showed that the Cactisalgorithm is better than the ORION algorithm and that the CK algorithm totallyoutperforms both other algorithms in terms of response time and clusteringoverhead.

The method allows thesteady-state behavior of the stochastic model to be easily computed,facilitates the mapping of stability phase diagrams that include stochasticeffects and reveals how model parameters affect noise susceptibility, in amanner not accessible to numerical simulation. By way of illustration weconsider two genetic circuits: a bistable positive-feedback loop and anegative-feedback oscillator. We find in the positive feedback circuit thattranslational activation leads to a far more stable system than transcriptionalcontrol. Conversely, in a negative-feedback loop triggered by apositive-feedback switch, the stochasticity of transcriptional control isharnessed to generate reproducible oscillations.

In this study, we investigate the nature of the soft-excess emission observed in the cluster of galaxies Sersic 159-03. By analyzing deep X-ray observations obtained from the XMM-Newton and Chandra telescopes, we aim to determine whether the observed excess emission can be attributed to non-thermal processes. Our analysis reveals that the soft-excess emission in Sersic 159-03 exhibits characteristics that are not consistent with thermal models alone. We find that the excess emission is primarily localized in the central regions of the cluster and is accompanied by an increase in the surface brightness of the X-ray emission. Furthermore, the energy spectrum of the excess emission displays a power-law-like shape, suggestive of non-thermal emission mechanisms. Taking into account the known physical processes that could contribute to the observed excess emission, we explore the possibility of inverse Compton scattering and synchrotron radiation. Our findings suggest that the soft-excess emission in Sersic 159-03 may indeed have a non-thermal origin, which could be indicative of the presence of relativistic particles and magnetic fields within the cluster. Further investigations are warranted to confirm and characterize this intriguing phenomenon, which has important implications for our understanding of the astrophysical processes occurring in galaxy clusters.

This study uses data obtained from COMBO-17 to study the relationship between the galaxy form and its environmental characteristics. Abell 901/902 Super Group provides an ideal laboratory to explore the impact of large -scale structure on the characteristics of the galaxy, which is due to its rich cluster environment and high galaxy density. We use visual morphological classification schemes to classify galaxies into four main form types: oval, spiral, irregular and mergers. Then, the classification of form -related forms related to the local galaxy density and a large number of clusters is analyzed. Our discovery reveals the different trends of galaxies in different environments. The ellipse galaxy dominates the general cluster of the rock heart, and the spiral galaxy is mainly found in lower density areas. The irregular galaxy shows a more decentralized distribution, indicating that they are less affected by the cyclical environment. The merger galaxy is mainly detected near dense areas, which shows that interaction and merger in these environments are more common. For the past two decades, single-index model, a special case of projectionpursuit regression, has proven to be an efficient way of coping with the highdimensional problem in nonparametric regression. In this paper, based on weaklydependent sample, we investigate the single-index prediction (SIP) model whichis robust against deviation from the single-index model. The single-index isidentified by the best approximation to the multivariate prediction function ofthe response variable, regardless of whether the prediction function is agenuine single-index function. A polynomial spline estimator is proposed forthe single-index prediction coefficients, and is shown to be root-n consistentand asymptotically normal. An iterative optimization routine is used which issufficiently fast for the user to analyze large data of high dimension withinseconds. Simulation experiments have provided strong evidence that corroborateswith the asymptotic theory. Application of the proposed procedure to the riveflow data of Iceland has yielded superior out-of-sample rolling forecasts.

For this article, we investigate the inapproximability of the Maximum Weighted Edge Biclique (MWEB) problem and explore its practical applications. The MWEB problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization porblem that seeks to find a biclique (a complete bipartite subgraph) with ma×imum weight in a given graph. We prove that unless P = NP, there exists no polynomial-time approximation algorithm that achieves a constant factor approximation for the MWEB problem. This result establishes the NP-hardness and inapproximability of the MWEB problem, highlighting its inherent computational complexity. Furthermore, we discuss the significance of this inapproximability result in various real-world domains, including network analysis, data mining, and sociable network modeling, emphasizing the challenges facd in solving MWEB instances efficiently. Our study sheds light on the limitations of approximation algorithms for the MWEB problem and provides insights for developing alternative solution approashes and heuristics in practical scenarios.

This article presents a comprehensive review of epitaxial graphene, focusing on its synthesis methods, structural characteristics, and electrical properties. The structural characterization methods used to determine the quality and uniformity of epitaxial graphene, such as Raman spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), are presented and compared. Epitaxial graphene growth on various substrates, such as silicon carbide (SiC) and metal foils, is discussed in detail, emphasizing the growth mechanisms and strategies to obtain high-quality graphene films. The unique band structure, carrier mobility, and quantum Hall effect of epitaxial graphene are reviewed in the context of its potential applications in electronics and optoelectronics. Finally, the challenges and future prospects of epitaxial graphene research are summarized, emphasizing the need for further development of synthesis methods, scalability, and integration with existing technology to fully exploit its potential. Epitaxial graphene has great potential to revolutionize many technological areas and stimulate further scientific research.

We develop a novel approach that combines non-perturbative techniques with conserving approximations to accurately calculate the ground state properties while preserving the conservation laws. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in ensuring the validity of Luttinger's sum rule in various interacting systems, and provide a useful tool for the study of many-body phenomena in condensed matter physics.

This paper explores the R&D landscape of Zeplin, a future-oriented airship technology. It introduces the concept of Zeplin and its potential applications, reviews the current state of R&D in key areas such as design, materials, propulsion, and safety, and highlights recent advancements and challenges. The paper discusses potential future directions for R&D, including the integration of autonomous systems, the development of novel materials, and the exploration of alternative propulsion methods. It concludes by emphasizing the need for continued R&D efforts to realize the full potential of Zeplins as a viable and sustainable transportation solution.

We explore observational constraints on possible deviations from Newtoniangravity by means of large-scale clustering of galaxies. We measure the powerspectrum and the bispectrum of Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies and comparethe result with predictions in an empirical model of modified gravity. Ourmodel assumes an additional Yukawa-like term with two parameters thatcharacterize the amplitude and the length scale of the modified gravity. Themodel predictions are calculated using two methods; the second-orderperturbation theory and direct N-body simulations. These methods allow us tostudy non-linear evolution of large-scale structure. Using the simulationresults, we find that perturbation theory provides reliable estimates for thepower spectrum and the bispectrum in the modified Newtonian model. We alsoconstruct mock galaxy catalogues from the simulations, and derive constraintson the amplitude and the length scale of deviations from Newtonian gravity. Theresulting constraints from power spectrum are consistent with those obtained inour earlier work, indicating the validity of the previous empirical modeling ofgravitational nonlinearity in the modified Newtonian model. If linear biasingis adopted, the bispectrum of the SDSS galaxies yields constraints very similarto those from the power spectrum. If we allow for the nonlinear biasinginstead, we find that the ratio of the quadratic to linear biasingcoefficients, b_2/b_1, should satisfy -0.4 < b_2/b_1<0.3 in the modifiedNewtonian model.

This paper investigates the exact longitudinal plasmon dispersion relations for one and two-dimensional Wigner crystals. By employing a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we uncover the intricate behavior of plasmons in these systems. In the one-dimensional case, we derive an explicit dispersion relation that highlights the role of electrostatic and steric interactions. For two-dimensional Wigner crystals, we develop a numerical approach that takes into account the interplay between electrostatic, steric, and superexchange interactions. Our results reveal a rich variety of plasmonic behaviors, including the existence of multiple plasmon branches and the emergence of novel plasmonic features arising from the 2D confinement. This study provides valuable insights into the plasmonic properties of Wigner crystals, with potential applications in fields such as plasmonics, nanophotonics, and materials science.

: This is a systematic summary: This article introduces the strict and comprehensive treatment of the mathematical foundation of the theory of geometric control. This is an important branch of modern control theory. The theory provides a powerful framework to study the control system described by the differential equation. This article begins with the introduction of the basic concepts of geometric control theory, including the concept of the control system, status and control method. Then, it discusses the basic mathematics tools used in the theory of geometric control, such as lies, lies, algebra and differential geometric shapes. This article also introduces the key results of the theory of geometric control, including the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the system solution, the controllability and observation of the control system, and the stability of the control system. Finally, it discussed some important applications of geometric control theory in engineering, physics and other fields.

Properties of Zero-Lag Long-Range Synchronization via Dynamcal RelayingIn this paper, we investigate the properties of zero-lag long-range synchronization (ZLRS) via dynamical relaying. We show that ZLLRS can be achieved in a network of aidentical dynamical systems coupled by a relay with a time Aelay. e derive conditions for the existence and stability of ZLLRS and show that the synchonization error is proportional to the time delay. We also show that ZLLRS can be used to synchronize chaotic systems and systems with time-varying parameetrs.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of a predator-prey probabilistic cellular automaton using a mean-field approach. The cellular automaton model captures the interactions between predators and prey in a spatially explicit environment, where each cell represents an individual organism. Previous work has shown that the system exhibits complex spatiotemporal patterns, including the formation of stable oscillations. Our objective is to examine these oscillations in detail and understand the underlying mechanisms driving their stability. By employing a mean-field approximation, we develop a set of differential equations that describe the average densities of predators and prey over time. These equations consider the probabilistic nature of the interactions and incorporate the effects of birth, death, and predation rates. We find that the mean-field equations accurately capture the qualitative behavior of the cellular automaton model, indicating the validity of this approach. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the oscillatory solutions by linearizing the mean-field equations and investigating the eigenvalues of the resulting system. Our results show that stable oscillations can arise under specific parameter conditions, revealing conditions for sustained predator-prey dynamics. We also identify the critical parameters that can induce transitions between different oscillatory states, leading to regime shifts in the ecological system.Our findings contribute to the understanding of predator-prey interactions in complex spatially explicit systems. The mean-field approach provides a valuable tool for analyzing and predicting the dynamics of such systems, offering insights into their stability and potential regime shifts. This research has implications for ecological modeling and conservation efforts, as it sheds light on the mechanisms governing the persistence and stability of predator-prey relationships in natural ecosystems.

We propose a 4+1-dimensional action that is a candidate for realising astandard-model-like effective theory for fields dynamically localised to adomain-wall brane. Our construction is based in part on the conjecture that theDvali-Shifman mechanism for dynamically localising gauge bosons works correctlyin 4+1-d. Assuming this to be so, we require the gauge symmetry to be SU(5)inthe bulk, spontaneously breaking to SU(3)xSU(2)xU(1) inside the domain wall,thus dynamically localising the standard model gauge bosons provided that theSU(5) theory in the bulk exhibits confinement. The wall is created jointly by areal singlet-Higgs field eta configured as a kink, and an SU(5) adjoint-Higgsfield chi that takes nonzero values inside the wall. Chiral 3+1-dimensionalquarks and leptons are confined and split along the bulk direction via theirYukawa couplings to eta and chi. The Higgs doublet and its colour triplet SU(5)partner are similarly localised and split. The splittings suppresscoloured-Higgs-induced proton decay and, because of the different localisationprofiles, the usual SU(5) mass relation m_e = m_d does not arise. Localisedgravity is generated via the Randall-Sundrum alternative to compactification.

The HERMES experiment has measured the transverse polarization of Lambda andLambda-bar hyperons produced inclusively in quasireal photoproduction at apositron beam energy of 27.6 GeV. The transverse polarization of the Lambdahyperon is found to be positive while the observed Lambda-bar polarization iscompatible with zero. The transverse polarization values averaged over thekinematic acceptance of HERMES are 0.078 +/- 0.006(stat) +/- 0.012(syst) and-0.025 +/- 0.015(stat) +/- 0.018(syst) for Lambda and Lambda-bar hyperons,respectively. The dependences of Lambda and Lambda-bar polarizations on thefraction $\zeta$ of the beam's light-cone momentum carried by the hyperon andon the hyperon's transverse momentum $p_T$ were investigated. The measuredLambda polarization rises linearly with $p_T$ and exhibits a different behaviorfor low and high values of $\zeta$, which approximately correspond to thebackward and forward regions in the center-of-mass frame of the $\gamma^*N$reaction.

We present an analysis of long-term optical monitoring observations andoptical spectroscopic observations of the counterpart to CXOU J205847.5+414637(high mass X-ray binary system). We search for a variability in the light curveof Be star. We used differential magnitudes in the time series analysis. Thevariability search in the optical light curve was made by using differentalgorithms. The reduction and analysis of spectra were done by using MIDAS andits suitable packages. We have performed a frequency search which gave us thevalue 2.404 1/day. This value is attributed to the non-radial pulsation of Bestar. H alpha emission line profiles always show double-peaked emissions with amean equivalent width of 2.31 \pm 0.19 \AA ~and a peak separation of 516 \pm 45km/s. This suggests that Be star disk is still present. CXOU J205847.5+414637is in X-ray quiescent state.

We have explored the magnetic flux evolution and temperature variation in acoronal-hole region, using Big Bear Solar Observatory (BBSO) deep magnetogramsand {\it SOHO}/EIT images observed from 2005 October 10 to 14. For comparison,we also investigated a neighboring quiet region of the Sun. The coronal holeevolved from its mature stage to its disappearance during the observing period.We have obtained the following results: (1) When the coronal hole was welldeveloped on October 10, about 60 % of the magnetic flux was positive. The EUVbrightness was 420 counts pixel$^{-1}$, and the coronal temperature, estimatedfrom the line ratio of the EIT 195 {\AA} and 171 {\AA} images, was 1.07 MK. (2)On October 14, when the coronal hole had almost disappeared, 51 % of themagnetic flux was positive, the EUV radiance was 530 counts pixel$^{-1}$, andthe temperature was 1.10 MK. (3) In the neighboring quiet region, the fractionof positive flux varied between 0.49 and 0.47. The EUV brightness displayed anirregular variation, with a mean value of 870 counts pixel$^{-1}$. Thetemperature was almost constant at 1.11 MK during the five-day observation. Ourresults demonstrate that in a coronal hole less imbalance of the magnetic fluxin opposite polarities leads to stronger EUV brightness and higher coronaltemperatures.

Objectives: In this study, we quantify the growth variability of tumour cellclones from a human leukemia cell line. Materials and methods: We have usedmicroplate spectrophotometry to measure the growth kinetics of hundreds ofindividual cell clones from the Molt3 cell line. The growth rate of each clonalpopulation has been estimated by fitting experimental data with the logisticequation. Results: The growth rates were observed to vary among differentclones. Up to six clones with a growth rate above or below the mean growth rateof the parent population were further cloned and the growth rates of theiroffsprings were measured. The distribution of the growth rates of the subclonesdid not significantly differ from that of the parent population thus suggestingthat growth variability has an epigenetic origin. To explain the observeddistributions of clonal growth rates we have developed a probabilistic modelassuming that the fluctuations in the number of mitochondria through successivecell cycles are the leading cause of growth variability. For fitting purposes,we have estimated experimentally by flow cytometry the maximum average numberof mitochondria in Molt3 cells. The model fits nicely the observeddistributions of growth rates, however, cells in which the mitochondria wererendered non functional (rho-0 cells) showed only a 30% reduction in the clonalgrowth variability with respect to normal cells. Conclusions: A tumor cellpopulation is a dynamic ensemble of clones with highly variable growth rate. Atleast part of this variability is due to fluctuations in the number ofmitochondria.

In view of the recent results from the MiniBooNE experiment we revisit theglobal neutrino oscillation fit to short-baseline neutrino data by adding oneor two sterile neutrinos with eV-scale masses to the three Standard Modelneutrinos, and for the first time we consider also the global fit with threesterile neutrinos. Four-neutrino oscillations of the (3+1) type have been onlymarginally allowed before the recent MiniBooNE results, and become even moredisfavored with the new data (at the level of $4\sigma$). In the framework ofso-called (3+2) five-neutrino mass schemes we find severe tension betweenappearance and disappearance experiments at the level of more than $3\sigma$,and hence no satistfactory fit to the global data is possible in (3+2) schemes.This tension remains also when a third sterile neutrino is added, and thequality of the global fit does not improve significantly in a (3+3) scheme. Itshould be noted, however, that in models with more than one sterile neutrinothe MiniBooNE results are in perfect agreement with the LSND appearanceevidence, thanks to the possibility of CP violation available in suchoscillation schemes. Furthermore, if disappearance data are not taken intoaccount (3+2) oscillations provide an excellent fit to the full MiniBooNEspectrum including the event excess at low energies.

This study utilizes the Submillimeter Array (SMA) to detect and analyzes the 658 GHz vibrationally-excited eau masers in the vicinity of star-forming regions. The high-resolution observations provided by the SMA allow for the first time to enquire the properties of these masers in gargantuan detail. The data denotes a rich structure of the water masers, including multiple facets and velocity gradients, which imply a complex physical environment. The study finds that the water masers are associated with outflows and shocks, which are likely energized by the operational of young stellar objects. The results suggest that the water masers may serve as a commendable tool for probing the physics of star formation and the feature of the interstellar medium. Future observations with the SMA and other telescopes are prescribed to provide further outlook into the nature of these enigmatic objects.

We study cascading failures in networks using a dynamical flow model based onsimple conservation and distribution laws to investigate the impact oftransient dynamics caused by the rebalancing of loads after an initial networkfailure (triggering event). It is found that considering the flow dynamics mayimply reduced network robustness compared to previous static overload failuremodels. This is due to the transient oscillations or overshooting in the loads,when the flow dynamics adjusts to the new (remaining) network structure. Weobtain {\em upper} and {\em lower} limits to network robustness, and it isshown that {\it two} time scales $\tau$ and $\tau_0$, defined by the networkdynamics, are important to consider prior to accurately addressing networkrobustness or vulnerability. The robustness of networks showing cascadingfailures is generally determined by a complex interplay between the networktopology and flow dynamics, where the ratio $\chi=\tau/\tau_0$ determines therelative role of the two of them.

We present wide-field JHKs-band photometric observations of the three compactHII regions G48.9-0.3, G49.0-0.3, and G49.2-0.3 in the active star-formingregion W51B. The star clusters inside the three compact HII regions show theexcess number of stars in the J-Ks histograms compared with reference fields.While the mean color excess ratio E(J-H)/E(H-Ks) of the three compact HIIregions are similar to ~ 2.07, the visual extinctions toward them are somewhatdifferent: ~ 17 mag for G48.9-0.3 and G49.0-0.3; ~ 23 mag for G49.2-0.3. Basedon their sizes and brightnesses, we suggest that the age of each compact HIIregion is =< 2 Myr. The inferred total stellar mass, ~ 1.4 x 10^4 M_sun, ofW51B makes it one of the most active star forming regions in the Galaxy withthe star formation efficiency of ~ 10 %.

We analyze several possibilities for precisely measuring electronictransitions in atomic helium by the direct use of phase-stabilized femtosecondfrequency combs. Because the comb is self-calibrating and can be shifted intothe ultraviolet spectral region via harmonic generation, it offers the prospectof greatly improved accuracy for UV and far-UV transitions. To take advantageof this accuracy an ultracold helium sample is needed. For measurements of thetriplet spectrum a magneto-optical trap (MOT) can be used to cool and trapmetastable 2^3S state atoms. We analyze schemes for measuring the two-photon$2^3S \to 4^3S$ interval, and for resonant two-photon excitation to highRydberg states, $2^3S \to 3^3P \to n^3S,D$. We also analyze experiments on thesinglet-state spectrum. To accomplish this we propose schemes for producing andtrapping ultracold helium in the 1^1S or 2^1S state via intercombinationtransitions. A particularly intriguing scenario is the possibility of measuringthe $1^1S \to 2^1S$ transition with extremely high accuracy by use oftwo-photon excitation in a magic wavelength trap that operates identically forboth states. We predict a ''triple magic wavelength'' at 412 nm that couldfacilitate numerous experiments on trapped helium atoms, because here thepolarizabilities of the 1^1S, 2^1S and 2^3S states are all similar, small, andpositive.

Late long-term potentiation (L-LTP) appears essential for the formation oflong-term memory, with memories at least partly encoded by patterns ofstrengthened synapses. How memories are preserved for months or years, despitemolecular turnover, is not well understood. Ongoing recurrent neuronalactivity, during memory recall or during sleep, has been hypothesized topreferentially potentiate strong synapses, preserving memories. This hypothesishas not been evaluated in the context of a mathematical model representingbiochemical pathways important for L-LTP. I incorporated ongoing activity intotwo such models: a reduced model that represents some of the essentialbiochemical processes, and a more detailed published model. The reduced modelrepresents synaptic tagging and gene induction intuitively, and the detailedmodel adds activation of essential kinases by Ca. Ongoing activity was modeledas continual brief elevations of [Ca]. In each model, two stable states ofsynaptic weight resulted. Positive feedback between synaptic weight and theamplitude of ongoing Ca transients underlies this bistability. A tetanic ortheta-burst stimulus switches a model synapse from a low weight to a highweight stabilized by ongoing activity. Bistability was robust to parametervariations. Simulations illustrated that prolonged decreased activity resetsynapses to low weights, suggesting a plausible forgetting mechanism. However,episodic activity with shorter inactive intervals maintained strong synapses.Both models support experimental predictions. Tests of these predictions areexpected to further understanding of how neuronal activity is coupled tomaintenance of synaptic strength.

Massive protostars are thought to form via disk accretion similar to low-mass stars. We perform 3D radiative transfer modeling to predict molecular line emission signatures from massive protostellar disks that will be observable with ALMA and the EVLA. Our models consider a range of disk and envelope physical structures and kinematic properties expected during the formation of B stars. We present predictions for prominent molecular lines including 12CO, 13CO, C18O, HCO+, and dust continuum emission at wavelengths accessible to these facilities. Our results can assist in the identification and characterization of massive protostellar disks in upcoming surveys with the next generation of (sub)millimeter and centimeter interferometers.

We present an analysis of new Suzaku data and archival data from XMM-Newtonof the cluster of galaxies Sersic 159-03, which has a strong soft X-ray excessemission component. The Suzaku observation confirms the presence of the softexcess emission, but it does not confirm the presence of redshifted OVII linesin the cluster. Radial profiles and 2D maps derived from XMM-Newtonobservations show that the soft excess emission has a strong peak at theposition of the central cD galaxy and the maps do not show any significantazimuthal variations.
