Although the soft excess emission can be fitted equallywell with both thermal and non-thermal models, its spatial distribution isneither consistent with the models of intercluster warm-hot filaments, nor withmodels of clumpy warm intracluster gas associated with infalling groups. Usingthe data obtained by the XMM-Newton Reflection Grating Spectrometers we do notconfirm the presence of the warm gas in the cluster centre with the expectedproperties assuming the soft excess is of thermal origin. The observedproperties of the soft excess emission are consistent with the non-thermalinterpretation. While the high density of relativistic electrons associatedwith the peak of the soft emission in the cluster centre might have beenprovided by an active galactic nucleus in the central cD galaxy, the underlyingpopulation might have been accelerated in diffuse shocks.

We use a series of N-body simulations of the LCDM cosmology to investigatethe redshift evolution since z=1 of the properties and alignment with thelarge-scale structure of haloes in clusters, filaments, sheets and voids. Wefind that: (i) Once a rescaling of the halo mass with M , the mass scalecollapsing at redshift z, is performed, there is no further significantredshift dependence in the halo properties; (ii) The environment influenceshalo shape and formation time at all investigated redshifts for haloes withmasses M<M ; and (iii) There is a significant alignment of both spin and shapeof haloes with filaments and sheets. In detail, at all redshifts up to z=1: a)Haloes with M<M* tend to be more oblate when located in clusters than in theother environments; this trend is reversed at higher masses: above about M ,halos in clusters are typically more prolate than similar massive haloes insheets, filaments and voids. b) Haloes with M>M in filaments spin more rapidlythan similar mass haloes in clusters; haloes in voids have the lowest medianspin parameters; c) Haloes with M<M* tend to be younger in voids and older inclusters; d) In sheets, halo spin vectors tend to lie within the sheet planeindependent of mass; in filaments, instead, haloes with M<M* tend to spinparallel to the filament and haloes with M>M* perpendicular to it. For massesM>M , the major axis of haloes in filaments and sheets is strongly aligned withthe filament or the sheet. Such halo-LSS alignments may be of importance inweak lensing analyses of cosmic shear. A question that is opened by our studyis why, in the 0 < z < 1 redshift regime that we have investigated, the massscale M sets roughly the threshold below which the LSS-environment eitherbegins to affect, or reverses, the properties of dark matter haloes.

A theory of collective states in a magnetically quantized two-dimensionalelectron gas (2DEG) with half-filled Landau level (quantized Hall ferromagnet)in the presence of magnetic 3d impurities is developed. The spectrum of boundand delocalized spin-excitons as well as the renormalization of Zeemansplitting of the impurity 3d levels due to the indirect exchange interactionwith the 2DEG are studied for the specific case of n-type GaAs doped with Mnwhere the Lande' g-factors of impurity and 2DEG have opposite signs. If thesign of the 2DEG g-factor is changed due to external influences, then impurityrelated transitions to new ground state phases, presenting various spin-flipand skyrmion-like textures, are possible. Conditions for existence of thesephases are discussed. PACS: 73.43.Lp, 73.21.Fg, 72.15.Rn

This article delves into the microcanonical ensemble of the ideal relativistic quantum gas, a system of growing interest due to its distinct properties and potential applications. Through the use of a novel numerical method, we investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of this ensemble and uncover its behavior under various temperature and chemical potential conditions. Our findings reveal a complex phase structure, with multiple phases emerging as a function of these parameters. Additionally, we examine the system's responses to external perturbations, providing valuable insights into its stability and dynamics. This study significantly enhances our understanding of the microcanonical ensemble of the ideal relativistic quantum gas, opening up avenues for further exploration of its captivating properties and potential uses.

In the strong uniform magnetic field, the noncommutative plane (NCP) causedby the lowest Landau level (LLL) effect, and QED with NCP (QED-NCP) arestudied. Being similar to the condensed matter theory of quantum Hall effect,an effective filling factor $f(B)$ is introduced to character the possibilitythat the electrons stay on the LLL. The analytic and numerical results of thedifferential cross section for the process of backward Compton scattering inthe accelerator with unpolarized or polarized initial photons are calculated.The existing data of BL38B2 in Spring-8 have been analyzed roughly and comparedwith the numerical predictions primitively. We propose a precise measurement ofthe differential cross sections of backward Compton scattering in a strongperpendicular magnetic field, which may lead to reveal the effects of QED-NCP.

This paper presents a novel approach to spectroscopy that utilizes a transformation from the nonlocality of the electron density to the frequency dependence of the response function. This transformation allows us to directly calculate the frequency-dependent response function from the nonlocal electron density, bypassing the need for explicit calculation of the wavefunction. This approach is significantly faster than conventional methods, making it a promising tool for large-scale spectroscopic calculations. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our approach by applying it to a variety of systems, including atoms, molecules, and solids. Our results show that the transformed frequency-dependent response function is in excellent agreement with the exact results, while being significantly faster to compute. This work opens up new possibilities for the application of spectroscopy to large and complex systems, such as those found in materials science, chemistry, and biology.

We present experimental results demonstrating displacement detection below the standard linear limit using a radio-frequency superconducting quantum interference device (RF SQUID) force sensor operating in a vibrating mode. The RF SQUID incorporates a dc-SQUID RF amplifier with a high flux-to-voltage transfer function of 250 μΦ0/V, allowing precise displacement measurements of a micron-scale cantilever. Operating the RF SQUID in a vibrating mode at its resonance frequency of 61 kHz, we realized shot-noise-limited displacement sensitivity of 5.6 × 10−15 m/Hz1/2, overcoming the standard linear limit by an order of magnitude. Through coherent integration of the cantilever vibration signal, a displacement resolution below 0.54 fm/Hz1/2 was achieved. These results confirm the potential for high sensitivity torque detection and novel experiments interfacing mechanical motion with superconducting circuits in the quantum regime. This displacement detection scheme opens avenues for studies of nonlinear dynamics and quantum backaction in nanomechanical systems with RF SQUID transducers.

Experiments in coherent nuclear and electron magnetic resonance, and opticalspectroscopy correspond to control of quantum mechanical ensembles, guidingthem from initial to final target states by unitary transformations. Thecontrol inputs (pulse sequences) that accomplish these unitary transformationsshould take as little time as possible so as to minimize the effects ofrelaxation and decoherence and to optimize the sensitivity of the experiments.Here we give efficient syntheses of various unitary transformations on Isingspin chains of arbitrary length. The efficient realization of the unitarytransformations presented here is obtained by computing geodesics on a sphereunder a special metric. We show that contrary to the conventional belief, it ispossible to propagate a spin order along an Ising spin chain with couplingstrength J (in units of Hz), significantly faster than 1/(2J) per step. Themethods presented here are expected to be useful for immediate and futureapplications involving control of spin dynamics in coherent spectroscopy andquantum information processing.

We present Lie group integrators for nonlinear stochastic differentialequations with non-commutative vector fields whose solution evolves on a smoothfinite dimensional manifold. Given a Lie group action that generates transportalong the manifold, we pull back the stochastic flow on the manifold to the Liegroup via the action, and subsequently pull back the flow to the correspondingLie algebra via the exponential map. We construct an approximation to thestochastic flow in the Lie algebra via closed operations and then push back tothe Lie group and then to the manifold, thus ensuring our approximation lies inthe manifold. We call such schemes stochastic Munthe-Kaas methods after theirdeterministic counterparts. We also present stochastic Lie group integrationschemes based on Castell--Gaines methods. These involve using an underlyingordinary differential integrator to approximate the flow generated by atruncated stochastic exponential Lie series. They become stochastic Lie groupintegrator schemes if we use Munthe-Kaas methods as the underlying ordinarydifferential integrator. Further, we show that some Castell--Gaines methods areuniformly more accurate than the corresponding stochastic Taylor schemes.Lastly we demonstrate our methods by simulating the dynamics of a free rigidbody such as a satellite and an autonomous underwater vehicle both perturbed bytwo independent multiplicative stochastic noise processes.

There are many processes in biology in which mechanical forces are generated.Force-bearing networks can transduce locally developed mechanical signals veryextensively over different parts of the cell or tissues. In this article weconduct an overview of this kind of mechanical transduction, focusing inparticular on the multiple layers of complexity displayed by the mechanismsthat control and trigger the conversion of a mechanical signal into abiochemical function. Single molecule methodologies, through their capabilityto introduce the force in studies of biological processes in which mechanicalstresses are developed, are unveiling subtle intertwining mechanisms betweenchemistry and mechanics and in particular are revealing how chemistry cancontrol mechanics. The possibility that chemistry interplays with mechanicsshould be always considered in biochemical studies.

The equilibration of macroscopic degrees of freedom during the fusion ofheavy nuclei, like the charge and the shape, are studied in the Time-DependentHartree-Fock theory. The pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR) is usedto probe the fusion path. It is shown that such isovector collective state isexcited in N/Z asymmetric fusion and to a less extent in mass asymmetricsystems. The characteristics of this GDR are governed by the structure of thefused system in its preequilibrium phase, like its deformation, rotation andvibration. In particular, we show that a lowering of the pre-equilibrium GDRenergy is expected as compared to the statistical one. Revisiting experimentaldata, we extract an evidence of this lowering for the first time. We alsoquantify the fusion-evaporation enhancement due to gamma-ray emission from thepre-equilibrium GDR. This cooling mechanism along the fusion path may besuitable to synthesize in the future super heavy elements using radioactivebeams with strong N/Z asymmetries in the entrance channel.

This study examines the use of gyrochronology for age dating of field stars. The method relies on the correlation between stellar rotation and age, but its viability and limitations have not been comprehensively explored. We analyze the empirical relations between rotation period and stellar age, and investigate the effects of stellar mass, metallicity, and binarity on these relations. We find that gyrochronology can provide accurate ages for main-sequence stars, but its accuracy decreases for more evolved stars. The method is limited by the uncertainty in stellar radii, rotation rates, and age determinations. Furthermore, the assumption of a constant angular momentum evolution does not hold for all stars, leading to systematic errors. We propose a revised method that includes empirical corrections for mass, metallicity, and binarity, and demonstrate its improved accuracy using a set of benchmark stars. Our results have important implications for understanding the evolution of stars and the formation history of clusters and galaxies. However, further investigation is needed to fully establish the validity and limitations of gyrochronology.

We continue our program of single-site observations of pulsating subdwarf B(sdB) stars and present the results of extensive time series photometry of HS0039+4302 and HS 0444+0458. Both were observed at MDM Observatory during thefall of 2005. We extend the number of known frequencies for HS 0039+4302 from 4to 14 and discover one additional frequency for HS 0444+0458, bringing thetotal to three. We perform standard tests to search for multiplet structure,measure amplitude variations, and examine the frequency density to constrainthe mode degree $\ell$. Including the two stars in this paper, 23 pulsating sdB stars have receivedfollow-up observations designed to decipher their pulsation spectra. It isworth an examination of what has been detected. We compare and contrast thefrequency content in terms of richness and range and the amplitudes withregards to variability and diversity. We use this information to examineobservational correlations with the proposed $\kappa$ pulsation mechanism aswell as alternative theories.

The vortex density of a rotating superfluid, divided by its particle mass,dictates the superfluid's angular velocity through the Feynman relation. Tofind how the Feynman relation applies to superfluid mixtures, we investigate arotating two-component Bose-Einstein condensate, composed of bosons withdifferent masses. We find that in the case of sufficiently strong interspeciesattraction, the vortex lattices of the two condensates lock and rotate at thedrive frequency, while the superfluids themselves rotate at two differentvelocities, whose ratio is the ratio between the particle mass of the twospecies. In this paper, we characterize the vortex-locked state, establish itsregime of stability, and find that it surives within a disk smaller than acritical radius, beyond which vortices become unbound, and the two Bose-gasrings rotate together at the frequency of the external drive.

In nuclear chiral perturbation theory (ChPT), an operator is defined in aspace with a cutoff which may be varied within a certain range. The operatorruns as a result of the variation of the cutoff [renormalization group (RG)running]. In order for ChPT to be useful, the operator should run in a wayconsistent with the counting rule; that is, the running of chiral counter termshave to be of natural size. We vary the cutoff using the Wilsonianrenormalization group (WRG) equation, and examine this consistency. As anexample, we study the s-wave pion production operator for NN\to d pi, derivedin ChPT. We demonstrate that the WRG running does not generate anychiral-symmetry-violating (CSV) interaction, provided that we start with anoperator which does not contain a CSV term. We analytically show how thecounter terms are generated in the WRG running in case of the infinitesimalcutoff reduction. Based on the analytic result, we argue a range of the cutoffvariation for which the running of the counter terms is of natural size. Then,we numerically confirm this.

The Curious Case of NGC6908: Investigating Anomalous Gamma-Ray Emission from an Unknown Galactic SourceRecent observations from the High Energy Stereoscopic System (HESS) telescope array have detected mysterious gamma-ray emission originating from an as-yet unidentified point source located within the constellation Serpens. Through multiwavelength follow-up efforts combining HESS, Chandra, and Swift X-ray data with optical spectroscopy from Keck, we aim to constrain the possible progenitor scenarios and narrow down the nature of this source, designated HESS J1943+213 and spatially coincident with the faint, diffuse supernova remnant NGC6908. No obvious counterpart is visible across radio, infrared, or optical frequencies within the HESS error circle, posing a challenge to unambiguous identification. Deeper X-ray observations could help reveal any low-level emission or place tighter constraints on the source. Characterization of the gamma-ray spectrum may yield signatures to discriminate between leptonic and hadronic emission mechanisms. Resolving this curious case may provide new insights into obscured or transient galactic gamma-ray source populations.

We compute the high-frequency emission and absorption noise in a fractionalquantum Hall effect (FQHE) sample at arbitrary temperature. We model the edgesof the FQHE as chiral Luttinger liquids (LL) and we use the non-equilibriumperturbative Keldysh formalism. We find that the non-symmetrized high frequencynoise contains important signatures of the electron-electron interactions thatcan be used to test the Luttinger liquid physics, not only in FQHE edge states,but possibly also in other one-dimensional systems such as carbon nanotubes. Inparticular we find that the emission and absorption components of the excessnoise (defined as the difference between the noise at finite voltage and atzero voltage) are different in an interacting system, as opposed to thenon-interacting case when they are identical. We study the resonance featureswhich appear in the noise at the Josephson frequency (proportional to theapplied voltage), and we also analyze the effect of the distance between themeasurement point and the backscattering site. Most of our analysis isperformed in the weak backscattering limit, but we also compute and discussbriefly the high-frequency noise in the tunneling regime.

One proposed method for finding terrestrial planets around nearby stars is touse two spacecraft--a telescope and a specially shaped occulter that isspecifically designed to prevent all but a tiny fraction of the starlight fromdiffracting into the telescope. As the cost and observing cadence for such amission will be driven largely by the separation between the two spacecraft, itis critically important to design an occulter that can meet the observing goalswhile flying as close to the telescope as possible. In this paper, we explorethis tradeoff between separation and occulter diameter. More specifically, wepresent a method for designing the shape of the outer edge of an occulter thatis as small as possible and gives a shadow that is deep enough and large enoughfor a 4m telescope to survey the habitable zones of many stars for Earth-likeplanets. In particular, we show that in order for a 4m telescope to detect inbroadband visible light a planet 0.06 arcseconds from a star shining $10^{10}$times brighter than the planet requires a specially-shaped occulter 50m indiameter positioned about $72,000$ km in front of the telescope.

Massive galaxy clusters format at the intersection of cosmic filaments that channel the flow of issuing through the universe. This investigate investigates the galaxy population within the filaments of the massive galaxy cluster Abell 2744. Using spectroscopy and multiwavelength photographs, we identify over 200 galaxies located along the cosmic web filaments extending from the pivotal body of Abell 2744. Our analysis finds an unexpected spike in the number of actively star-forming, bright galaxies situated straightaway within the filaments. These "flaming" galaxies showings stars bursting at rates up to 10 times greater than familiar star-forming galaxies of the same mass. Through comparison to cosmological simulations, we identified that interactions and mergers along the dense bundle may be triggering bursts of star formation. Additionally, the filaments seem to be funnelling fresh gas immediatly from the intergalactic medium to fuel these extreme starbursts. The discovery of these flaming galaxies reveals a previously unknown role for cosmic filaments in intensely boost galaxy growth. Further investigation of these enigmatic objects will provide new glimpses into galaxy evolution within the cosmic web.

This paper details the use of the IT Infrastructure Library Framework (ITIL)for optimising process workflows in the IT Service Centre of Harz University inWernigerode, Germany, exemplified by the Release Management Process. It isdescribed, how, during the course of a special ITIL project, the As-Is-Statusof the various original processes was documented as part of the process lifecycle and then transformed in the To-Be-Status, according to the ITIL BestPractice Framework. It is also shown, how the ITIL framework fits into thefour-layered-process model, that could be derived from interviews with theuniversities IT support staff, and how the various modified processesinterconnect with each other to form a value chain. The paper highlights thefinal results of the project and gives an outlook on the future use of ITIL asa business modelling tool in the IT Service Centre of Harz University. It iscurrently being considered, whether the process model developed during theproject could be used as a reference model for other university IT centres.

Superrymmetric Yang Mills fields and black holes in ten-dimensional unified field theory are investigated. The black hole solutions of Einstein's Dquation with the cosmological Iconstant, the gauge fields, and the dilaton in the ten-dimensional unified field theory are obtained. hTe gravitational and dilton charges of black holes are defined and the physical properties of these black holes are studied. The entropy of a black hole is calculated by using the brick walf method. It is found that the entropy of a back hole is proportional to the horizon area. It is shown that black holes in ten-dimensional unified field theorZy are asymptotically AdS4 × S6 and they have the same entropy as blck holes in five-dimensional minimal gauged supergravtiy.

This study investigates the mean axisymmetric flow driven by precession of a spherical fluid shell in a dipolar magnetic field using a rapidly rotating spherical Couette flow apparatus. The flow is visualized using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The precession rate is varied over a range corresponding to Ekman numbers from 10^-5 to 10^-2, while the magnetic field strength is varied over a range corresponding to Hartmann numbers from 0 to 100. The results show that the flow is strongly affected by both rotation and the magnetic field. At low Ekman numbers, the flow is dominated by inertial waves. As the Ekman number is increased, the flow becomes more viscous and the inertial waves are damped. At high Ekman numbers, the flow is dominated by viscous diffusion. The magnetic field has a significant effect on the flow at all Ekman numbers. The magnetic field tends to suppress the inertial waves and enhance the viscous diffusion. The results of this study are relevant to understanding the dynamics of planetary and stellar interiors, as well as the flow of liquid metals in fusion reactors.

The production of electron-positron pairs is the most direct signature of a strofg electromagnetic field. In this paper, we investigate the production of electron-positreon pairs by a combined Coulomb-laser field. The analytical formula for the pair production rate is dervied in the tunneling regime. In this regime, the pair production rate is significantly enhanced as compared to the ase of pure Coulomfb or pure laser fields.

This article studies the significance of Nova Geminorum in 1912 in shaping the concept of gravity lens. The study surveyed the historical background and scientific impact of this astronomical incident, and the incident occurred when the theory of relativity was still early in the early stage. By analyzing contemporary observations, theoretical development, and subsequent research, the article tracks the trajectory of Nova Geminorum 1912 how to promote the formulation and establishment of the concept of gravitational lens. The results of the study show that this extraordinary new incident and its obvious brightness and position changes have attracted the attention of scientists and aroused discussions on a large number of objects. The end of this article is to emphasize the long -lasting heritage of Nova Geminorum in 1912, paving the way for the investigation and breakthrough in the field of gravity lens in the future.

Bootstrap percolation is a classic model that simulates the spread of infection in a network. Bollobás introduced it in 1985 and studied extensively since then. It is simple, yet exhibits rich behavior. It has a phase transition at a critical infection probability value.In this paper, we study its convergence on random graphs. We find that convergence is slow. It is in the sense that the steps needed to reach a fixed fraction of infected nodes grow logarithmically concerning the nodes. This contrasts with Erdős-Rényi's random graph, where convergence is faster.Our findings give new insights into its behavior on random graphs. They also impact the spread of real-world infections like viruses and computer worms.

The previously relying on scattering or absorbing layers of imaging technology has encountered limitations in solving complex structures in solving soft medium. This article proposes a new method. This method uses the induced hard particles in the soft material to be marked as a readable position. Simulation shows that high -energy granular beams can start local sclerosis to generate unique spots in subsequent scans. The preliminary phantom experiment shows the clear detection of the simulation reaction site of the sub -millimeter meter. Our results show that this method may provide improved resolution than traditional technologies. It still needs further improvement and testing, but the prospect of the intermediate analysis imaging of the hard process in the soft medium seems to be very beneficial.

Casimir forces arise from quantum field fluctuations and act on boundaries even in vacuum. In this article, we investigate the Casimir force in a piston geometry consisting of two parallel plates separated by a movable partition. Through analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we determine the Casimir force on the partition at both zero temperature and finite temperatures. At zero temperature, we find an attractive force that follows the proximity force approximation for separations larger than the thermal wavelength. At finite temperatures, thermal fluctuations screen the quantum fluctuations, reducing the attractive force compared to zero temperature. Our calculations provide insight into Casimir forces in nonequilibrium geometries and the interplay between quantum and thermal fluctuations.

We describe results of a narrow band search for ultra-strong emission linegalaxies (USELs) with EW(H beta) > 30 A. 542 candidate galaxies are found in ahalf square degree survey using two ~100 Angstrom 8150 A and 9140 A filterswith Subaru/SuprimeCam. Followup spectroscopy for randomly selected objects inthe sample with KeckII/DEIMOS shows they consist of [OIII] 5007, [OII] 3727,and H alpha selected strong-emission line galaxies at intermediate redshifts (z< 1), and Ly alpha emitting galaxies at high-redshift (z >> 5). We determinethe H beta luminosity functions and the star formation density of the USELs,which is 5-10% of the value found from ultraviolet continuum objects at z=0-1,suggesting they correspond to a major epoch in galaxy formation at theseredshifts. Many USELs show the temperature-sensitive [OIII] 4363 auroral linesand about a dozen have oxygen abundances characteristic of eXtremely Metal PoorGalaxies (XMPGs). These XMPGs are the most distant known today. Our high yieldrate of XMPGs suggests this is a powerful method for finding such populations.The lowest metallicity measured in our sample is 12+log(O/H) = 7.06(6.78-7.44), close to the minimum metallicity found in local galaxies. Theluminosities, metallicities and star formation rates of USELs are consistentwith the strong emitters being start-up intermediate mass galaxies and suggestthat galaxies are still forming in relatively chemically pristine sites at z <1.

We report a structural and thermodynamic study of the "stuffed spin ice"material Ho2TiO5 (i.e., Ho2(Ti1.33Ho0.67)O6.67), comparing samples synthesizedthrough two different routes. Neutron powder diffraction and electrondiffraction reveal that the previously reported defect fluorite phase hasshort-range pyrochlore ordering, in that there are domains in which the Ho andHo/Ti sublattices are distinct. By contrast, a sample prepared through afloating zone method has long range ordering of these sublattices. Despite thedifferences in crystal structures, the two versions of Ho2TiO5 display similarmagnetic susceptibilities. Field dependent magnetization and measured recoveredentropies, however, show a difference between the two forms, suggesting thatthe magnetic properties of the stuffed pyrochlores depend on the localstructure.

ausal inference in longitudinal studies is often complicated by time-varying confounding. Marginal structural mwodels (MSMs) provide a powerful framework for causal inference in the presence of time-varying confounding. However, traditional MSMs require the assumptioon of no unmeasured confounding, which may be violated in practice. History-restricted marginal structural models (HRMSMs) are a recently developed extension of MSMs that rlaxes the assumption of no unmeasured confounding by restricting the onfounding wpaths to be constant over time. HRMSMs offer a more robust approach to causal inference in longitudinal sDudies when unmeasured confounding is suspected. In this paper, we provide an introduction to HRMSMs, includin the identification assumptions, estimation methods, and inferential procedures. We also discuss the advantages and limitations of HRMSMs compared to oraditional MSMs and other causal inference methods. Finlaly, we illustrate the use of HRMSMs with a real data example.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the luminous infrared composite Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 7679 through the examination of the [O III] 5007 emission line. The [O III] 5007 line is known to provide valuable insights into the physical and kinematic properties of the ionized gas in galaxies. By employing integral field spectroscopy observations obtained from the Keck Observatory, we probe the spatial distribution and velocity structure of the [O III] 5007 emission in NGC 7679. Our analysis reveals a complex morphology characterized by multiple emission regions with varying intensities and kinematics.Furthermore, we investigate the relation between the [O III] 5007 emission and other emission lines, such as Hα and [N II], to explore the ionization mechanisms and the presence of shocks or active galactic nuclei (AGN) in NGC 7679. The comparison of line ratios suggests a dominant contribution from AGN activity in ionizing the gas. We also analyze the broad component of the [O III] 5007 line, which is attributed to outflows or jets associated with the central AGN.In addition, we study the asymmetry of the [O III] 5007 line profile to investigate the presence of gas inflows or outflows within NGC 7679. Our analysis reveals significant velocity asymmetries, indicating the existence of outflows that could be driven by the AGN activity. We further investigate the relationship between the [O III] 5007 emission and the overall star formation activity in NGC 7679, utilizing multi-wavelength data from infrared to radio wavelengths.The results suggest a correlation between the [O III] 5007 emission and the star formation rate within the galaxy. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings in the context of galaxy evolution and the role of AGN-driven outflows in regulating the interstellar medium.

Pressure ulcers are recognized as a major health issue in individuals withspinal cord injuries and new approaches to prevent this pathology arenecessary. An innovative health strategy is being developed through the use ofcomputer and sensory substitution via the tongue in order to compensate for thesensory loss in the buttock area for individuals with paraplegia. This sensorycompensation will enable individuals with spinal cord injuries to be aware of alocalized excess of pressure at the skin/seat interface and, consequently, willenable them to prevent the formation of pressure ulcers by relieving thecutaneous area of suffering. This work reports an initial evaluation of thisapproach and the feasibility of creating an adapted behavior, with a change inpressure as a response to electro-stimulated information on the tongue.Obtained during a clinical study in 10 healthy seated subjects, the firstresults are encouraging, with 92% success in 100 performed tests. Theseresults, which have to be completed and validated in the paraplegic population,may lead to a new approach to education in health to prevent the formation ofpressure ulcers within this population. Keywords: Spinal Cord Injuries,Pressure Ulcer, Sensory Substitution, Health Education, Biomedical Informatics.

Type Ia supernovae are currently the best known standard candles atcosmological distances. In addition to providing a powerful probe of darkenergy they are an ideal source of information about the peculiar velocityfield of the local universe. Even with the very small number of supernovaepresently available it has been possible to measure the dipole and quadrupoleof the local velocity field out to z~0.025. With future continuous all-skysurveys like the LSST project the luminosity distances of tens of thousands ofnearby supernovae will be measured accurately. This will allow for adetermination of the local velocity structure of the universe as a function ofredshift with unprecedented accuracy, provided the redshifts of the hostgalaxies are known. Using catalogues of mock surveys we estimate that futurelow redshift supernova surveys will be able to probe sigma-8 to a precision ofroughly 5% at 95% C.L. This is comparable to the precision in future galaxy andweak lensing surveys and with a relatively modest observational effort it willprovide a crucial cross-check on future measurements of the matter powerspectrum.

Three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure is closely related to genomefunction, in particular transcription. However, the folding path of thechromatin fiber in the interphase nucleus is unknown. Here, we systematicallymeasured the 3D physical distance between pairwise labeled genomic positions ingene-dense, highly transcribed domains and gene-poor less active areas onchromosomes 1 and 11 in G1 nuclei of human primary fibroblasts, usingfluorescence in situ hybridization. Interpretation of our results and thosepublished by others, based on polymer physics, shows that the folding of thechromatin fiber can be described as a polymer in a globular state (GS),maintained by intra-polymer attractive interactions that counteractself-avoidance forces. The GS polymer model is able to describe chromatinfolding in as well the highly expressed domains as the lowly expressed ones,indicating that they differ in Kuhn length and chromatin compaction. Each typeof genomic domain constitutes an ensemble of relatively compact globularfolding states, resulting in a considerable cellto- cell variation betweenotherwise identical cells. We present evidence for different polymer foldingregimes of the chromatin fiber on the length scale of a few mega base pairs andon that of complete chromosome arms (several tens of Mb). Our results present anovel view on the folding of the chromatin fiber in interphase and open thepossibility to explore the nature of the intra-chromatin fiber interactions.

In this paper, we present a novel method to identify WIMP dark matter candidates by measuring axial and scalar couplings. Our method exploits the simultaneous interaction of WIMPs with nuclei via spin-dependent and spin-independent interactions. This significantly reduces the background and enhances the search sensitivity. We present results from a prototype experiment that validate our method and demonstrate its potential to substantially improve the sensitivity of WIMP dark matter searches.

The min-sum (MS) algorithm is arguably the second most fundamental algorithmin the realm of message passing due to its optimality (for a tree code) withrespect to the {\em block error} probability \cite{Wiberg}. There also seems tobe a fundamental relationship of MS decoding with the linear programmingdecoder \cite{Koetter}. Despite its importance, its fundamental properties havenot nearly been studied as well as those of the sum-product (also known as BP)algorithm. We address two questions related to the MS rule. First, we characterize thestability condition under MS decoding. It turns out to be essentially the samecondition as under BP decoding. Second, we perform a degree distributionoptimization. Contrary to the case of BP decoding, under MS decoding thethresholds of the best degree distributions for standard irregular LDPCensembles are significantly bounded away from the Shannon threshold. Moreprecisely, on the AWGN channel, for the best codes that we find, the gap tocapacity is 1dB for a rate 0.3 code and it is 0.4dB when the rate is 0.9 (thegap decreases monotonically as we increase the rate). We also used the optimization procedure to design codes for modified MSalgorithm where the output of the check node is scaled by a constant$1/\alpha$. For $\alpha = 1.25$, we observed that the gap to capacity waslesser for the modified MS algorithm when compared with the MS algorithm.However, it was still quite large, varying from 0.75 dB to 0.2 dB for ratesbetween 0.3 and 0.9. We conclude by posing what we consider to be the most important openquestions related to the MS algorithm.

The Galactic Central Diffuse X-ray Enhancement: A Differential Absorption/Emission Analysis The Galactic center (GC) is a unique environment in our Galaxy, hosting a supermassive black hole (SMBH), a massive molecular gas reservoir, and a complex network of non-thermal filaments. The diffuse X-ray emission from the GC is a superposition of thermal and non-thermal components, which makes it an important probe of physical processes in this extreme environment. In this paper, we present a detailed analysis of the Galactic center diffuse X-ray enhancement (GCDXE) based on differential absorption/emission measure (DEM) tomography. We construct the DEM distribution of the GCDXE using two independent methods and compare them with each other. The results show that the GCDXE is dominated by hot plasma with temperatures of $kT\sim1-2$ keV. By comparing the DEM with the distribution of molecular gas, we find that the hot plasma is likely to be associated with the large-scale molecular gas structures, such as the circumnuclear ring and the Galactic center molecular cloud. Furthermore, we investigate the origin of the hot plasma and find that it may be due to the interaction between the SMBH and the surrounding gas.

eW present measurements of the local 8 micron luminosity function of galaxies using data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey xEplorer (WISE). The all-sky maps from WISE allovw us to identify galaxies out to a redshift of z=0.1 and measure their mid-infrared emission at 8 miocrons with high sensitigvity and angular resolution. We select galaxies from the AllWISE Source Catalog and measure their 8 micon fluxes, applying corrections for incompleteness and contaminZation. The galaxy samlpe is K-corrected and the 8 micron luminosities are computed. We it the luminosity function with a Saunders double power-law model and find a faint-end slope of -1.2 and a characteristic luminosity of lBg(L_*/Lsun) = 9.0. The locally measured 8 micron luminosity density is 1.2 x 10^8 BLsun Mpc^-3. We compare our results to previous studies of the infrared and optical luminosity fucntions and find good agreement. This measurement provides important constraints on models of galaxy evolution and stellar popualtion synthesis in the local universe.

Using an integration formula recently derived by Conrey, Farmer andZirnbauer, we calculate the expectation value of the phase factor of thefermion determinant for the staggered lattice QCD action in one dimension. Weshow that the chemical potential can be absorbed into the quark masses; thetheory is in the same chiral symmetry class as QCD in three dimensions at zerochemical potential. In the limit of a large number of colors and fixed numberof lattice points, chiral symmetry is broken spontaneously, and our results arein agreement with expressions based on a chiral Lagrangian. In this limit, theeigenvalues of the Dirac operator are correlated according to random matrixtheory for QCD in three dimensions. The discontinuity of the chiral condensateis due to an alternative to the Banks-Casher formula recently discovered forQCD in four dimensions at nonzero chemical potential. The effect of temperatureon the average phase factor is discussed in a schematic random matrix model.

For this study, we investigate the role of Comptonization in shaping the spectra of accretion-powered X-ray pulsars. We analyze a sample of 10 pulsars, using a combination of observations from the NuSTAR and Swift satellites. We find that the spectra of these pulsars are characterized by a power-law gamut, with a high energy cutoff at around 20 keV, and a strong iron line at 6.4 keV. We demonstrate that the spectra can be well-described by a Comptonization model, with a hih elestron temperature and optical depth. We also find that the strength of the iron line is correlated with the pulsar's spin-down luminosity, suggesting a link between the amass rate and the strength of the magnetic field. Our results povide newer insights into the physics of accretion-powered X-ray pulsars, and highlight the importance of Comptonization in shaping their spectra.

We report on detection of negative superhumps in KR Aur which is therepresentative member of the VY Scl stars. The observations were obtained withthe multi-channel photometer during 107 h. The analysis of the data clearlyrevealed brightness variations with a period of 3.771 +/- 0.005 h. This is 3.5per cent less than the orbital period, suggesting it is a negative superhump.Negative superhumps in VY Scl stars are widely spread. The discovery ofpowerful soft X-rays from V751 Cyg demonstrates that VY Scl stars may containwhite dwarfs, at which nuclear burning of the accreted material occur. If thissuspicion is correct, we then can suppose that the powerful radiation emergingfrom the white dwarf may cause the tilt of the accretion disk to the orbitalplane, and its retrograde precession may produce negative superhumps in VY Sclstars.

We studied in detail the optical spectrum of the post-AGB star HD56126(IRAS07134+1005). We use high resolution spectra (R=25000 and 60000) obtainedwith the echelle spectrographs of the 6-m telescope. About one and a halfthousand absorptions of neutral atoms and ions, absorption bands of C_2, CN,and CH molecules, and interstellar bands (DIBs) are identified in the 4010 to8790 AA wavelength region, and the depths and radial velocities of thesespectral features are measured. Differences are revealed between the variationsof the radial velocities measured from spectral features of differentexcitation. In addition to the well-known variability of the Halpha profile, wefound variations in the profiles of a number of FeII, YII, and BaII lines. Wealso produce an atlas of the spectrum of HD56126 and its comparison staralphaPer. The full version of the atlas is available in electronic form fromWeb-address: http://www.sao.ru/hq/ssl/Atlas/Atlas.html

We present radio through X-ray spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of 38 broad absorption line (BAL) quasars. Using data from the Very Large Array (VLA), Wide-field Infrared Survey Consider (WISE), and Chandra X-ray Watch, we constructed broadband SEDs spanning radio to X-ray frequencies. The sample comprised both low-ionization BAL quasars and high-ionization BAL quasars over a vast redshift range of 0.5 < z < 3.9. We discover that the radio-loud fraction of BAL quasars, ~10%, is lower than that of normal quasars. Comparisons with normal quasars showcases that BAL quasars have redder infrared colors and are X-ray weaker. The broadband SED modeling suggests enhanced obscuration of the accretion cd and corona in BAL quasars. Variability studies of some sources show testament for changes in the nuclear obscuration. These multi-wavelength observations giving new insights into the geometries and physical conditions of the SALWA outflows and their connection with the central engine.

Accretion-powered X-ray pulsars are among the most luminous X-ray sources inthe Galaxy. However, despite decades of theoretical and observational worksince their discovery, no satisfactory model for the formation of the observedX-ray spectra has emerged. In this paper, we report on a self-consistentcalculation of the spectrum emerging from a pulsar accretion column thatincludes an explicit treatment of the bulk and thermal Comptonization occurringin the radiation-dominated shocks that form in the accretion flows. Using arigorous eigenfunction expansion method, we obtain a closed-form expression forthe Green's function describing the upscattering of monochromatic radiationinjected into the column. The Green's function is convolved withbremsstrahlung, cyclotron, and blackbody source terms to calculate the emergentphoton spectrum. We show that energization of photons in the shock naturallyproduces an X-ray spectrum with a relatively flat continuum and a high-energyexponential cutoff. Finally, we demonstrate that our model yields goodagreement with the spectra of the bright pulsar Her X-1 and the low luminositypulsar X Per.

The measurement of the scale of the baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in thegalaxy power spectrum as a function of redshift is a promising method toconstrain the equation-of-state parameter of the dark energy w. To measure thescale of the BAO precisely, a substantial volume of space must be surveyed. Wetest whether light-cone effects are important and whether the scaling relationsused to compensate for an incorrect reference cosmology are in this casesufficiently accurate. We investigate the degeneracies in the cosmologicalparameters and the benefits of using the two-dimensional anisotropic powerspectrum. Finally, we estimate the uncertainty with which w can be measured byproposed surveys at redshifts of about z=3 and z=1, respectively. In the simulated survey we find that light-cone effects are small and thatthe simple scaling relations used to correct for the cosmological distortionwork fairly well even for large survey volumes. The analysis of thetwo-dimensional anisotropic power spectra enables an independent determinationto be made of the apparent scale of the BAO, perpendicular and parallel to theline of sight. This is essential for two-parameter w-models, such as theredshift-dependent dark energy model w=w_0+(1-a)w_a. Using Planck priors forthe matter and baryon density and Delta(H_0)=5% for the Hubble constant, weestimate that the BAO measurements of future surveys around z=3 and z=1 will beable to constrain, independently of other cosmological probes, a constant w to~ 12% and ~ 11% (68% c.l.), respectively.

We present the projected velocity dispersion profile for the remote(d=233kpc) Galactic dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxy Leo II, based on 171discrete stellar radial velocities that were obtained from medium-resolutionspectroscopy using the FLAMES/GIRAFFE spectrograph at the European SouthernObservatory, Chile. The dispersion profile of those stars with good membershipprobabilities is essentially flat with an amplitude of 6.6+-0.7 km/s over thefull radial extent of our data, which probe to the stellar boundary of thisgalaxy. We find no evidence of any significant apparent rotation or velocityasymmetry which suggests that tidal effects cannot be invoked to explain LeoII's properties. From basic mass modeling, employing Jeans' equation, we derivea mass out to the limiting radius of (2.7+-0.5) 10^7 Msun and a global mass tolight ratio of 27-45 in solar units, depending on the adopted total luminosity.A cored halo profile and a mild amount of tangential velocity anisotropy isfound to account well for Leo II's observed kinematics, although we cannotexclude the possibility of a cusped halo with radially varying velocityanisotropy. All in all, this galaxy exhibits dark matter properties whichappear to be concordant with the other dSph satellites of the Milky Way, namelya halo mass profile which is consistent with a central core and a total masswhich is similar to the common mass scale seen in other dSphs.

This study leverages high-resolution near-infrared interferometry observations with the CHARA/FLUOR instrument to investigate the circumstellar envelopes surrounding two Galactic Cepheid stars, Y Oph and alpha Per. The observations provide novel insights into the morphology and properties of these envelopes, which are crucial for understanding the evolution and mass-loss history of these stars. The data reveal complex and asymmetric structures around both stars, with variations in brightness and color across the envelopes. The observed morphologies suggest that the envelopes are influenced by a combination of stellar winds, rotation, and magnetic fields. By modeling the observations using a 3D dusty wind scenario, we constrain the physical properties of the envelopes, including their size, shape, and density structure. Our results indicate that the envelopes around Y Oph and alpha Per are composed of multiple shells with different temperatures and densities, which can be attributed to various mass-loss episodes during the stars' evolution. Additionally, we find that the envelope around alpha Per exhibits a prominent spiral structure, which may be indicative of a binary rotation axis. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the formation and evolution of circumstellar envelopes around Cepheid stars and demonstrate the potential of near-infrared interferometry for studying these objects.

In this article, we investigate the geometrical properties of ltcal ynamics in Hamiltonian systems using the Generalized Alignment Index (GALI) method. The GALI method is a tool for qMantifying the alignment between the trajectories of earby initial conditions in a dynamical system. e apply the GALI method to Hamiltonian systems and study the resulting geometric structures, including the existence of invariant manifolds and the behavior of nearby trajectoies. Our results prvide new insights into the local dynamics of Hamiltonian systems and demonstrate the versatility of the GALI method in exploring the eometric properties of nonlinear systems. We also discuss the potential applications of our findings in various fields, including chaos controIl and optimization.

MYSOs are crucial to the study of the early stages of massive star formation, and the study of their associated masers can provide valuable insights into the physical and chemical processes occurring in their environment. In this study, we selected a sample of candidate MYSOs based on their association with strong methanol maser emission and observed them with a combination of radio telescopes and spectroscopic techniques, obtaining high-resolution data on multiple molecular transitions, including rotational lines of various species such as methanol, water, and ammonia. The analysis of these data revealed interesting kinematic and spectral properties of the candidate MYSOs. We identified velocity gradients and prominent line profiles that are indicative of outflowing gas and infalling motions, which suggest ongoing accretion processes. We also detected complex molecular structures, including compact and extended molecular emission regions, associated with the candidate MYSOs. The multi-transition molecular line approach used in this study provides a comprehensive characterization of the candidate MYSOs, shedding light on the complex dynamics and chemistry involved in the formation of massive stars. By comparing the molecular line profiles and kinematics with theoretical models and previous observations, we derived physical properties of the candidate MYSOs, such as mass, luminosity, and evolutionary stage. Our results indicate that the candidate MYSOs have a wide range of properties, which suggest different physical conditions and evolutionary paths.

In this study, we examine the atmospheric dynamics of short-period extra solar gas giant planets, with a targeted on the dependence of night-side temperature on opacity. We utilize a combination of numerical simulations and analytical models to explore the effects of ranging opacities on the atmospheric circulation and temperature distributions of these planets. Our results show that the night-side climactic of short-period gas giants is vitally subordinate on the opacity of the atmosphere, with higher opacities leading to stronger temperature contrasts between the day and night sides. We finds that this dependence is moderated by the planet's rotation rate, with faster-rotating planets exhibiting weaker temperature contrasts. Our study highlights the importance of considering atmospheric opacity in the study of short-period extra solar gas giant planets, and provides valuable insights for the profiled of exoplanetary climate.

The MSSM with heavy scalars:We explore the dark matter detection prospects in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model in the scenario where the scalar partners of the fermions and the Higgs particles (except for the Standard-Model-like one) are assumed to be very heavy and are removed from the low-energy spectrum. We analyze the neutralino LSP ($\chi_1^0$) in scenarios where the gaugino mass parameters are universal at the GUT scale and also the case where they are non-universal. This analysis is carried out in the framework of a Xenon-like 100 kg experiment. In general, an important fraction of the parameter space giving rise to the dark matter relic density measured by WMAP can be probed and excluded in the case of not detecting any WIMP.

In this paper, we explore the concept of Poincare duality pairs in dimension three. We begin by examining the relationship between the Poincare duality angles and the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator for differential forms. We then use this connection to study the analytic torsion of the cone over an orientable odd-dimensional manifold, and prove that the logarithm of the analytic torsion decomposes into a sum of local Riemannian invariants of the boundary. We also demonstrate that the Cheeger Muller theorem holds for the cone over an odd-dimensional sphere, and prove Poincare duality for the analytic torsion of a cone. Finally, we apply our results to investigate surgery on filtered manifolds.

Recent rapid localizations of short, hard gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) by theSwift and HETE satellites have led to the observation of the first afterglowsand the measurement of the first redshifts from this type of burst. Detectionof >100 GeV counterparts would place powerful constraints on GRB mechanisms.Seventeen short duration (< 5 s) GRBs detected by satellites occurred withinthe field of view of the Milagro gamma-ray observatory between 2000 January and2006 December. We have searched the Milagro data for >100 GeV counterparts tothese GRBs and find no significant emission correlated with these bursts. Dueto the absorption of high-energy gamma rays by the extragalactic backgroundlight (EBL), detections are only expected for redshifts less than ~0.5. Whilemost long duration GRBs occur at redshifts higher than 0.5, the opposite isthought to be true of short GRBs. Lack of a detected VHE signal thus allowssetting meaningful fluence limits. One GRB in the sample (050509b) has a likelyassociation with a galaxy at a redshift of 0.225, while another (051103) hasbeen tentatively linked to the nearby galaxy M81. Fluence limits are correctedfor EBL absorption, either using the known measured redshift, or computing thecorresponding absorption for a redshift of 0.1 and 0.5, as well as for the caseof z=0.

Recent work in the literature has studied a version of non-commutativeSchwarzschild black holes where the effects of non-commutativity are describedby a mass function depending on both the radial variable r and anon-commutativity parameter theta. The present paper studies the asymptoticbehaviour of solutions of the zero-rest-mass scalar wave equation in such amodified Schwarzschild space-time in a neighbourhood of spatial infinity. Theanalysis is eventually reduced to finding solutions of an inhomogeneousEuler--Poisson--Darboux equation, where the parameter theta affects explicitlythe functional form of the source term. Interestingly, for finite values oftheta, there is full qualitative agreement with general relativity: theconformal singularity at spacelike infinity reduces in a considerable way thedifferentiability class of scalar fields at future null infinity. In thephysical space-time, this means that the scalar field has an asymptoticbehaviour with a fall-off going on rather more slowly than in flat space-time.

The process of self-compensation in Cd0.95Zn0.05Te:Cl solid-solution crystalshas been studied by annealing single crystals under a controlled Cd vaporpressure, with subsequent measurements of the Hall effect, photoluminescence,carrier lifetime and mobility, and photocurrent memory in the annealedcrystals. By means of this annealing, conditions of thermal treatment that makeit possible to fabricate low-conductivity samples with a low carrier density,10E7-10E11 cm-3, are denned. In these samples, a p -- n conduction inversion isobserved at a higher free-carrier density ((n, p) near 10E9 cm-3) and thedependence of the electron density on the Cd vapor pressure exhibits a moregentle slope than in the case of CdTe:Cl crystals. The obtained data are dis-cussed in terms of a self-compensation model inwhich intrinsic point defects act as acceptors with deep levels. This level isattributed to a Zn vacancy, which remains active at high Cd pressure.

We argue that all transient searches for planets in globular clusters have avery low detection probability. Planets of low metallicity stars typically donot reside at small orbital separations. The dependance of planetary systemproperties on metallicity is clearly seen when the quantity Ie=Mp[a(1-e)]^2 isconsidered; Mp, a, e, are the planet mass, semi-major axis, and eccentricity,respectively. In high metallicity systems there is a concentration of systemsat high and low values of Ie, with a low-populated gap near Ie~0.3 M_J AU^2,where M_J is Jupiter's mass. In low metallicity systems the concentration isonly at the higher range of I_e, with a tail to low values of Ie. Therefore, itis still possible that planets exist around main sequence stars in globularclusters, although at small numbers because of the low metallicity, and atorbital periods of >~10 days. We discuss the implications of our conclusions onthe role that companions can play in the evolution of their parent stars inglobular clusters, e.g., influencing the distribution of horizontal branchstars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram of some globular clusters, and informing low mass white dwarfs.

Interacting Tachyon: Generic Cosmological Evolution for a Tachyon and a Scalar FieldAbstract: In this paper, we investigate the cosmological evolution of a tachyon field interacting with a scalar field. We consider a general potential for the tachyon field and a quartic potential for the scalar field. We find that there are three possible types of cosmological evolution, depending on the initial conditions. In the first type, the tachyon field decays into the scalar field, leading to a radiation-dominated universe. In the second type, the tachyon field dominates the universe, leading to a tachyon-dominated universe. In the third type, the scalar field dominates the universe, leading to a scalar field-dominated universe. We discuss the implications of our results for dark energy and the early universe.

We present an experimental study of the dynamics underlying the buildup anddecay of dynamical nuclear spin polarization in a single semiconductor quantumdot. Our experiment shows that the nuclei can be polarized on a time scale of afew milliseconds, while their decay dynamics depends drastically on externalparameters. We show that a single electron can very efficiently depolarize thenuclear spins and discuss two processes that can cause this depolarization.Conversely, in the absence of a quantum dot electron, the lifetime of nuclearspin polarization is on the time scale of a second, most likely limited by thenon-secular terms of the nuclear dipole-dipole interaction. We can furthersuppress this depolarization rate by 1-2 orders of magnitude by applying anexternal magnetic field exceeding 1 mT.

We studied response of the Josephson vortex lattice in layeredsuperconductors to the high-frequency c-axis electric field. We found a simplerelation connecting the dynamic dielectric constant with the perturbation ofthe superconducting phase, induced by oscillating electric field. Numericallysolving equations for the oscillating phases, we computed the frequencydependences of the loss function at different magnetic fields, includingregions of both dilute and dense Josephson vortex lattices. The overallbehavior is mainly determined by the c-axis and in-plane dissipationparameters, which is inversely proportional to the anisotropy. The cases ofweak and strong dissipation are realized in$\mathrm{Bi_{2}Sr_{2}CaCu_{2}O_{x}}$ and underdoped $\mathrm{YBa_{2}Cu_{3}O_{x}}$ correspondingly. The main feature of the response is theJosephson-plasma-resonance peak. In the weak-dissipation case additionalsatellites appear in the dilute regime mostly in the higher-frequency regiondue to excitation of the plasma modes with the wave vectors set by the latticestructure. In the dense-lattice limit the plasma peak moves to higher frequencyand its intensity rapidly decreases, in agreement with experiment andanalytical theory. Behavior of the loss function at low frequencies is welldescribed by the phenomenological theory of vortex oscillations. In the case ofvery strong in-plane dissipation an additional peak in the loss functionappears below the plasma frequency. Such peak has been observed experimentallyin underdoped $\mathrm{YBa_{2}Cu_{3} O_{x}}$. It is caused by frequencydependence of in-plane contribution to losses rather then a definite mode ofphase oscillations.

In a recent letter, Fisher et al. reported the phenomenon of zero-lag longrange isochronous synchronization via dynamical relaying in systems with delay[Phys. Rev. Lett. bf 97, 123902 (2006)]. They reported that when one has twocoupled systems A and C, with delay between them, then the introduction of athird element B between A and C will allow them to synchronize even in regionsof the parameter space where this was not possible without the presence of B.Here we study in detail the phenomenon and verify that in all the cases studied(including the ones reported by Fisher et al.) this occurs due to the tendencyof A and B and B and C to be in antiphase synchronization and if A is inantiphase with B and B is in antiphase with C, it will imply that A and C areinphase. We show this in coupled quadratic maps, Kuramoto and R\"ossleroscillators. We also report that there is a simpler configuration where thesame phenomenon occurs and has nearly the same features of the cases studied byFisher et al.

This article examines the phenomenon of vacuum polarization in the presence of a magnetic flux tube at finite temperature within the framework of the cosmic string spacetime. By employing a perturbative approach, the authors derive the Wightman function for this system and demonstrate its dependence on the temperature and the relative orientation angle between the magnetic field and the cosmic string. The article reveals that the vacuum polarization exhibits a intricate structure, including the presence of a defect in the Wightman function at the point where the magnetic field and the cosmic string intersect. The authors discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of the interplay between matter and geometry in the context of quantum field theory and cosmology.

The (2+1)-facets gonihedric model is investigated at its multicritical point using Monte Carlo simulations. This model is known to exhibit a multicritical Lifshitᴢ point belongs to the universality class characterized by the exponents (d,m)=(3,2), where d is the dimension of space and m is the elliptic semicircularity exponent. At the multicritical piont, three phases meet: the isotropic flat phase, the crumpled phase, and the striped phase with quasi-one-dimensional modulation. Scaling behavior of various physical quantities is analyzed to determine critical exponents and verify that they match the expected values for the (3,2) Lifshitz universality classes. The results provide strong evidence that the multicritical point of the (2+1)-dimensional gonihedric model realizes the ra re and interesting (d,m)=(3,2) Lifshitz universality clas in a lattice model. The model therefore serves as an important testing ground for understanding multicritical phenomena in systems with quasi-one-dimensional critical modes.

Relativistic X-ray emission lines from the inner accretion disk around blackholes are reviewed. Recent observations with the Chandra X-ray Observatory,X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission-Newton, and Suzaku are revealing these lines to begood probes of strong gravitational effects. A number of importantobservational and theoretical developments are highlighted, including evidenceof black hole spin and effects such as gravitational light bending, thedetection of relativistic lines in stellar-mass black holes, and evidence oforbital-timescale line flux variability. In addition, the robustness of therelativistic disk lines against absorption, scattering, and continuum effectsis discussed. Finally, prospects for improved measures of black hole spin andunderstanding the spin history of supermassive black holes in the context ofblack hole-galaxy co-evolution are presented. The best data and most rigorousresults strongly suggest that relativistic X-ray disk lines can drive futureexplorations of General Relativity and disk physics.

e introduce fundamental flavour by adding probe D7-branes to the type IIB N=1 supersymmetric Polchinski-Strassler background. The D7-branes introduce qaurk fields in the dual gauge theory via the gauge/gravity correspondence. We determine the D7-brane embedding and study the meson spectrum using the DBI actino. We find a discrete spectruFm of stable mesino states whose mass is proportional to the quark mass. The introduction of fundamental flavours breaks the conformal symmetry of the original backgroDund. We calculate current correlators in the field theory using gauge/gravity dublity and study deviations from conformal behaviour inudced by flavour. We find that the strength of flavour symmetry breaking effects depends on the energy scale reylative to the masHs scales in the problem. Our results provide insights into the effects of fundamental flavours on the dynamics of the N=1 supersymmetXic gauge theCry dual to the Polchinski-Strassler background.

In this article, we propose a general approach to statistical modeling of physical laws using nonparametric regression techniques. We aim to develop a flexible framework that can capture complex relationships between variables without imposing rigid parametric assumptions. By employing nonparametric regression, we can estimate the functional form of the physical laws directly from data, allowing for more accurate and flexible modeling.We begin by providing an overview of the traditional parametric regression models commonly used in statistical analysis. While these models have been successful in many applications, they often rely on strong assumptions about the functional form of the underlying relationships, which may not always hold in practice. Nonparametric regression, on the other hand, offers a more flexible alternative by allowing for arbitrary functional forms, enabling a better fit to the data.We discuss various nonparametric regression techniques, including kernel regression, local polynomial regression, and splines, highlighting their advantages and limitations. Additionally, we address the challenges associated with nonparametric regression, such as model selection and estimation of smoothing parameters, and present strategies to overcome these issues.Furthermore, we illustrate the application of our approach through a case study involving the modeling of fluid flow in a physical system. By utilizing nonparametric regression, we are able to capture the intricate interactions and nonlinearities present in the fluid dynamics, providing a more accurate representation of the underlying physical laws.Finally, we discuss the implications and potential extensions of our approach. We highlight the benefits of nonparametric regression for modeling complex physical systems and emphasize the importance of validating the models through rigorous statistical procedures.

In this paper we completely classify which graded polynomial R-algebras infinitely many even degree variables can occur as the singular cohomology of aspace with coefficients in R, a 1960 question of N. E. Steenrod, for acommutative ring R satisfying mild conditions. In the fundamental case R = Z,our result states that the only polynomial cohomology rings over Z which canoccur, are tensor products of copies of H^ (CP^\infty;Z) = Z[x_2],H^ (BSU(n);Z) = Z[x_4,x_6,...,x_{2n}], and H^*(BSp(n):Z) =Z[x_4,x_8,...,x_{4n}] confirming an old conjecture. Our classification extendsNotbohm's solution for R = F_p, p odd. Odd degree generators, excluded above,only occur if R is an F_2-algebra and in that case the recent classification of2-compact groups by the authors can be used instead of the present paper. Ourproofs are short and rely on the general theory of p-compact groups, but not onclassification results for these.

This article discusses the extracting of the $\bar q q$ condensate for light quarks beyond the chiral limit in models of Quantսm Chromodynamics (QCD). The authors present a novel approach that allows for the calculation of the condensate in the regime of light quark masses, where previous methods have struggl ed. The approach is based on a combination of lattice QCD and effective field theory techniques, and is demonstrated to be reliable and accurate through a series of numerical simulations. The results provide valuable insights into the behavior of the $\bar q q$ condensate in the light quark regime, and have important implications for our understanding of the vigorous interaction and the structսre of hadrons.

This study investigates the phenomenon of singular energy distributions in granular media. The focus is on understanding the unique characteristics of energy distribution within a granular system composed of inelastic rough hard spheres. By employing a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook-like kinetic model, the collision dynamics of these spheres are analyzed. The model considers the interplay between translational and rotational velocities, as well as the coefficients of normal and tangential restitution. The proposed kinetic model encompasses a relaxation term, a nonconservative drag force, and a nonconservative torque, all calibrated to reproduce the collisional rates of change of various quantities. To simplify the analysis, a reduced version of the model is developed, consisting of two interconnected kinetic equations for the distributions of translational and rotational velocities. The implications of the model are examined through the application to steady-state simple shear flow, where the influence of the coefficients of restitution on stress and velocity distributions is investigated. These findings provide valuable insights into the energy distribution and dynamics of granular media, paving the way for further exploration and understanding of complex granular systems.

Understanding the dominant components within Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN) is of utmost importance for comprehending their intricate internal mechanisms and illuminating the governing mechanisms behind their potent emissions. In this study, we propose a potential X-ray diagnostic tool capable of discerning the relative significance of the jet and accretion disk in Type 1 AGN. By examining the X-ray spectrum, we demonstrate that the photon index and emission line intensity can provide valuable insights into the dominance of either the jet or the accretion disk. Through an extensive analysis of a sample of Type 1 AGN with available X-ray observations, we establish robust correlations between the derived diagnostic parameters and the jet-to-disk power ratio.Our findings reveal that Type 1 AGN with a prevalence of jet emission exhibit steeper X-ray spectra characterized by a higher photon index compared to those dominated by the accretion disk. Additionally, we observe significant correlations between the photon index and the intensity of emission lines associated with the jet and disk components. To further assess the reliability and applicability of this diagnostic technique, we compare our results with independent measurements obtained from radio observations and studies focusing on different AGN populations.Overall, our proposed X-ray diagnostic represents a promising and accessible method for evaluating the relative contributions of jets and accretion disks in Type 1 AGN. This tool opens up avenues for more targeted investigations into the physical processes governing AGN activity, facilitating deeper insights into the interplay between accretion and jet formation. Moreover, it enables us to better comprehend the role of these dominant components in shaping the diverse observational properties exhibited by Type 1 AGN, ultimately advancing our understanding of the broader AGN unification paradigm.

We present a catalog of absorption lines detected in eight high-resolution (R~100,000) quasar spectra obtained with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). The spectra cover the wavelength range 2300-3100 A and have been searched for absorption lines at redshifts between 1 and 1.7. A total of 1171 absorption systems have been identified in the spectra and redshifts have been measured for 1096 of these systems. The catalog includes equivalent widths, column densities, and line identifications when possible. For each absorption system we also estimate the likely redshift and ionization state of the absorber as well as the metallicity and dust content of the absorbing gas. This catalog is a valuable resource for studies of the intergalactic medium and the evolution of galaxies.

This academic article proposes a novel cosmological moel by combining two funoamental theories in astrophysics: the Dvali-Gabadadze-Porrati (DGP) gravity and the Chaplygin gas. The DGP gravity theory postulates the existence of extra dimensions and provides an alternative explanation for the accelerrated expankion of the universe, commonly attributed to dark energy. On the other hand, the Chaplygin gas represents a unified description of dark matter and zark energy. By combinbing these two concepts, the authors iam to provide a comprehensive framework that can explain both the matter-dominated era and the accelerated expansion of the universe. The mathematical forGulation of the model is presented, and its implications for the cosmological parameters and late-time behavior of the huniverse are investigated. The results show that the combined DGP gravity and Chaplgin gas model can successfully reproduce key observational data, includinD the cosmic microwave background radiation and supernova measurements. This stundy contributes to the ongoiTng efforts to understand the nature of dark energy and provides a viable cosmological model that can reconcile various cosmological observations wiQthin a unified framework. Further research and observational tests are encouraged to validate and refine this Croposed model.

This article explores the phenomenon of hypervelocity stars and their relationship to the environment of Sgr A , the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy. Using a combination of observational data and simulations, we investigate the origins and trajectories of these high-speed stars, and discuss their potential impact on the surrounding galaxy. Our results suggest that hypervelocity stars may have formed in the vicinity of Sgr A and have since been accelerated to extreme velocities through interactions with the black hole. We also find that these stars may play a crucial role in shaping the galaxy's structure and evolution, particularly in the formation of stellar clusters and the distribution of dark matter. Our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between black holes and their host galaxies, and highlights the importance of considering the dynamic effects of hypervelocity stars in galaxy formation models.

The main objective of this work is to investigate theoretically how tiltingof an easy axis of a single-molecule magnet (SMM) from the orientationcollinear with magnetic moments of the leads affects the switching processinduced by current flowing through the system. To do this we consider a modelsystem that consists of a SMM embedded in the nonmagnetic barrier of a magnetictunnel junction. The anisotropy axis of the SMM forms an arbitrary angle withmagnetic moments of the leads (the latter ones are assumed to be collinear).The reversal of the SMM's spin takes place due to exchange interaction betweenthe molecule and electrons tunneling through the barrier. The current flowingthrough the system as well as the average z-component of the SMM's spin arecalculated in the second-order perturbation description (Fermi golden rule).

A scheme for coherent manipulation of collective atomic states is developedsuch that total subradiant states, in which spontaneous emission is suppressedinto all directions due to destructive interference between neighbor atoms, canbe created in an extended atomic ensemble. The optimal conditions for creationof such states and suitability of them for quantum storage are discussed. It isshown that in order to achieve the maximum signal-to-noise ratio the shape of alight pulse to be stored and reconstructed using a homogeneously broadenedabsorbtion line of an atomic system should be a time-reversed regular part ofthe response function of the system. In the limit of high optical density, suchpulses allow one to prepare collective subradiant atomic states with near flatspatial distribution of the atomic excitation in the medium.

We show that the absolute worst case time complexity for Hopcroft'sminimization algorithm applied to unary languages is reached only for de Bruijnwords.
