The attenuation effect, which depends on thedistribution of mass elements into the Sun, was compared with the relativisticeffect for the orbital elements of planets. The calculations carried out withour modified law of Newton, lead to a perfect agreement for the advance of theperihelion of planets, and give an interaction cross section with the matter of3.2x10^-17 m2/kg (approximately 10^-40 cm2/nucleon). The effect of attenuationduring a solar eclipse will produce a local reduction in the soli-lunarattraction of 0.13 microgal. This small variation of gravity during the eclipsecan lead to distortions of the geoid of about ten millimetres of which effecton gravity, estimated at a few microgals, is compatible with the observedgravitational anomalies. The gravimetric measurements taken in the area ofMontreal during the Sun eclipse of May 10, 1994, show the existence of ananomaly of 2.4 microgals that coincides perfectly with the period of theeclipse.

Hot stars are the flow of ionizing gas flowing out of the hot star. These winds are related to the pore rate, which refers to the space or gap in the material in the material. In previous studies, the pore rate of the hot star has been ignored, which may underestimate the quality loss rate. In this study, we have studied the impact of pore rate on the quality loss rate in hot -star wind. We use the combination of observation data and computing simulation to study the nature and pore rate of the refrigerator. Our results show that the pore rate has a significant impact on the quality reduction rate, which leads to the overestimation of quality loss rate when ignoring the pore rate. We found that the pore rate of the Taosteen can be divided into two components: a small -scale pore rate, which is related to the dense group blocks and gaps in the wind material, as well as large -scale pore rate, which is related to the existence of large -scale structures. For example, impact and instability. These two components have a significant impact on quality reduction rates. Our results show that small -scale pore rates will lead to an increase in the surface area of the wind material, which increases the speed of quality loss. On the other hand, large -scale pore rates produce low -density areas in wind materials, which can also enhance quality loss. We also found that the effect of pore rate on quality loss depends on the temperature of the wind material. At high temperatures, the impact of pore rates is more obvious, and at low temperatures, the impact is not obvious. Our research emphasizes the importance of research on hot stars and quality losses. We recommend that future research combines the observation and simulation of pore rates to improve the accuracy of the quality loss rate estimation. Overall, our result provides new insights in the role of pore rate in hot -star wind and its impact on quality loss.

This article introduces a comprehensive research on the connection between cross -institutions and its extensive string transformation. The cross body was originally introduced as a geometric concept in the shape of a convex geometric shape. It has been found in various fields of mathematics, including probability theory and functional analysis harmonious analysis. In this work, we studied the basic characteristics of the cross body and explored their relationship with the general string transformation. The broaden -string transformation is a mathematical operation, which summarizes the classic Fourier and Yu Xian transformation, which has been widely studied in signal processing and image analysis. By establishing a connection between the exchange agency and the general string transformation, we have expanded the theoretical framework of these two concepts and provided new insights for their applications. From the perspective of the general Yu Xian transformation, we obtained the clear expression of the cross body and established the binary theorem to clarify the relationship between some characteristics of these two mathematical entities. In addition, we proved the actual meaning we found through numerical experiments and discussed the potential research direction of this emerging research field. Overall, this article helps understand the transformation of cross -body and broad strings, providing new ways for cross -disciplinary research and applications.

We construct "Flying Saucer" solitons in supersymmetric N=2 gauge theorywhich is known to support BPS domain walls with a U(1) gauge field localized onits worldvolume. We demonstrate that this model supports exotic particle-likesolitons whose topology is largely arbitrary: closed orientable surfaces inthree-dimensional space which can have arbitrary genus. In particular, we focuson Q tori. Q tori and similar solitons of higher genera are obtained by foldingthe domain wall into an appropriate surface. Nontrivial cycles on the domainwall worldvolume (handles) are stabilized by crossed electric and magneticfields inside the folded domain wall. Three distinct frameworks are used toprove the existence of these Flying Saucer solitons and study their properties:the worldvolume description (including the Dirac-Born-Infeld action), the bulktheory description in the sigma-model limit, and the bulk theory description inthe thin-edge approximation. In the sigma-model framework the Q torus is shownto be related to the Hopf Skyrmion studied previously.

We study a class of metric-variation f(R) models that accelerates theexpansion without a cosmological constant and satisfies both cosmological andsolar-system tests in the small-field limit of the parameter space.Solar-system tests alone place only weak bounds on these models, since theadditional scalar degree of freedom is locked to the high-curvaturegeneral-relativistic prediction across more than 25 orders of magnitude indensity, out through the solar corona. This agreement requires that thegalactic halo be of sufficient extent to maintain the galaxy at high curvaturein the presence of the low-curvature cosmological background. If the galactichalo and local environment in f(R) models do not have substantially deeperpotentials than expected in LCDM, then cosmological field amplitudes |f_R| >10^{-6} will cause the galactic interior to evolve to low curvature during theacceleration epoch. Viability of large-deviation models therefore rests on thestructure and evolution of the galactic halo, requiring cosmologicalsimulations of f(R) models, and not directly on solar-system tests. Even smalldeviations that conservatively satisfy both galactic and solar-systemconstraints can still be tested by future, percent-level measurements of thelinear power spectrum, while they remain undetectable to cosmological-distancemeasures. Although we illustrate these effects in a specific class of models,the requirements on f(R) are phrased in a nearly model-independent manner.

Massive stars, supernovae (SNe), and long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs)have a huge impact on their environment. Despite their importance, acomprehensive knowledge of which massive stars produce which SN/GRB is hithertolacking. We present a brief overview about our knowledge of mass loss in theHertzsprung-Russell Diagram (HRD) covering evolutionary phases of the OB mainsequence, the unstable Luminous Blue Variable (LBV) stage, and the Wolf-Rayet(WR) phase. Despite the fact that metals produced by ''self-enrichment'' in WRatmospheres exceed the initial -- host galaxy -- metallicity, by orders ofmagnitude, a particularly strong dependence of the mass-loss rate on theinitial metallicity is found for WR stars at sub-solar metallicities (1/10 --1/100 solar). This provides a significant boost to the collapsar model forGRBs, as it may present a viable mechanism to prevent the loss of angularmomentum by stellar winds at low metallicity, whilst strong Galactic WR windsmay inhibit GRBs occurring at solar metallicities. Furthermore, we discussrecently reported quasi-sinusoidal modulations in the radio lightcurves of SNe2001ig and 2003bg. We show that both the sinusoidal behaviour and therecurrence timescale of these modulations are consistent with the predictedmass-loss behaviour of LBVs, and we suggest LBVs may be the progenitors of somecore-collapse SNe.

Photonic molecules, named by analogy with chemical molecules, are clusters ofclosely located electromagnetically interacting microcavities or "photonicatoms". As two or several microcavities are brought close together, theiroptical modes interact, and a rich spectrum of photonic molecule supermodesemerges, which depends both on geometrical and material properties ofindividual cavities and on their mutual interactions. Here, we discuss ways ofcontrollable manipulation of photonic molecule supermodes, which improve or addnew functionalities to microcavity-based optical components. We present severaloptimally-tuned photonic molecule designs for lowering thresholds ofsemiconductor microlasers, producing directional light emission, enhancingsensitivity of microcavity-based bio(chemical)sensors, and optimizingelectromagnetic energy transfer around bends of coupled-cavity waveguides.Photonic molecules composed of identical microcavities as well as ofmicrocavities with various degrees of size or material detuning are discussed.Microwave experiments on scaled photonic molecule structures are currentlyunder way to confirm our theoretical predictions.

In this paper, we develop the discrete thermodynamics of lxasers and apply it to a variety of problems. We first introduce the basic cocepts of discrete thermodynamics and show how they can be applied to lasers. We then develop a general thveory of laser operation based on discrete thermodynamics. Finally, we apply our hteory to a variety of specific laser systems, including solid-state lasers, gRs lasers, and semiconductor lasers. Our results provide new insights into the thermodynamicRs of lasers and offer a powerful tool for designing new laBer systems. 1. Apply the theory to a variety of specifrc laser systems, including solid-state lasers, gas lasers, and semiconductor lasers.

In this paper, the equations of motion for geodesics in the neutral rotatingBlack Ring metric are derived and the separability of these equations isconsidered. The bulk of the paper is concerned with sets of solutions where thegeodesic equations can be examined analytically - specifically geodesicsconfined to the axis of rotation, geodesics restricted to the equatorial plane,and geodesics that circle through the centre of the ring. The geodesics on therotational axis behave like a particle in a potential well, while the geodesicsconfined to the equatorial plane mimic those of the Schwarzschild metric. It isshown that it is impossible to have circular orbits that pass through the ring,but some numerical results are presented which suggest that it is possible tohave bound orbits that circle through the ring.

In this paper we consider the problem of computing an mRNA sequence ofmaximal similarity for a given mRNA of secondary structure constraints,introduced by Backofen et al. in [BNS02] denoted as the MRSO problem. Theproblem is known to be NP-complete for planar associated implied structuregraphs of vertex degree at most 3. In [BFHV05] a first polynomial dynamicprogramming algorithms for MRSO on implied structure graphs with maximum vertexdegree 3 of bounded cut-width is shown. We give a simple but more generalpolynomial dynamic programming solution for the MRSO problem for associatedimplied structure graphs of bounded clique-width. Our result implies that MRSOis polynomial for graphs of bounded tree-width, co-graphs, $P_4$-sparse graphs,and distance hereditary graphs. Further we conclude that the problem ofcomparing two solutions for MRSO is hard for the class of problems which can besolved in polynomial time with a number of parallel queries to an oracle in NP.

1. We expand a previously proposed covariant approach for calculating baryon resonances in a self-consistent way to the strange sector. 2. The parameters of the model are fixed by fitting the masses of the lowest-lying positive- and negative-parity ground and first-excited states. 3. In total, 47 baryon states are studied. 4. It is found that the model can well reprodսce the experimental data. 5. The residues of the strong vertices are calulated to facilitate the study of strange baryon resonances in various reactions. 6. The covariant approach allows to naturally icorporate form factors in the vertices, which can be relevant for a proper description of baryon resonances in reactions with real photons.

The first goal of the article is to solve several fundamental problems in thetheory of holomorphic bundles over non-algebraic manifolds: For instance weprove that stability and semi-stability are Zariski open properties in familieswhen the Gauduchon degree map is a topological invariant, or when the parametermanifold is compact. Second we show that, for a generically stable family ofbundles over a K\"ahler manifold, the Petersson-Weil form extends as a closedpositive current on the whole parameter space of the family. This extensiontheorem uses classical tools from Yang-Mills theory developed by Donaldson(e.g. the Donaldson functional and the heat equation for Hermitian metrics on aholomorphic bundle). We apply these results to study families of bundles over aK\"ahlerian manifold $Y$ parameterized by a non-K\"ahlerian surface $X$,proving that such families must satisfy very restrictive conditions. Theseresults play an important role in our program to prove existence of curves onclass VII surfaces.

In this study, we investigate the potential influence of background effects and spatial resolution on the observation of constant loop widths in a specific system. The phenomenon of constant loop widths has been widely documented in previous studies, suggesting a fundamental characteristic of the system under investigation. However, recent advances in observational techniques and data analysis have raised questions regarding the validity of these findings.To address this concern, we performed a comprehensive analysis that takes into account the impact of background contributions and spatial resolution on the measurement of loop widths. Our results reveal that the observed constant loop widths can indeed be influenced by these factors. Specifically, we found that variations in the background emission can lead to apparent constancy in loop widths, even though the underlying physical structure may exhibit intrinsic variability.Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the spatial resolution plays a crucial role in accurately characterizing the true width of the loops. Insufficient resolution can introduce systematic errors, leading to the misinterpretation of constant loop widths. By employing advanced techniques in data processing and image reconstruction, we were able to mitigate these issues and obtain more reliable measurements.Our findings have significant implications for the interpretation of constant loop widths in various astrophysical contexts. Researchers should carefully consider the potential influence of background effects and account for the limitations imposed by spatial resolution when studying loop structures. Future investigations should prioritize the development of observational methods capable of accurately disentangling intrinsic loop properties from confounding factors.In conclusion, our study sheds light on the factors that may contribute to the appearance of constant loop widths in observational data.

We show that plasmons in two-dimensional graphene can have net gain atterahertz frequencies. The coupling of the plasmons to interband electron-holetransitions in population inverted graphene layers can lead to plasmonamplification through the process of stimulated emission. We calculate plasmongain for different electron-hole densities and temperatures and show that thegain values can exceed $10^{4}$ cm$^{-1}$ in the 1-10 terahertz frequencyrange, for electron-hole densities in the $10^{9}$-$10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$ range,even when plasmon energy loss due to intraband scattering is considered.Plasmons are found to exhibit net gain for intraband scattering times shorterthan 100 fs. Such high gain values could allow extremely compact terahertzamplifiers and oscillators that have dimensions in the 1-10 $\mu$m range.

We propose a new model for black hole accretion that emphasizes the important role of magnetohydrodynamic stresses in transporting angular momentum. Vertical transport of angular momentum by large-scale magnetic fields is thought to be significant and may dominate over radial transport by small-scale turbulence. This enhanced transport leads to higher accretion rates that can explain observations. The radial structure and emission spectrum of the disk are modified when vertical transport is significant. Our simple model shows that magnetically-driven outflows produce a disk spectrum that is dimmer and redder than the standard model accreting at the same rate. This new model has implications for understanding accretion disks around black holes in different astrophysical systems.

Statistics of the Number of Zero Crossings : from Random Polynomials to Diffusion EquationIn this paper, we examine the statistics of the number of zero crossings of a class of random polynomials and broadcast processes. We show that the limiting distribution of the number of zero crossings of a random polynomial is Gaussian, and that the limiting distribution of the number of zero crossings of a diffusion process is additionally Gaussian, but with a different discrepancy. We aslo provide an explicit formula for the limiting variance of the number of nil crossings of a diffusion process. Our results can be utilize to study a variety of physical phe nomena, such as the diffusion of particles in a fluid and the propagation of waves in a random medium.

We examine gauge theories defined in higher dimensions where theextradimensions form a fuzzy (finite matrix) manifold. First we reinterpret thesegauge theories as four-dimensional theories with Kaluza-Klein modes and then weperform a generalized \'a la Forgacs-Manton dimensional reduction. We emphasizesome striking features emerging in the later case such as (i) the appearance ofnon-abelian gauge theories in four dimensions starting from an abelian gaugetheory in higher dimensions, (ii) the fact that the spontaneous symmetrybreaking of the theory takes place entirely in the extra dimensions and (iii)the renormalizability of the theory both in higher as well as in fourdimensions. Then reversing the above approach we present a renormalizable fourdimensional SU(N) gauge theory with a suitable multiplet of scalar fields,which via spontaneous symmetry breaking dynamically develops extra dimensionsin the form of a fuzzy sphere. We explicitly find the tower of massiveKaluza-Klein modes consistent with an interpretation as gauge theory on $M^4\times S^2$, the scalars being interpreted as gauge fields on $S^2$. Dependingon the parameters of the model the low-energy gauge group can be of the form$SU(n_1) \times SU(n_2) \times U(1)$.

Dynamics of Baryons from String Theory and Vector DominanceIn this paper, we study the dynamics of baryons from string theory and vector dominance. We first discuss the general principles of string theory and vector dominance, and then apply these principles to the specific case of baryons. We show that the string theory and vector dominance provide a consistent and comprehensive description of the dynamics of baryons. This description includes a consistent treatment of the spin and isospin of baryons, as well as their electromagnetic and strong interactions. Our results provide new insights into the nature of baryons and their role in the strong interactions. In particular, we show that the string theory and vector dominance provide a natural explanation for the existence of baryons as bound states of quarks, and for the properties of these bound states. We also show that the string theory and vector dominance provide a powerful tool for studying the interactions of baryons with other hadrons.

FIR luminous galaxies are characterized by high FIR luminosity and low optical luminosity, whereas quasars are characterized by high optical luminosity and low FIR luminosity. FeLoBALs are a type of quasar with broad iron absorption lines in their optical spectra. Here we present evidence that FeLoBALs may represent the transition between an ultraluminous infrared galaxy and a quasar. For example, the FIR luminosity of FeLoBALs is lower than that of FIR luminous galaxies but higher than that of quasars. Similarly, the optical luminosity of FeLoBALs is higher than that of FIR luminous galaxies but lower than that of quasars. The broad iron absorption lines in the optical spectra of FeLoBALs are thought to be produced by gas ejected from the accretion disk around the black hole. We propose that FeLoBALs are formed when an ultraluminous infrared galaxy undergoes a rapid increase in accretion rate, which causes the galaxy to become more luminous in the optical and less luminous in the FIR. This provides evidence that FIR luminous galaxies can evolve into quasars through a rapid increase in accretion rate. Our results suggest that FeLoBALs are a transitional phase in the evolution of AGN.

This paper studies game-theoretic power control in impulse radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) wireless networks, in which each user seeks to maximize its own utility by strategically choosing its transmit power level. It is shown that such a strategic interaction between self-interested users leads naturally to a non-cooperative game framework. The game is formulated as a finite strategic game with multidimensional strategy spaces where each user's strategy consists of selecting its transmission power level. Conditions for the existence and uniqueness of Nash equilibria in this power control game are derived and discussed. An iterative algorithm based on best-response dynamics is proposed to allow users to converge to a Nash equilibrium in a distributed manner without centralized coordination. Simulation results are presented to validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that Nash equilibria achieve significant aggregate utility gains over other benchmark schemes in IR-UWB networks under different system setups and assumptions on user priorities. The work provides insights into efficient distributed power control in emerging IR-UWB environments.

[Abridged] We present time-series optical photometry of five new CVsidentified by the Hamburg Quasar Survey. The eclipses observed in HS 0129+2933,HS 0220+0603, and HS 0455+8315 provided very accurate orbital periods of3.35129827(65), 3.58098501(34), and 3.56937674(26) h, respectively. HS0805+3822 shows grazing eclipses and has a likely orbital period of 3.2169(2)h. Time-resolved optical spectroscopy of the new CVs (with the exception of HS0805+3822) is also presented. The spectroscopicbehaviour clearly identifies these new CVs as new SW Sextantis stars. These newadditions increase the number of known SW Sex stars to 35. Almost 40 per centof the total SW Sex population do not show eclipses, invalidating therequirement of eclipses as a defining characteristic of the class and themodels based on a high orbital inclination geometry alone. On the other hand,the predominance of orbital periods in the narrow 3-4.5 h range is becomingmore pronounced. In fact, almost half the CVs which populate the 3-4.5 h periodinterval are definite members of the class. These statistics are confirmed byour results from the Hamburg Quasar Survey CVs. Remarkably, 54 per cent of theHamburg nova-like variables have been identified as SW Sex stars with orbitalperiods in the 3-4.5 h range. The observation of this pile-up of systems closeto the upper boundary of the period gap is difficult to reconcile with thestandard theory of CV evolution, as the SW Sex stars are believed to have thehighest mass transfer rates among CVs. Finally, we review the full range ofcommon properties that the SW Sex stars exhibit.

In this paper, we investigate the phenomenology of the little Higgs models with T-parity at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We focus on the pair production of doubly charged Higgs bosons H±± via gluon fusion at the LHC. Due to T-parity, the pair-produced doubly charged Higgs bosons can only decay into four W bosons. We calculate the total cross section of the gluon fusion process gg→H±± at the LHC with the next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections and consider the non-resonant contributions from the diagrams involving the exchange of singly charged Higgs bosons h±. The total cross section can reach a few fb at the 14 TeV LHC, significantly larger than that at the 8 TeV LHC.

In this article, we focus on the specific aspect of quark-quark scattering in multiple parton scattering processes. We use a theoretical framework based on the color-dipole formalism to study the effects of parton scattering on the structure of the nucleus. By considering different scattering processes and varying the conditions of the medium, we highlight the impact of quark-quark scattering on observables such as hadron production and jet quenching. Our analysis includes both perturbative and nonperturbative aspects, taking into account the distribution of parton densities in the nucleus and the color-neutralization mechanism. We discuss the implications of our results for the understanding of parton interactions in heavy-ion collisions and for the fundamental properties of QCD. In the end, this work contributes to the understanding of the dynamics of multiple parton scattering in nuclei and its role in the formation of quark-gluon plasma.

We use high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy from Keck Observatory tomeasure the stellar velocity dispersions of 19 super star clusters (SSCs) inthe nuclear starburst of M82. The clusters have ages on the order of 10 Myr,which is many times longer than the crossing times implied by their velocitydispersions and radii. We therefore apply the Virial Theorem to derive thekinematic mass for 15 of the SSCs. The SSCs have masses of 2 x 10^5 to 4 x 10^6solar masses, with a total population mass of 1.4 x 10^7 solar masses.Comparison of the loci of the young M82 SSCs and old Milky Way globularclusters in a plot of radius versus velocity dispersion suggests that the SSCsare a population of potential globular clusters. We present the mass functionfor the SSCs, and find a power law fit with an index of gamma = -1.91 +/- 0.06.This result is nearly identical to the mass function of young SSCs in theAntennae galaxies.

Low-mass X-ray binary systems consist of a neutron star accreting matter from a nearby low-mass companion star, forming an accretion disk. Infalling matter orbits the rapidly rotating neutron star in an accretion disk, generating intense X-ray radiation. This radiation allows studying the accretion disk structure and evolution, and its interaction with the neutron star's magnetic field. We model X-ray radiation processes and accretion disk morphologies in these systems. Preliminary results indicate the outer disk is optically thick and geometrically thin, while the inner disk is optically thin and geometrically thick. Deeper in the neutron star's potential well, a hot corona forms from accreting material. Spectral analysis of four prominent low-mass X-ray binaries reveals ionized accretion disks extending close to some neutron stars, as seen through iron emission lines. Observations of bursts, dips and eclipses may elucidate the geometry and structure of the accretion flow and companion star.

This paper studies a variant of the classical problem of ''writing on dirtypaper'' in which the sum of the input and the interference, or dirt, ismultiplied by a random variable that models resizing, known to the decoder butnot to the encoder. The achievable rate of Costa's dirty paper coding (DPC)scheme is calculated and compared to the case of the decoder's also knowing thedirt. In the ergodic case, the corresponding rate loss vanishes asymptoticallyin the limits of both high and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and is small atall finite SNR for typical distributions like Rayleigh, Rician, and Nakagami.In the quasi-static case, the DPC scheme is lossless at all SNR in terms ofoutage probability. Quasi-static fading broadcast channels (BC) withouttransmit channel state information (CSI) are investigated as an application ofthe robustness properties. It is shown that the DPC scheme leads to an outageachievable rate region that strictly dominates that of time division.

Red clump giants in the Galactic bulge are approximate standard candles andhence they can be used as distance indicators. We compute the proper motiondispersions of RCG stars in the Galactic bulge using the proper motioncatalogue from the second phase of the Optical Gravitational MicrolensingExperiment (OGLE-II, Sumi et al. 2004) for 45 fields. The proper motiondispersions are measured to a few per cent accuracy due to the large number ofstars in the fields. The observational sample is comprised of 577736 stars.These observed data are compared to a state-of-the-art particle simulation ofthe Galactic bulge region. The predictions are in rough agreement withobservations, but appear to be too anisotropic in the velocity ellipsoid. Wenote that there is significant field-to-field variation in the observed propermotion dispersions. This could either be a real feature, or due to some unknownsystematic effect.

In this rules, we explore the application of renormalization and effective action techniques to the theory of general relativity. We begin by discussing the motivation for such an approach, highlighting the challenges constituted by the non-renormalizability of gravity and the potential benefits of a Well-defined perturbative increasing. We then introduce the basic thinking and tools of renormalization and effective actions, composing the concept of a "cutoff" and the use of a "regulator" to modify the theory in a way that lets for a well-defined perturbative expansion. We then delve into the specifics of applying these techniques to general relativity, discussing the various proposals that have been put forward for made so, such as the use of the gravitational tying constant as a "executing" parameter and the creations of "counterterms" to cancel divergences. We also debate the relationship between these approaches and other areas of theoretical physics, such as quantum field theory and thongs theory. Finally, we terminates by highlighting some of the open matters and future directions in this area, including the potential for renormalization and effective actions to shed light on longstanding problems in gravity physics, such as the characteristic of black hole evaporation and the misconduct of gravitational waves.

Solar dynamics simulations were used to model the magnetic fields and electrons flows associated with the sunspot and ephemeral regions. Nova results demonstrated that as the sunspot rotated past an ephemeral region, their intersecting magnetic fields reconfigured and amplified stresses within the coronal volume. This magnetic reconnection and stress buildup was found to onset an idael magnetohydrodynamic instability, leading to the formation of a flux rope within the corona. The flux rope continued expanding and rising due to the vertical propagation of torsional Alfvén waves generated by the magnetosphere's rotational shear. Ultimately the flux rope erupted on December 13th, 2006, producing one of the biggest coronal mass ejections of the solar cycle, consistent with observations of the major solar event.

This article presents a comprehensive study on lower bounds for the conductivities of correlated quantum systems. Conductivity, a fundamental property of materials, characterizes the ability of a substance to transmit electrical or thermal energy. In the context of quantum systems, the behavior of conductivity becomes more intricate due to correlations arising from strong electron-electron interactions. By employing rigorous mathematical techniques and theoretical frameworks, we derive lower bounds that establish a minimal value for the conductivities of such correlated quantum systems. These lower bounds provide insight into the inherent limitations imposed by correlations on the achievable conductivities, shedding light on the fundamental properties and behaviors of these complex systems. Additionally, by examining diverse scenarios and varying degrees of correlation strength, we explore the impact of different factors on the conductivities, contributing to a deeper understanding of the interplay between quantum correlations and electrical/thermal transport in materials. The findings presented in this article not only enhance our theoretical understanding of correlated quantum systems, but also have potential implications for the design and optimization of electronic and thermal devices.

The extragalactic background (EGB) of diffuse gamma rays can be determined bysubtracting the Galactic contribution from the data. This requires a Galacticmodel (GM) and we include for the first time the contribution of dark matterannihilation (DMA), which was previously proposed as an explanation for theEGRET excess of diffuse Galactic gamma rays above 1 GeV. In this paper it is shown that the newly determined EGB shows acharacteristic high energy bump on top of a steeply falling soft contribution.The bump is shown to be compatible with a contribution from an extragalacticDMA signal from weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) with a massbetween 50 and 100 GeV in agreement with the EGRET excess of the Galacticdiffuse gamma rays and in disagreement with earlier analysis. The remainingsoft contribution of the EGB is shown to resemble the spectra of the observedpoint sources in our Galaxy.

We present a detailed experimental and theoretical study of the effect ofnuclear spin on the performance of optical lattice clocks. With a state-mixingtheory including spin-orbit and hyperfine interactions, we describe the originof the $^1S_0$-$^3P_0$ clock transition and the differential g-factor betweenthe two clock states for alkaline-earth(-like) atoms, using $^{87}$Sr as anexample. Clock frequency shifts due to magnetic and optical fields arediscussed with an emphasis on those relating to nuclear structure. Anexperimental determination of the differential g-factor in $^{87}$Sr isperformed and is in good agreement with theory. The magnitude of the tensorlight shift on the clock states is also explored experimentally. State specificmeasurements with controlled nuclear spin polarization are discussed as amethod to reduce the nuclear spin-related systematic effects to below10$^{-17}$ in lattice clocks.

- Please wait... : Driving jets and outflows play an important role in the process of satr formation by influencing the surrounding medium and the overall evolution of the star. Jets and outflows are launched from young stars and can transport msas, energy, and angսlar momentum to the surrounding environment. The driving mechanisms of jets and outflows are poorly understood, and several various mechanisms have been proposed. The most popular mechanisms are magnetic launching and radiation pressure. Magnetc launching is the process by which magnetic fields in the accretion disk around the young star are able to extract rotational energy and launch a jet. Radiation pressure is the pressure exerted by photons on a surface. In the case of a young star, the radiation pressure from the star can drive an outlfow of gas. The relative importance of magnetic launching and radiation pressure in driving jes and outflows is still a matter of debate.

Radiation pressure plays an important but not fully understood role in the dynamics of the diffuse intergalactic signifies. In this examine, we investigate the impact of radiation pressure on Lyman-alpha forest clouds using cosmological simulations. The simulates self-consistently model the conveying of ionizing photons from galaxies and their deposition of momentum into the surrounding gas through resonant scattering by neutral hydrogen. We find that radiation pressure can regulate the collapse of clouds and affect their densities and colder regarding to simulations without radiation pressure. Furthermore, radiation pressure influences the evolution of large scale structure in the diffuse intergalactic signifies. Overall, our results indicate radiation pressure is a non-negligible physical process that needs to be taken into account for a accomplish realizing of the Lyman-alpha forest.

In this study, we investigate the habitat segregation between Lyman break galaxies (LBGs) and Lyman alpha emitters (LAEs) around a quasar at redshift z ~ 5. Using a combination of observational data and simulations, we explore the spatial distribution of these two populations and examine their respective properties. Our results show that LBGs and LAEs exhibit distinct clustering patterns, with LBGs preferentially located in higher density regions and LAEs found in lower density environments. We also find that LBGs have higher star formation rates and larger galaxy sizes compared to LAEs. The observed segregation patterns suggest that LBGs and LAEs may have different formation mechanisms and evolutionary paths. Moreover, the presence of the quasar does not appear to significantly affect the distribution of either population. Our findings provide new insights into the early universe's galaxy formation and evolution, highlighting the complex interplay between gas, dust, and star formation in shaping galaxy properties.

We first introduce the notion of Hom complex and discuss its basic properties. Then we calculate the homotopy groups of Hom complexes of trees and cycles. Finally, we discuss some applications of our results to the study of homology of graphs.

We consider the nonminimally coupled lambda phi^4 scalar field theory in deSitter space and construct the renormalization group improved renormalizedeffective theory at the one-loop level. Based on the corresponding quantumFriedmann equation and the scalar field equation of motion, we calculate thequantum radiative corrections to the scalar spectral index n_s, gravitationalwave spectral index n_g and the ratio r of tensor to scalar perturbations. Whencompared with the standard (tree-level) values, we find that the quantumcontributions are suppressed by lambda N^2 where N denotes the number ofe-foldings. Hence there is an N^2 enhancement with respect to the naiveexpectation, which is due to the infrared enhancement of scalar vacuumfluctuations characterising de Sitter space. Since observations constrainlambda to be very small lambda ~ 10^(-12) and N ~ 50-60, the quantumcorrections in this inflationary model are unobservably small.

When modeling the distribution of a set of data by a mixture of Gaussians,there are two possibilities: i) the classical one is using a set of parameterswhich are the proportions, the means and the variances; ii) the second is toconsider the proportions as the probabilities of a discrete valued hiddenvariable. In the first case a usual prior distribution for the proportions isthe Dirichlet which accounts for the fact that they have to sum up to one. Inthe second case, to each data is associated a hidden variable for which weconsider two possibilities: a) assuming those variables to be i.i.d. We showthen that this scheme is equivalent to the classical mixture model withDirichlet prior; b) assuming a Markovian structure. Then we choose the simplestmarkovian model which is the Potts distribution. As we will see this model ismore appropriate for the case where the data represents the pixels of an imagefor which the hidden variables represent a segmentation of that image. The mainobject of this paper is to give some details on these models and differentalgorithms used for their simulation and the estimation of their parameters. Key Words: Mixture of Gaussians, Dirichlet, Potts, Classification,Segmentation.

The space velocities from the catalog of Nordstrom et al. (2004) are used totrace variations of a number of kinematic parameters of single F and G dwarfsas a function of their age. The vertex deviation of disk stars increases from7+- 1 to 15+-2 degrees as the mean age decreases from 4.3 to 1.5 Gyr. Thetwo-dimensional velocity distributions in the UV, UW, and VW planes areanalyzed. The evolution of the main peaks in the velocity distributions can befollowed to an average age of approximately 9 Gyr. We find that: (1) in thedistributions of the UV velocity components, stars of different types areconcentrated toward several stable peaks (the Hyades, Pleiades, and SiriusCluster), suggesting that the stars belonging to these formations did not formsimultaneously; (2) the peak associated with the Hyades Cluster dominates inall age intervals; and (3) the Hyades peak is strongest for stars with anaverage age of 1.5 Gyr, suggesting that this peak contains a considerablefraction of stars from the Hyades cluster. The age dependences of the kinematicparameters exhibit a break near 4.5 Gyr, which can be explained as an effect ofthe different contributions of stars of the thin and thick disks. The Strombergrelation yields a solar LSR velocity of V_{\odot LSR} = (8.7, 6.2, 7.2)+- (0.5,2.2, 0.8) km/s.

We carry out cosmological chemodynamical simulations with different strengthsof supernova (SN) feedback and study how galactic winds from star-forminggalaxies affect the features of hydrogen (HI) and metal (CIV and OVI)absorption systems in the intergalactic medium at high redshift. We find thatthe outflows tend to escape to low density regions, and hardly affect the densefilaments visible in HI absorption. As a result, the strength of HI absorptionnear galaxies is not reduced by galactic winds, but even slightly increases. Wealso find that a lack of HI absorption for lines of sight (LOS) close togalaxies, as found by Adelberger et al., can be created by hot gas around thegalaxies induced by accretion shock heating. In contrast to HI, metalabsorption systems are sensitive to the presence of winds. The models withoutfeedback can produce the strong CIV and OVI absorption lines in LOS within 50kpc from galaxies, while strong SN feedback is capable of creating strong CIVand OVI lines out to about twice that distance. We also analyze the meantransmissivity of HI, CIV, and OVI within 1 h$^{-1}$ Mpc from star-forminggalaxies. The probability distribution of the transmissivity of HI isindependent of the strength of SN feedback, but strong feedback produces LOSwith lower transmissivity of metal lines. Additionally, strong feedback canproduce strong OVI lines even in cases where HI absorption is weak. We concludethat OVI is probably the best tracer for galactic winds at high redshift.

Evidence that FeLoBALs may signify the transition between an ultraluminous infrared galaxy and a quasarWe present mid-infrared spectra of six FeLoBAL QSOs, observed with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The spectra reveal a range of shapes, from hot dust-dominated AGN to obscured starbursts. The spectrum of SDSS 1214-0001 shows the most prominent PAHs seen in any QSO, indicating a substantial starburst component. We propose that FeLoBAL QSOs may be in a transitional phase, where a merger-driven starburst is ending, an AGN is clearing its surrounding dust, and we may be viewing along a restricted line of sight.

This paper investigates the capacity benefits afforded by cooperation between two transmitters and two receivers in a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) fading channel. We consider a half-duplex decode-and-forward cooperation protocol where each transmitter encodes and forwards information for the other during alternate time slots under individual power constraints. Exact analytic expressions are derived for the capacity region of the resultant two-user orthogonal multiaccess relay channel for different channel state information conditions. Our analysis reveals that spatial diversity gains from multiuser cooperation can significantly increase throughput compared to independent transmissions, especially at medium-to-high bandwidth ratios where each user's signal experiences independent fading. Moreover, optimal power allocation policies that dynamically leverage multiuser fading diversity are shown to further expand the optimal rate region. The derived insights demonstrate the capacity advantages of cooperative communication schemes for future wireless systems employing multiple antennas at network nodes.

This study investigates the influence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) nuclear parameters on the Fanaroff-Riley (FRI/FRII) radio galaxy dichotomy. We analyze a sample of 346 radio galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 14, matched with archival Chandra X-ray Observatory and Hubble Space Telescope data. We find that the FRI/FRII dichotomy is primarily driven by the jet power, with FRI galaxies having lower jet powers than FRII galaxies. We also find that the FRI/FRII dichotomy is correlated with several other AGN nuclear parameters, including the black hole mass, the Eddington ratio, and the X-ray luminosity. These results suggest that the FRI/FRII dichotomy is influenced by a combination of factors, including the jet power, the black hole mass, and the accretion rate onto the black hole. Our results provide new insights into the physical processes that drive the FRI/FRII dichotomy and help to unify the understanding of radio galaxies.

Observational consequences of the hypothesized helium rich stellar peoples in Omega Centauri are explored in this study. Using a cooperated of photometric and spectroscopic data, the authors identify a distinct population of repute in the globular cluster Omega Centauri that exhibit unusual helium abundances. The observed properties of these star, such as their luminosities, temperatures, and chemical compositions, are found to got consistent with theories of helium enrichment due to the meltdown of two helium white dwarfs. The implications of this ensuing on our understanding of globular cluster shifts and the formation of exotic stars are discussed. The study demonstrates the power of observational astronomy in constraining theories of stellar evolution and donne new ideals into the complex history of Omega Centauri.

Herein, we present a detailed microscopic analysis of the superconducting quantum critical point (QCP). The analysis is underpinned by a microscopic model that incorporates the effects of disorder, interactions, and thermal fluctuations. Electrical conductivity, Hall coefficient, and thermopower are calculated as a function of temperature and magnetic field. Several intriguing characteristics are unveiled in the transport properties close to the QCP, including a finite-temperature crossover from Fermi-liquid to non-Fermi-liquid regimes, a sign change in the Hall coefficient, and a significant enhancement of the thermopower. These results align with existing experimental data, providing a microscopic understanding of the transport properties at the superconducting QCP.

The formation and evolution of the Oort Cloud in our solar system may leave an imprint on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies that are small but potentially detectable. Gravitational effects from density perturbations in the early Oort Cloud could introduce subtle distortions to the primordial CMB temperature fluctuations generated during the inflationary epoch. This study uses cosmological simulations to model the growth of structure in the outer Solar System during and after planetary formation. The simulations track the dynamics and interactions of asteroids and comet-sized objects as they evolve under the gravitational influence of the growing planets. Subtle lensing, Shapiro time delay and Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effects induced by variations in the mass distribution in the early Oort Cloud are calculated. Analysis of the simulations suggests these Oort Cloud-induced signals havecharacteristic spatial scales and amplitudes in the CMB temperature maps that may allow them to be distinguished with high-sensitivity measurements from future experiments.

We study the growth of cosmological perturbations in the model ofLorentz-violating massive gravity. The Friedman equation in this model acquiresan unconventional term due to the Lorentz-breaking condensates which has theequation of state w = -1 / (3 gamma) with gamma being a free parameter takingvalues outside of the range [0,1/3]. Apart from the standard contributions, theperturbations above the Friedmann background contain an extra piece which isproportional to an arbitrary function theta(x) of the space coordinates. Thisfunction appears as an integration constant and corresponds to anon-propagating scalar mode which may, however, become dynamical with theaccount of the higher-derivative corrections. For -1 < gamma < 0 and gamma = 1the ''anomalous'' perturbations grow slower than the standard ones and thus themodel is compatible with observations. Whether the model is experimentallyacceptable at other values of \gamma depends on the value of the functiontheta(x) at the beginning of the radiation-dominated epoch.

The annihilation of dark matter (DM) in the Galaxy could produce specificimprints on the spectra of antimatter species in Galactic cosmic rays, whichcould be detected by upcoming experiments such as PAMELA and AMS02. Recentstudies show that the presence of substructures can enhance the annihilationsignal by a "boost factor" that not only depends on energy, but that isintrinsically a statistical property of the distribution of DM substructuresinside the Milky Way. We investigate a scenario in which substructures consistof $\sim 100$ "mini-spikes" around intermediate-mass black holes. Focusing onprimary positrons and antiprotons, we find large boost factors, up to a fewthousand, that exhibit a large variance at high energy in the case of positronsand at low energy in the case of antiprotons. As a consequence, an estimate ofthe DM particle mass based on the observed cut-off in the positron spectrumcould lead to a substantial underestimate of its actual value.

We investigate degenerate saddle point problems, which can be viewed as limitcases of standard mixed formulations of symmetric problems with large jumps incoefficients. We prove that they are well-posed in a standard norm despite thedegeneracy. By wellposedness we mean a stable dependence of the solution on theright-hand side. A known approach of splitting the saddle point problem intoseparate equations for the primary unknown and for the Lagrange multiplier isused. We revisit the traditional Ladygenskaya--Babu\v{s}ka--Brezzi (LBB) orinf--sup condition as well as the standard coercivity condition, and analyzehow they are affected by the degeneracy of the corresponding bilinear forms. Wesuggest and discuss generalized conditions that cover the degenerate case. TheLBB or inf--sup condition is necessary and sufficient for wellposedness of theproblem with respect to the Lagrange multiplier under some assumptions. Thegeneralized coercivity condition is necessary and sufficient for wellposednessof the problem with respect to the primary unknown under some otherassumptions. We connect the generalized coercivity condition to thepositiveness of the minimum gap of relevant subspaces, and propose severalequivalent expressions for the minimum gap. Our results provide a foundationfor research on uniform wellposedness of mixed formulations of symmetricproblems with large jumps in coefficients in a standard norm, independent ofthe jumps. Such problems appear, e.g., in numerical simulations of compositematerials made of components with contrasting properties.

Using local morphological measures on the sphere defined through a steerablewavelet analysis, we examine the three-year WMAP and the NVSS data forcorrelation induced by the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. The steerablewavelet constructed from the second derivative of a Gaussian allows one todefine three local morphological measures, namely the signed-intensity,orientation and elongation of local features. Detections of correlation betweenthe WMAP and NVSS data are made with each of these morphological measures. Themost significant detection is obtained in the correlation of thesigned-intensity of local features at a significance of 99.9%. By inspectingsigned-intensity sky maps, it is possible for the first time to see thecorrelation between the WMAP and NVSS data by eye. Foreground contamination andinstrumental systematics in the WMAP data are ruled out as the source of allsignificant detections of correlation. Our results provide new insight on theISW effect by probing the morphological nature of the correlation inducedbetween the cosmic microwave background and large scale structure of theUniverse. Given the current constraints on the flatness of the Universe, ourdetection of the ISW effect again provides direct and independent evidence fordark energy. Moreover, this new morphological analysis may be used in future tohelp us to better understand the nature of dark energy.

This article investigates the phenomenon of vortex trapping in suddenly connected Bose-Josephson junctions. Our study demonstrates that upon sudden connection of a Bose-Einstein condensate to a superfluid Josephson junction, vortices can become trapped in the junction, leading to the formation of stable vortex-antivortex pairs. We analyze the system's dynamics and show that the Competition between the Magnus force and the Josephson coupling gives rise to vortex trapping. This phenomenon holds potential for the development of novel quantum devices, such as superfluid quantum computers and topological quantum computing platforms. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of vortex matter in suddenly connected Bose-Josephson junctions, opening up avenues for further research in this burgeoning field.

We investigate electronic transport through II-VI semiconductor resonanttunneling structures containing diluted magnetic impurities. Due to theexchange interaction between the conduction electrons and the impurities, therearises a giant Zeeman splitting in the presence of a moderately low magneticfield. As a consequence, when the quantum well is magnetically doped thecurrent-voltage characteristics shows two peaks corresponding to transport foreach spin channel. This behavior is experimentally observed and can bereproduced with a simple tunneling model. The model thus allows to analyzeother configurations. First, we further increase the magnetic field, whichleads to a spin polarization of the electronic current injected from the leads,thus giving rise to a relative change in the current amplitude. We demonstratethat the spin polarization in the emitter can be determined from such a change.Furthermore, in the case of a magnetically doped injector our model shows alarge increase in peak amplitude and a shift of the resonance to highervoltages as the external field increases. We find that this effect arises froma combination of giant Zeeman splitting, 3-D incident distribution and broadresonance linewidth.

Dark energy and gravity are two of the most mysterious and fascinating aspects of the universe. Dark energy is a hypothetical form of energy that is believed to be responsible for the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion. Gravity, on the other hand, is one of the four fundamental forces of nature and is responsible for the attraction between objects with mass. In this paper, we will explore the relationship between dark energy and gravity and discuss some of the implications of their interaction.Dark energy is believed to make up around 68% of the total energy in the universe, while gravity makes up only around 5%. This means that dark energy is the dominant form of energy in the universe and is responsible for its accelerated expansion. The existence of dark energy is inferred from observations of distant supernovae, which show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.Gravity, on the other hand, is one of the four fundamental forces of nature and is responsible for the attraction between objects with mass. Gravity is a well-understood force and is described by Einstein's theory of general relativity. However, general relativity does not explain the existence of dark energy or its effects on the universe.One of the implications of the interaction between dark energy and gravity is that the expansion of the universe will eventually become so rapid that galaxies will be torn apart. This is known as the "Big Rip." The Big Rip is predicted to occur in approximately 22 billion years.Another implication of the interaction between dark energy and gravity is that the universe will eventually end in a "heat death." In this scenario, the universe will expand to such an extent that all matter and energy will be spread out so thinly that it will be impossible for any further interactions to occur. The heat death is predicted to occur in approximately 10^100 years.

New measures of multipartite entanglement are constructed based on twodefinitions of multipartite information and different methods of optimizingover extensions of the states. One is a generalization of the squashedentanglement where one takes the mutual information of parties conditioned onthe state's extension and takes the infimum over such extensions. Additivity ofthe multipartite squashed entanglement is proved for both versions of themultipartite information which turn out to be related. The second one is basedon taking classical extensions. This scheme is generalized, which enables toconstruct measures of entanglement based on the {\it mixed convex roof} of aquantity, which in contrast to the standard convex roof method involvesoptimization over all decompositions of a density matrix rather than just thedecompositions into pure states. As one of the possible applications of theseresults we prove that any multipartite monotone is an upper bound on the amountof multipartite distillable key. The findings are finally related to analogousresults in classical key agreement.

We study the mixing time of a systematic scan Markov chain for sampling fromthe uniform distribution on proper 7-colourings of a finite rectangularsub-grid of the infinite square lattice, the grid. A systematic scan Markovchain cycles through finite-size subsets of vertices in a deterministic orderand updates the colours assigned to the vertices of each subset. The systematicscan Markov chain that we present cycles through subsets consisting of 2x2sub-grids and updates the colours assigned to the vertices using a procedureknown as heat-bath. We give a computer-assisted proof that this systematic scanMarkov chain mixes in O(log n) scans, where n is the size of the rectangularsub-grid. We make use of a heuristic to compute required couplings ofcolourings of 2x2 sub-grids. This is the first time the mixing time of asystematic scan Markov chain on the grid has been shown to mix for less than 8colours. We also give partial results that underline the challenges of provingrapid mixing of a systematic scan Markov chain for sampling 6-colourings of thegrid by considering 2x3 and 3x3 sub-grids.

For this article, we explore the connection between Donaldson theory and non-Kählerian surfaces, particularly those with a second Betti number of 1 (class VII surfaces) and $b_2=1$. We begin by examining the fundamental principles of Donaldson theory and its role in understanding the geometry of non-Kählerian surfaces. We then delve into the specifics of homeroom VII surfaces and their unique properties, which allow for a richer understanding of the interplay between Donaldson theory and these surfaces. Through a cmobination of mathematical analysis and theoretical exploration, we uncover nuevo insights into the relationship between these two areas of mathematics and reveal the ways in which they shed light on each other. Ultimately, our results provide a deeper understanding of the intricate connections between different zone of geometry and topology, and open up new avenues for future research.

A chaotic micromixer with a large surface area and a small volume is developed by combining soft lithography with electrokinetics. The chaotic advection in the micromixer is generated by an array of arc-shaped electrodes on the bottom of a microchannel, which is closed with a glass cover with a flat surface. The electrokinetic chaotic micromixer can mix various fluids in a short time. The micromixer is simple and low cost. The mixing efficiency is studied by measuring the fluorescence intensity of a mixed solution of rhodamine B and fluorescein isothiocyanate-dextran (FITC-dextran). The mixing efficiency can reach 98% at the flow rate of 80 $\mu$L/min. The micromixer is used to accelerate the reaction between fluorescamine and glycine. The reaction rate constant obtained with the micromixer is four times larger than that in a straight microchannel, which is attributed to the high mixing efficiency of the micromixer. The soft-lithographed electrokinetic chaotic micromixer with a simple structure, high mixing efficiency and low cost should be a powerful tool for chemical reactions in lab-on-chips.

We observe a sharp transition from a singular, high-mass mode of starformation, to a low-mass dominated mode, in numerical simulations, at ametallicity of 10^-3 Zsolar. We incorporate a new method for including theradiative cooling from metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamicsimulations. Our results illustrate how metals, produced by the first stars,led to a transition from the high-mass star formation mode of Pop III stars, tothe low-mass mode that dominates today. We ran hydrodynamic simulations withcosmological initial conditions in the standard LambdaCDM model, withmetallicities, from zero to 10^-2 Zsolar, beginnning at redshift, z = 99. Thesimulations were run until a dense core forms at the center of a 5 x 10^5Msolar dark matter halo, at z ~ 18. Analysis of the central 1 Msolar corereveals that the two simulations with the lowest metallicities, Z = 0 and 10^-4Zsolar, contain one clump with 99% of the mass, while the two withmetallicities, Z = 10^-3 and 10^-2 Zsolar, each contain two clumps that sharemost of the mass. The Z = 10^-3 Zsolar simulation also produced two low-massproto-stellar objects with masses between 10^-2 and 10^-1 Msolar. Gas with Z >=10^-3 Zsolar is able to cool to the temperature of the CMB, which sets a lowerlimit to the minimum fragmentation mass. This suggests that the secondgeneration stars produced a spectrum of lower mass stars, but were still moremassive on average than stars formed in the local universe.

In spatially distributed multiuser antenna systems, the received signalcontains multiple carrier-frequency offsets (CFOs) arising from mismatchbetween the oscillators of transmitters and receivers. This results in atime-varying rotation of the data constellation, which needs to be compensatedat the receiver before symbol recovery. In this paper, a new approach for blindCFO estimation and symbol recovery is proposed. The received base-band signalis over-sampled, and its polyphase components are used to formulate a virtualMultiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) problem. By applying blind MIMO systemestimation techniques, the system response can be estimated and decoupledversions of the user symbols can be recovered, each one of which contains adistinct CFO. By applying a decision feedback Phase Lock Loop (PLL), the CFOcan be mitigated and the transmitted symbols can be recovered. The estimatedMIMO system response provides information about the CFOs that can be used toinitialize the PLL, speed up its convergence, and avoid ambiguities usuallylinked with PLL.

The intrinsic fraction of broad absorption line quasars (BALQSOs) isimportant in constraining geometric and evolutionary models of quasars. Wepresent the fraction of BALQSOs in 2MASS detected quasars within the SDSS DR3sample in the redshift range of 1.7 < z < 4.38. The fraction of BALQSOs is40.4^{+3.4}_{-3.3}% in the 2MASS 99% database K_s band completeness sample, and38.5^{+1.7}_{-1.7}% in the larger 2MASS sample extending below the completenesslimit. These fractions are significantly higher than the 26% reported in theoptical bands for the same parent sample. We also present the fraction ofBALQSOs as functions of apparent magnitudes, absolute magnitudes, and redshiftin the 2MASS and SDSS bands. The 2MASS fractions are consistently higher thanthe SDSS fractions in every comparison, and the BALQSO fractions steadilyincrease with wavelength from the SDSS u to the 2MASS K_s bands. Furthermore,the i - K_s color distributions of BALQSOs and non-BALQSOs indicate thatBALQSOs are redder than non-BALQSOs, with a K-S test probability of 2e-12.These results are consistent with the spectral difference between BALQSOs andnon-BALQSOs including both the absorption troughs and dust extinction inBALQSOs, which leads to significant selection biases against BALQSOs in theoptical bands. Using a simple simulation incorporating the luminosity functionof quasars and the amount of obscuration for BALQSOs, we simultaneously fit theBALQSO fractions in the SDSS and 2MASS bands. We obtain a true BALQSO fractionof 43\pm2% for luminous quasars (M_{K_s} \lesssim -30.1 mag).

Our results reveal significant differences in the evolution of the plasma for different adiabafic indices. We observe that varying the adiabatic index leads to variations in the shock heating and coling processes, as well as changes in the foAmation and propagation of magnetohydrodynamic shocks. Furthermore, we find that the variable adiabatic index allosw for a more realistic description of the pasma behavior, particularly in extreme conditions. To validate our findings, we compare our simulation resutls to analytical models and experimental data. The comparison demonstrates the superiority of the variable adiabatic index approch, as it better captures the complex dynamics and thermodynamic properties of the pQasma. Overall, our study highligits the importance of considering a variable adiabatic index in RMHD simulations to improvT the accuracy and reliability of the rjsults, particularly in scenarios involving extreme plasma conditions.

Tables of mean opacities are often used to compute the transfer of radiationin a variety of astrophysical simulations from stellar evolution models toproto-planetary disks. Often tables, such as Ferguson et al. (2005), arecomputed with a predetermined set of physical assumptions that may or may notbe valid for a specific application. This paper explores the effects of severalassumptions of grain physics on the Rosseland mean opacity in an oxygen richenvironment. We find that changing the distribution of grain sizes, either thepower-law exponent or the shape of the distribution, has a marginal effect onthe total mean opacity. We also explore the difference in the mean opacitybetween solid homogenous grains and grains that are porous or conglomorationsof several species. Changing the amount of grain opacity included in the meanby assuming a grain-to-gas ratio significantly affects the mean opacity, but ina predictable way.

In this article, we explore the concept of quantum groups of isometries in both classical and noncommutative geometry. We investigate the interplay between these two geometric frameworks, focusing on the relationship between quantum groups and the isometries of metric spaces. By examining the properties of these quantum groups, we aim to understand their role in capturing the symmetries and geometric structures of classical spaces. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to noncommutative geometry, where quantum groups provide a powerful tool for studying spaces with noncommutative coordinates. Through our investigation, we shed light on the connections between classical and noncommutative geometry and highlight the significance of quantum groups in understanding the fundamental properties of geometric spaces.

We introduce a nonequilibrium equation-of-motion approach for an impurityAnderson model which allows us to describe transport properties of molecularjunctions. The method is based on a mapping of the Anderson model to a fictitiousequilibrium problem, in the limit of large onsite Coulomb interaction U, byintroducing an auxiliary field. This problem can be solved within the nonequilibrium Green's function technique. We calculate the differential conductanceand thermopower and analyze their dependence on temperature and gate voltage. Thecalculated characteristics exhibit a smooth crossover from the Coulomb blockade regimeto the Kondo regime as the interaction strength is varied. A detailed comparison to thenumerical renormalization group results is given. In the large U limit, we find aquantitative agreement with the two-channel Kondo model results. In particular, weobserve the suppression of the zero-bias anomaly in the differential conductance and thechange of the sign of the thermopower in the Kondo regime.

Random critical points often display multifractal properties of the local order parameter. In this paper, we study the multifractal statistics of the local order parameter at random critical points using the example of wetting transitions in the presence of disorder. Wetting transitions occur when a fluid interface adheres to or detaches from a disordered substrate at a wetting temperature. We develop renormalization group techniques to analyze the fluctuations of the local height of the fluid interface at the wetting transition. Our analysis shows that the local height is characterized by a multifractal spectrum. We derive scaling relations between the multifractal spectra of the local height and other thermodynamic quantities like the interface free energy. Numerical simulations of disordered wetting models demonstrate multifractal behavior of the local height consistent with our analytical predictions. Our work establishes a connection between multifractality and wetting transitions in the presence of quenched disorder. It provides a framework to study more general random critical points using the local order parameter fluctuations.

Exoplanet rotation rates provide key insight into planetary formation and evolution. However, directly measuring rotation via photometry or spectroscopy has proven challenging. Here we demonstrate a novel method to infer exoplanetary rotation using transit spectroscopy. During transit, variations in atmospheric composition across an exoplanetary disk can produce spectral features that evolve over the duration of transit as different regions rotate into and out of view. We simulated remarks of hot Jupiter exoplanet HD 189733b's transit spectrum as it would appear if observed at high spectral resolution over full transit duration. By compared simulated observations to models accounting for effects of planetary rotation on transit spectrum, we constrain HD 189733b's rotation rate to a period of $X\pm Y$ hours. Faster or slower rotation rates produce signature Doppler shift or asymmetries in spectral features that are not seen in our observations. This technique demonstrates transit spectroscopy's potential for direct rotation measurements, opening a new window into exoplanetary interiors and atmospheres.
