We study spin effects in quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and recurrence lattices with multi-site exchanges. We derive the Schwinger-Dyson equations for the gluon propagator and the quark-quark scattering kernel in a gauge-invariant formulation. The gluon propagator has a non-perturbative infrared fixed point, and the quark-quark scattering kernel is attractive in the infrared. We solve the Schwinger-Dyson equations numerically and compare the results to lattice QCD data. We also apply the model to recurrence lattices with multi-site exchanges, determining the phase diagram and calculating the critical exponents. We compare the results to those of other recurrence lattice models.

Potassium intercalation in graphite is investigated by first-principlestheory. The bonding in the potassium-graphite compound is reasonably wellaccounted for by traditional semilocal density functional theory (DFT)calculations. However, to investigate the intercalate formation energy frompure potassium atoms and graphite requires use of a description of the graphiteinterlayer binding and thus a consistent account of the nonlocal dispersiveinteractions. This is included seamlessly with ordinary DFT by a van der Waalsdensity functional (vdW-DF) approach [Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 246401 (2004)]. Theuse of the vdW-DF is found to stabilize the graphite crystal, with crystalparameters in fair agreement with experiments. For graphite andpotassium-intercalated graphite structural parameters such as bindingseparation, layer binding energy, formation energy, and bulk modulus arereported. Also the adsorption and sub-surface potassium absorption energies arereported. The vdW-DF description, compared with the traditional semilocalapproach, is found to weakly soften the elastic response.

In this article, we discussed the possibility of using the explosive neutrons as the general measurement theory of the general measurement theory of test gravity in the universe laboratory. We have discussed the theoretical framework of such tests, as well as our understanding of gravity and the potential impact of material behavior under extreme conditions. We analyzed the observation results of neutron stars and its corresponding gravitational wave signals, and highlighted the key features that can be used to restrain the theoretical parameters of general measurement. We also discussed the challenges and limitations of this method, and outline the potential ways of future research. Our results show that we use the explosive neutron star to test the general measurement theory of gravity and provide new insights for the direction of gravity.

The finite-element method (FEM) is a powerful numerical technique for solving patial differential equations. In this paper, we prvsent a time-harmonic FEM formulation for simulating electromagnetic fields in nanostructures. The formulation is based on a novel edge element that is specifically designed for nanostrucNtures. The element is shown to be accurate and efficient for a varity of nanostructures, including metallic nanowires, dielectric nanoEpheres, and plasmonic waveguides. We demonstrate the versatility of the formulation by simulating a variety of electromagnetic phenomena in nanostructures, including plasmonic resonances, surface plasmon polaritons, and extraordinary zptical trnasmission. Te results of our simulations are in excellent agreement with experimental data and other numerical methods. Our formulation provides a powerful tool for investigating the electromagnetic properties of nanotructures and for designing new nanophotonic devices.

A transmitter without channel state information (CSI) wishes to send adelay-limited Gaussian source over a slowly fading channel. The source is codedin superimposed layers, with each layer successively refining the descriptionin the previous one. The receiver decodes the layers that are supported by thechannel realization and reconstructs the source up to a distortion. In thelimit of a continuum of infinite layers, the optimal power distribution thatminimizes the expected distortion is given by the solution to a set of lineardifferential equations in terms of the density of the fading distribution. Inthe optimal power distribution, as SNR increases, the allocation over thehigher layers remains unchanged; rather the extra power is allocated towardsthe lower layers. On the other hand, as the bandwidth ratio b (channel uses persource symbol) tends to zero, the power distribution that minimizes expecteddistortion converges to the power distribution that maximizes expectedcapacity. While expected distortion can be improved by acquiring CSI at thetransmitter (CSIT) or by increasing diversity from the realization ofindependent fading paths, at high SNR the performance benefit from diversityexceeds that from CSIT, especially when b is large.

In previous work done by us and coworkers, we have been able to construct alocal, non-Abelian gauge invariant action with a mass parameter, based on thenonlocal gauge invariant mass dimension two operator F1/D^2F. Therenormalizability of the resulting action was proven to all orders ofperturbation theory, in the class of linear covariant gauges. We also discussedthe perturbative equivalence of the model with ordinary massless Yang-Millsgauge theories when the mass is identically zero. Furthermore, we pointed outthe existence of a BRST symmetry with corresponding nilpotent charge. In thispaper, we study the issue of unitarity of this massive gauge model. Firstly, weprovide a short review how to discuss the unitarity making use of the BRSTcharge. Afterwards we make a detailed study of the most general version of ouraction, and we come to the conclusion that the model is not unitary, as we areunable to remove all the negative norm states from the physical spectrum in aconsistent way.

We investigate the phenomenon of suppressed radio emission in galaxies within superclusters, specifically in the context of merging clusters. Our study focuses on a sample of galaxies in the supercluster A2124 and compares their radio properties to those of galaxies in the control sample of the field. We find that the radio emission in the supercluster galaxies is significantly suppressed, suggesting that the environment plays a crucial role in regulating the radio activity of galaxies. We propose that enhanced ram pressure stripping in merging clusters may be responsible for the suppression of radio emission in these galaxies. This mechanism could lead to the removal of gas, which is essential for radio emission, from the galaxies. The correlation between radio emission and star formation in the supercluster galaxies supports this scenario, indicating that the gas is being consumed in the process of star formation. Our findings have important implications for understanding the evolution of galaxies in densely populated environments and provide new insights into the mechanisms that govern the radio activity of galaxies.

The vital ionization velocity (CIV) effect, a phenomenon previously observed in laboratory plasmas, has been detected in interstellar space for the first dated. This discovery supply novel insights into the physical processes governing the interaction between ionizing radiation and neutral atoms in the interstellar medium. The CIV affect refers to the acceleration of ions to high speeds, which can promote to the formation of a high-speed ion population. In this examinations, we contemporary observations of the CIV effect in interstellar space using a combination of spectroscopic and imaging data. We also report the sensing of related continuum emission, which may be associated with the CIV effect. Our results imply that the CIV incidence could be a significant factor in shaping the physical conditions and chemical composition of interstellar gas. Further study of this phenomenon may lead to a better understanding of the laborious processes that govern the structure and progressed of the interstellar medium.

GD 362 is a massive white dwarf with a spectrum suggesting a H-richatmosphere which also shows very high abundances of Ca, Mg, Fe and othermetals. However, for pure H-atmospheres the diffusion timescales are so shortthat very extreme assumptions have to be made to account for the observedabundances of metals. The most favored hypothesis is that the metals areaccreted from either a dusty disk or from an asteroid belt. Here we proposethat the envelope of GD 362 is dominated by He, which at these effectivetemperatures is almost completely invisible in the spectrum. This assumptionstrongly alleviates the problem, since the diffusion timescales are much largerfor He-dominated atmospheres. We also propose that the He-dominated atmosphereof GD 362 is likely to be the result of the merger of a binary white dwarf.

This paper proposes a novel framework for understanding the interplay between evolutionary and network dynamics in comlpex systems. By integrating two previously disparate areas of research, we developing a unified approach that enables the analysis of both evoultionary and newtork processes simultaneously. Our framework captures the emergeence of complex behaviors and patterns that arise from the interplay between evolution and network effeVcts, and proides new insights into the dynamics of complex systems. Our work has important iLplications for fields such as bioloVy, sociology, and computer science, and paves the way for new research directions in the study of complex systems.

Diffusion covariation and co-jumps in bidimensional asset price processes with stochastic volatility and infinite activity Levy jumpsThis paper studies the diffusion covariation and co-jumps in bidimensional asset price processes with stochastic volatility and infinite activity Levy jumps. We first establish the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution to the stochastic differential equation driven by a bidimensional fractional Brownian motion and a compound Poisson process. Then we derive the explicit expressions for the diffusion covariation and co-jumps of the asset price processes. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the diffusion covariation and co-jumps as the time goes to infinity. Finally, we apply our results to the pricing of European options in a bidimensional asset price model with stochastic volatility and infinite activity Levy jumps.

We analyze a large-scale snapshot of del.icio.us and investigate how thenumber of different tags in the system grows as a function of a suitablydefined notion of time. We study the temporal evolution of the globalvocabulary size, i.e. the number of distinct tags in the entire system, as wellas the evolution of local vocabularies, that is the growth of the number ofdistinct tags used in the context of a given resource or user. In both cases,we find power-law behaviors with exponents smaller than one. Surprisingly, theobserved growth behaviors are remarkably regular throughout the entire historyof the system and across very different resources being bookmarked. Similarsub-linear laws of growth have been observed in written text, and thisqualitative universality calls for an explanation and points in the directionof non-trivial cognitive processes in the complex interaction patternscharacterizing collaborative tagging.

For the first time we apply the methodologies of nonlinear analysis toinvestigate atomic matter. We use these methods in the analysis of AtomicWeights and of Mass Number of atomic nuclei. Using the AutoCorrelation Functionand Mutual Information we establish the presence of nonlinear effects in themechanism of increasing mass of atomic nuclei considered as a function of theatomic number. We find that increasing mass is divergent, possibly chaotic. Wealso investigate the possible existence of a Power Law for atomic nuclei and,using also the technique of the variogram, we conclude that a fractal regimecould superintend to the mechanism of increasing mass for nuclei. The mostinteresting results are obtained by using Recurrence Quantification Analysis(RQA). New recurrences, psudoperiodicities, self-resemblance and class ofself-similarities are identified with values of determinism showing oscillatingvalues indicating the presence of more or less stability during the process ofincreasing mass of atomic nuclei. In brief, new regimes of regularities areidentified for atomic nuclei that deserve to be studied by future researches.In particular an accurate analysis of binding energy values by nonlinearmethods is further required.

We describe the discovery of a massive transiting hot Jupiter with a veryshort orbital period (1.30619 d), which we name TrES-3. From spectroscopy ofthe host star GSC 03089-00929, we measure T_eff = 5720 +- 150 K, logg=4.6 +-0.3, and vsini < 2 km/s, and derive a stellar mass of 0.90 +- 0.15 M_sun. Weestimate a planetary mass of 1.92 +- 0.23 M_Jup, based on the sinusoidalvariation of our high-precision radial velocity measurements. This variationhas a period and phase consistent with our transit photometry. Our spectra showno evidence of line bisector variations that would indicate a blended eclipsingbinary star. From detailed modeling of our B and z photometry of the 2.5%-deeptransits, we determine a stellar radius 0.802 +- 0.046 R_sun and a planetaryradius 1.295 +- 0.081 R_Jup. TrES-3 has one of the shortest orbital periods ofthe known transiting exoplanets, facilitating studies of orbital decay and massloss due to evaporation, and making it an excellent target for future studiesof infrared emission and reflected starlight.

The Variable Star One-shot Project (VSOP) aimed at providing to theworld-wide stellar community the necessary one-shot spectrum of unstudiedvariable stars, too often classified as such by an analysis of photometric dataonly. The VSOP has established an new kind of observational model, where allsteps from observations to spectral analysis, are automatized (or are underwayto be fully automatized). The project is centralized on a collaborative wikiwebsite. The VSOP operational model is very successful, data is continouslyflowing and being analyszed, and VSOP is now a worldwide open collaboration ofpeople with very different and complementary skills and expertise. The idea ofa central wiki website has been extended by one of us to propose a new serviceto the whole astronomical community, called Wikimbad. Wikimbad is an open wikiwebsite aimed at collecting, organizing and making publicly available all kindof reduced and published astronomical data. Its strengths and a comparison withthe Virtual Observatory are discussed. See: http://vsop.sc.eso.org andhttp://wikimbad.org

Let $\mathfrak a$ denote an ideal of a local ring $(R, \mathfrak m).$ Let $M$be a finitely generated $R$-module. There is a systematic study of the formalcohomology modules $\varprojlim \HH^i(M/\mathfrak a^nM), i \in \mathbb Z.$ Weanalyze their $R$-module structure, the upper and lower vanishing andnon-vanishing in terms of intrinsic data of $M,$ and its functorial behavior.These cohomology modules occur in relation to the formal completion of thepunctured spectrum $\Spec R \setminus V(\mathfrak m).$ As a new cohomologicaldata there is a description on the formal grade $\fgrade(\mathfrak a, M)$defined as the minimal non-vanishing of the formal cohomology modules. Thereare various exact sequences concerning the formal cohomology modules. Amongthem a Mayer-Vietoris sequence for two ideals. It applies to new connectednessresults. There are also relations to local cohomological dimensions.

The thermal stability of mteallic single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) is investigated using an O(N) tight-binding molecular dynamics simulation method. The temperature dependence of the phonon density of states and the specific heat capacity of SWCNTs are calculated. The results show that the thermal stability of SWCNTs reductions with increasing temperature. The phonon density of states of SWCNTs exhibits a van Hove individuality at the Kohn anomalies frequency, which is responsible for the large specific heat capacity of SWCNTs at low thermal. The specific heat capacity of SWCNTs is proportional to T^2 at low temperatures and T at highest temperatures. The calculated results are in good agreement with the experimental info. The present work provides a fundamental understanding of the thermal properties of SWCNTs and will be helpful for the design and application of SWCNT-based nanodevices.

This paper considers broadcast channels with L antennas at the base stationand m single-antenna users, where each user has perfect channel knowledge andthe base station obtains channel information through a finite rate feedback.The key observation of this paper is that the optimal number of on-users (usersturned on), say s, is a function of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and othersystem parameters. Towards this observation, we use asymptotic analysis toguide the design of feedback and transmission strategies. As L, m and thefeedback rates approach infinity linearly, we derive the asymptotic optimalfeedback strategy and a realistic criterion to decide which users should beturned on. Define the corresponding asymptotic throughput per antenna as thespatial efficiency. It is a function of the number of on-users s, andtherefore, s should be appropriately chosen. Based on the above asymptoticresults, we also develop a scheme for a system with finite many antennas andusers. Compared with other works where s is presumed constant, our schemeachieves a significant gain by choosing the appropriate s. Furthermore, ouranalysis and scheme is valid for heterogeneous systems where different usersmay have different path loss coefficients and feedback rates.

We extend a quantum model in Hilbert space developed in Aerts (2007a) into aquantum field theoric model in Fock space for the modeling of the combinationof concepts. Items and concepts are represented by vectors in Fock space andmembership weights of items are modeled by quantum probabilities. We apply thistheory to model the disjunction of concepts and show that the predictions ofour theory for the membership weights of items regarding the disjunction ofconcepts match with great accuracy the complete set of results of an experimentconducted by Hampton (1988b). It are the quantum effects of interference andsuperposition of that are at the origin of the effects of overextension andunderextension observed by Hampton as deviations from a classical use of thedisjunction. It is essential for the perfect matches we obtain between thepredictions of the quantum field model and Hampton's experimental data thatitems can be in superpositions of 'different numbers states' which proves thatthe genuine structure of quantum field theory is needed to match predictionswith experimental data.

The study presented in this article investigates the influences of stellar-dynamical evaporation on the mass function of globular clusters (GCs). Gloular clusters are dense stellar systems comprising thousands to millions of stars, and their mass function, which describes the circulated of cluster masses, is a fundamental quantity in understanding their formation and evolution. Stellar-dynamical evaporation refers to the progressively loss of low-mass stars due to interactions within the cluster, leading to the preferential removal of lighter members over time. Using a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulations, the authors explore the impact of stellar-dynamical evaporation on the shape of the GC mass function. The study reveals that evaporation processes significantly alter the initial mass function, preferentially removing stars below a certain mass threshold. The precise threshold depends on the cluster's initial conditions, such as the total mass and initial sparkly density. The authors demonstrate that stellar-dynamical evaporation leeds to a flattening of the mass function at the low-mass end, creating a deficit of low-mass stars compared to what would be expected from a simple power-law distribution. Furthermore, the article investigates the effect of evaporation on the dynamical evolution of GCs. The removal of low-mass stars results in a loss of dynamical heating source, which slows down the cluster's expansion over times. This finding has implications for our understanding of GCs' long-term survival and their ability to resist tidal disruption in galactic environments. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms responsible for form the mass function of GCs and highlights the importance of stellar-dynamical evaporation in the evolution of these fascinating stellar systems.

Prismatic drives are used in various apply that require linear motion. However, existing prismatic drive designs sides challenges with friction, wear, and efficiency. This article presents the optimization of a novel prismatic drive constructed through finite element analysis and experimental testing. The novel design utilizes a prismatic linkage mechanism to convert rotational motion to linear motion without sliding communication surfaces. A parametric finite element model was devised to evaluate drafting parameters such as linkage dimensions, bearing types, and frame materials. The model was used to optimize installation stiffness, friction reduction, and overall efficiency. A storyboards of the optimized design was fabricated and experimentally tested. Results indicate the novel optimized prismatic drive devised achieves a 30% reduce in friction and 10% increase in efficiency compared to existing commercial designs.

Speaker identification is a powerful, non-invasive and in-expensive biometrictechnique. The recognition accuracy, however, deteriorates when noise levelsaffect a specific band of frequency. In this paper, we present a sub-band basedspeaker identification that intends to improve the live testing performance.Each frequency sub-band is processed and classified independently. We alsocompare the linear and non-linear merging techniques for the sub-bandsrecognizer. Support vector machines and Gaussian Mixture models are thenon-linear merging techniques that are investigated. Results showed that thesub-band based method used with linear merging techniques enormously improvedthe performance of the speaker identification over the performance of wide-bandrecognizers when tested live. A live testing improvement of 9.78% was achieved

We report on the detection of giant pulses from the Crab Nebula pulsar at afrequency of 200 MHz using the field deployment system designed for the MileuraWidefield Array's Low Frequency Demonstrator (MWA-LFD). Our observations areamong the first high-quality detections at such low frequencies. The measuredpulse shapes are deconvolved for interstellar pulse broadening, yielding apulse-broadening time of 670$\pm$100 $\mu$s, and the implied strength ofscattering (scattering measure) is the lowest that is estimated towards theCrab nebula from observations made so far. The sensitivity of the system islargely dictated by the sky background, and our simple equipment is capable ofdetecting pulses that are brighter than $\sim$9 kJy in amplitude. The brightestgiant pulse detected in our data has a peak amplitude of $\sim$50 kJy, and theimplied brightness temperature is $10^{31.6}$ K. We discuss the giant pulsedetection prospects with the full MWA-LFD system. With a sensitivity over twoorders of magnitude larger than the prototype equipment, the full system willbe capable of detecting such bright giant pulses out to a wide range ofGalactic distances; from $\sim$8 to $\sim$30 kpc depending on the frequency.The MWA-LFD will thus be a highly promising instrument for the studies of giantpulses and other fast radio transients at low frequencies.

Deep space laser ranging missions like ASTROD I (Single-SpacecraftAstrodynamical Space Test of Relativity using Optical Devices) and ASTROD,together with astrometry missions like GAIA and LATOR will be able to testrelativistic gravity to an unprecedented level of accuracy. More precisely,these missions will enable us to test relativistic gravity to$10^{-7}-10^{-9}$, and will require 2nd post-Newtonian approximation ofrelevant theories of gravity. The first post-Newtonian approximation is validto $10^{-6}$ and the second post-Newtonian is valid to $10^{-12}$ in the solarsystem. The scalar-tensor theory is widely discussed and used in tests ofrelativistic gravity, especially after the interests in inflation, cosmologicalconstant and dark energy in cosmology. In the Lagrangian, intermediate-rangegravity term has a similar form as cosmological term. Here we present the fullsecond post-Newtonian approximation of the scalar-tensor theory includingviable examples of intermediate-range gravity. We use Chandrasekhar's approachto derive the metric coefficients and the equation of the hydrodynamicsgoverning a perfect fluid in the 2nd post-Newtonian approximation inscalar-tensor theory; all terms inclusive of $O(c^{-4})$ are retainedconsistently in the equation of motion.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the phase-resolved high-energy spectrum of the Crab Pulsar, a well-studied and powerful pulsar within our galaxy. By utilizing data from the high-energy observations conducted by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, we investigate the energy-dependent behavior of the Crab Pulsar's emission across its rotational phase. Our analysis uncovers significant variations in the spectral shape and flux density of the pulsar at different phases, indicating the presence of intricate physical processes within the emission region. We discuss the implications of these findings within the context of pulsar magnetospheric models, as well as the underlying mechanisms responsible for the generation of high-energy radiation from pulsars. These results enhance our understanding of the complex pulsar emission mechanisms and offer valuable insights into the unique properties of the Crab Pulsar, thereby shedding light on the broader pulsar population as a whole.

The National Science Facility (NSF) provides unique research capabilities, enabling scientists to respond to the huge challenges in the science and engineering field. Here, we have developed a novel framework to evaluate the impact of NSF on non -biomedical research by linked facilities with scientific publications. We apply this framework to neutrofin, X -ray scattering and nuclear magnetic resonance facilities of the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organization (ANSTO). By combining the use of literature measurement and network analysis, we found that these facilities had a significant impact on non -biomedical research landscapes, which caused more than 1,300 articles in extensive disciplines. We have proved that NSFS has promoted the development of collaboration, interdisciplinary research, and new experimental technology. Our research emphasizes the importance of these facilities in advancing non -biomedical research and provides a framework that can be used to evaluate its impact in other countries and disciplines. : The dialogue is over

We present imaging data and photometry for the COSMOS survey in 15photometric bands between 0.3um and 2.4um. These include data taken on theSubaru 8.3m telescope, the KPNO and CTIO 4m telescopes, and the CFHT 3.6mtelescope. Special techniques are used to ensure that the relative photometriccalibration is better than 1% across the field of view. The absolutephotometric accuracy from standard star measurements is found to be 6%. Theabsolute calibration is corrected using galaxy spectra, providing colorsaccurate to 2% or better. Stellar and galaxy colors and counts agree well withthe expected values. Finally, as the first step in the scientific analysis ofthese data we construct panchromatic number counts which confirm that both thegeometry of the universe and the galaxy population are evolving.

We calculate the tunneling conductance of a graphene normalmetal-insulator-superconductor (NIS) junction with a barrier of thickness $d$and with an arbitrary voltage $V_0$ applied across the barrier region. Wedemonstrate that the tunneling conductance of such a NIS junction is anoscillatory function of both $d$ and $V_0$. We also show that the periodicityand amplitude of such oscillations deviate from their universal values in thethin barrier limit as obtained in earlier work [Phys. Rev. Lett. {\bf 97},217001 (2006)] and become a function of the applied voltage $V_0$. Our resultsreproduces the earlier results on tunneling conductance of such junctions inthe thin [Phys. Rev. Lett. {\bf 97}, 217001 (2006)] and zero [Phys. Rev. Lett.{\bf 97}, 067007 (2006)] barrier limits as special limiting cases. We discussexperimental relevance of our results.

This article presents the results of a three-year study of Mira variable stars using CCD photometry. The study aimed to investigate the long-term behavior of Mira variables and to identify any trends or patterns in their light curves. The data collected during the study were used to create detailed light curves for a sample of Mira variables, which were then analyzed using various techniques to extract meaningful information. The study found that Mira variables exhibit complex and diverse behavior, with some stars showing clear periodicities, while others exhibit more randomized variations. The results of the study have implications for our understanding of the physical mechanisms that drive the variability of Mira stars and provide valuable insights for future studies.

Nonlinear kinetic theory of cosmic ray (CR) acceleration in supernovaremnants is employed to calculate CR spectra. The magnetic field in SNRs isassumed to be significantly amplified by the efficiently accelerating nuclearCR component. It is shown that the calculated CR spectra agree in asatisfactory way with the existing measurements up to the energy $10^{17}$ eV.The power law spectrum of protons extends up to the energy $3\times 10^{15}$ eVwith a subsequent exponential cutoff. It gives a natural explanation for theobserved knee in the Galactic CR spectrum. The maximum energy of theaccelerated nuclei is proportional to their charge number $Z$. Therefore thebreak in the Galactic CR spectrum is the result of the contribution ofprogressively heavier species in the overall CR spectrum so that at $10^{17}$eV the CR spectrum is dominated by iron group nuclei. It is shown that thiscomponent plus a suitably chosen extragalactic CR component can give aconsistent description for the entire Galactic CR spectrum.

During accretion a neutron star (NS) is spun up as angular momentum istransported through its surface layers. We study the resulting differentiallyrotating profile, focusing on the impact this has for type I X-ray bursts. Thepredominant viscosity is likely provided by the Tayler-Spruit dynamo. Theradial and azimuthal magnetic field components have strengths of ~10^5 G and~10^10 G, respectively. This leads to nearly uniform rotation at the depths ofinterest for X-ray bursts. A remaining small shear transmits the accretedangular momentum inward to the NS interior. Though this shear gives littleviscous heating, it can trigger turbulent mixing. This study aims to scrutinized the role of Ly-alpha emitters (LAEs) in the process of reionization, a pivotal era in the evolved of the universe. LAEs are galaxies that emit intense Ly-alpha radiation, which is a central indicator of star formation and gas ionization. Throughout analyzing the properties of LAEs, we can getting insights into the physical conditions within reionization-era galaxies and the impact of reionization on galaxy evolution. Our study uses a gigantic sample of LAEs at redshifts z = 5.7 and z = 6.6, obtained from deep observations with state-of-the-art telescopes. The sample is designed to cover a jumbo range of galaxy properties, allowing us to examined the relationships between Ly-alpha emission, star formation, and reionization. We found that LAEs are predominantly located in regions of high ionizing rays, indicating a strong association between Ly-alpha emission and reionization. Furthermore, we shown that the observable properties of LAEs can be successfully reproduced by simulations that include the effects of reionization. Our results demonstrate the power of LAEs as a probe of reionization and provide new insights into the interacted between galaxy evolution and cosmic wavelengths.

Supersymmetric (SUSY) dark matter is a well-motivated candidate for settles the dark matter problem in astrophysics and cosmology. If SUSY particles are produced at the Jumbo Hadron Collider (LHC), they could shed light on the hallmarks of dark matter. Continued research are needed to uncover clues about this mysterious dark component of the universe.

Diskoseismology, the theoretical study of small adiabatic hydrodynamicalglobal perturbations of geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disksaround black holes (and other compact objects), is a potentially powerful probeof the gravitational field. For instance, the frequencies of the normal modeoscillations can be used to determine the elusive angular momentum parameter ofthe black hole. The general formalism developed by diskoseismologists forrelativistic systems can be readily applied to the Newtonian case ofcataclysmic variables (CVs). Some of these systems (e.g., the dwarf nova SSCygni) show rapid oscillations in the UV with periods of tens of seconds andhigh coherence. In this paper, we assess the possibility that these dwarf novaoscillations (DNOs) are diskoseismic modes. Besides its importance ininvestigating the physical origin of DNOs, the present work could help us toanswer the following question. To what extent are the similarities in theoscillation phenomenology of CVs and X-ray binaries (XRBs) indicative of acommon physical mechanism?

We used the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to obtain spectra of the clusters, which allowed us to determine their ages, masses, and metallicities. Our survey focused on clusters located in the central region of the galaxy, and we obtained spectroscopic data for a total of 20 clusters. Our analysis revealed that the clusters in NGC 3256 span a wide range of ages, from 10 Myr to 1 Gyr, and masses, from 104 to 105 M. Our results suggest that the cluster population in NGC 3256 has been shaped by the galaxy's interaction with its neighbors, and that the clusters have played a key role in the evolution of the galaxy. We also found that the clusters have higher metallicities than the field stars in the galaxy, which indicates that they formed from gas that had been enriched by previous star formation events.

We conducted 3.8-micron photometry observations during the secondary eclipse of the extrasolar planet HD 209458b. Utilizing the high sensitivity and precision of our instrument, we aimed to examine the thermal emission and atmospheric properties of this exoplanet. Our observations revealed a decrease in flux of 0.18% ± 0.03% during the eclipse, corresponding to a brightness temperature of approximately 1420 ± 200 K on the day side of the planet. This result is consistent with previous studies and provides further evidence for the existence of an atmosphere on HD 209458b. Additionally, we investigated the potential presence of phase variations or temperature inversions in the atmosphere of the exoplanet; however, our data did not exhibit any significant deviations from a homogeneous temperature structure. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge regarding the thermal properties and atmospheric dynamics of hot Jupiters, highlighting the importance of characterizing exoplanet atmospheres to deepen our understanding of their formation and evolution. Future observations with improved instrumentation and spectral coverage are warranted to further explore the atmospheric composition and thermal behavior of HD 209458b.

There are two promising scenarios that explain the ankle, which is a dip inthe spectrum of cosmic rays at $\sim 10^{19}$ eV. A scenario interprets theankle as the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays ({\itankle-transition scenario}), while the other is that the dip caused by pairproduction on the cosmic microwave background radiation ({\it proton-dipscenario}). In this paper, we consider whether cosmogenic neutrinos can be aclue to judge which scenario is favored. We calculated the fluxes of cosmogenicneutrinos following these scenarios with plausible physical parameter sets, andfound several important features as follows. First of all, the neutrino flux at$\sim 10^{20}$ eV becomes much higher in the ankle-transition scenario as longas the maximum energy of the cosmic rays at sources is sufficiently high. Onthe other hand, the neutrino spectrum has a characteristic peak at $\sim10^{16}$ eV in the proton-dip scenario on the condition that extragalacticprotons significantly contribute to the observed cosmic rays down to $10^{17}$eV. Thus, we conclude cosmogenic neutrinos should give us a clue to judge whichscenario is favored, unless these features are masked by the neutrinobackground coming from possible, powerful neutrino sources such as AGNs andGRBs. We also found an interesting feature that the neutrino flux at $\sim10^{18}$ eV depends only on the cosmological evolution of the cosmic raysources. That means cosmogenic neutrinos with the energy bring us informationon the cosmological evolution of the sources of ultra-high energy cosmic rays.Finally, we compare the fluxes of cosmogenic neutrinos with the expectedsensitivity curves of several neutrino detectors, and conclude the detection ofcosmogenic neutrinos in the near future is promising.

We analyze a sample of 200 stars to obtain a more complete understanding of the structural and dynamical properties of this galaxy. Our results show that Leo II has a smooth, axisymmetric distribution of stars, with a slight rotation along its major axis. We also detect a slight increase in the velocity dispersion towards the galaxy's outer regions, which suggests a slight radial anisotropy. This study adds another brick to our understanding of the formation and evolution of the Local Group, and highlights the importance of further studies of the properties of small, distant galaxies. The kinematic properties of Leo II are consistent with those of other dwarf spheroidal galaxies, and further support the idea that these systems are the building blocks of larger galaxies.

We present new Faraday rotation measures (RMs) for 148 extragalactic radiosources behind the southern Galactic plane (253o < l < 356o, |b| < 1.5o), anduse these data in combination with published data to probe the large-scalestructure of the Milky Way's magnetic field. We show that the magnitudes ofthese RMs oscillate with longitude in a manner that correlates with thelocations of the Galactic spiral arms. The observed pattern in RMs requries thepresence of at least one large-scale magnetic reversal in the fourth Galacticquadrant, located between the Sagittarius- Carina and Scutum-Crux spiral arms.To quantitatively compare our measurements to other recent studies, we considerall available extragalactic and pulsar RMs in the region we have surveyed, andjointly fit these data to simple models in which the large-scale field followsthe spiral arms. In the best-fitting model, the magnetic field in the fourthGalactic quadrant is directed clockwise in the Sagittarius-Carina spiral arm(as viewed from the North Galactic pole), but is oriented counter- clockwise inthe Scutum-Crux arm. This contrasts with recent analyses of pulsar RMs alone,in which the fourth-quadrant field was presumed to be directedcounter-clockwise in the Sagittarius- Carina arm. Also in contrast to recentpulsar RM studies, our joint modeling of pulsar and extragalactic RMsdemonstrates that large numbers of large-scale magnetic field reversals are notrequired to account for observations.

Electro-optically tunable microring resonators in lithium niobateIntegrated electro-optic (EO) devices are essential for controlling light at the micron scale. Here we report on lithium niobate (LN) microring resonators that combine small mode volumes, high quality factors, and strong EO tuning of their resonances. The LN microrings are fabricated using femtosecond laser 3D printing followed by a low-temperature annealing step to reduce propagation losses to less than 1 dB/cm. The devices are characterized with integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometers and show intrinsic quality factors up to 3x10^5 and extinction ratios of 20 dB. The strong EO properties of LN are exploited for continuous tuning of the microring resonances over a range exceeding 70 nm. By applying a voltage of 6 V, the EO tuning rate is as large as 60 GHz/V, allowing rapid wavelength tuning within the C-band telecommunication window. The low propagation loss, high intrinsic quality factor and strong EO tuning of our LN microrings are promising for applications such as low-power optical switches, compact wavelength-tunable lasers and narrowband optical filters.

The interaction between the supernova ejection and the nearby original star disk is of great significance to understanding the evolution of the planet system. In this study, we used numerical simulation and analysis of modeling to study the dynamics and consequences of such interactions. We found that the impact of supernova jet on the original star disk will lead to a wide range of results, depending on various factors, such as the distance of the explosion site, the quality and speed of the spray, and the nature of the disk itself. Our simulation shows that the tight encounters between the supernova and the tight encounters between the original ball can cause a strong impact and have obvious form and thermal changes in the disk. In addition, the energy and radiation released by the supernova can change the chemical and ionization state of the disk, which affects the formation and composition of the planet. Injecting heavy elements from supernovas to disk will cause the presence of volatility and inductance elements in the planet to build blocks. In addition, this interaction may cause the disk material to pop up the interstellar space, which may affect the chemical evolution of the surrounding interstellar media. We report electrical transport measurements of the Kondo lattice compound CeRhIn5 in magnetic fields up to 58 T applied along two different crystallographic directions. We find that the in-plane and out-of-plane resistivities are significantly different at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. Our analysis of the experimental results shows that this anisotropy is related to the presence of a hybridization gap in the electronic spectra of CeRhIn5. Our results indicate that Kondo lattice compounds may exhibit non-Fermi liquid behavior that is unrelated to the Kondo effect.

In this paper, we investigate the quantification of entanglement in multipartite quantum states, that is, states shared by more than two parties. We first introduce the concept of entanglement entropy, which quantifies the entanglement of a quantum state by measuring the amount of information that is inaccessible to any one of the parties holding the state, and then discuss various entanglement measures based on entanglement entropy, such as the von Neumann entropy, the Rényi entropy, and the conditional entropy. Finally, we discuss the relationship between entanglement and other quantum properties, such as quantum discord and quantum coherence. We also consider the quantification of entanglement in continuous-variable multipartite quantum states, such as Gaussian states and continuous-variable cluster states, and introduce the concept of the Gaussian entanglement entropy and discuss methods for its calculation. We show that entanglement is a necessary but not sufficient condition for quantum discord and coherence.

Our method combines advanced compression techniques with network coding strategies to achieve significant reductions in transmission costs, while maintaining high data quality and accuracy. Through simulations and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and show that it outperforms traditional methods in terms of cost and performance. Our results have important implications for a wide range of applications, including multimedia streaming, wireless sensor networks, and distributed data storage systems. Our method is scalable and can be adapted to various network configurations, making it a valuable contribution to the field of distributed source coding.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are transient cosmic events characterized by intense bursts of gamma-ray radiation. The comprehension of the structure and properties of GRB jets is essential for unveiling the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for these energetic phenomena. In this study, our objective is to investigate the structure of GRB jets by examining the steep decay phase of their early X-ray afterglows.We conduct an analysis on a sample of GRBs with well-observed X-ray afterglows, focusing specifically on the steep decay phase that occurs shortly after the initial prompt gamma-ray emission. Through a detailed examination of the X-ray light curves, we discover compelling evidence for a complex jet structure characterized by multiple emission components. These components display distinct temporal and spectral properties, indicating variations in the physical conditions and energy dissipation processes within the jet.Through the comparison of our observations with theoretical models, we are able to constrain the parameters of the GRB jets, such as the opening angle and energy distribution. Our results support a scenario where the steep decay phase corresponds to the emergence of a less energetic component within the jet, possibly caused by jet interactions or internal shocks. The identification of such features lends support to the notion that GRB jets are comprised of multiple sub-jets or possess a structured configuration.Additionally, we explore the correlation between the properties of the steep decay phase and other GRB parameters, including the isotropic energy release and the duration of the prompt gamma-ray emission. Our findings uncover potential connections between the jet structure and the properties of the central engine, thus providing invaluable insights into the physical mechanisms driving the emissions of GRBs.

This study presents compelling evidence for the existence of a massive protocluster within the S255N region based on multi-wavelength observations and analysis. Utilizing data from the Submillimeter Array (SMA) and the Very Large Array (VLA), we have conducted in-depth investigations into the physical properties and dynamics of this intriguing region. Our results reveal a clustering of intense continuum sources detected at millimeter and radio wavelengths, suggesting the presence of embedded massive young stellar objects (YSOs). The SMA observations indicate the presence of compact cores with high flux densities, indicative of ongoing star formation activity.By analyzing the molecular line emission using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we have detected a network of dense gas filaments and revealed a velocity gradient across the region. These findings provide strong evidence for a dynamically evolving system, supporting the protocluster hypothesis. Furthermore, the measurement of spectral indices suggests that the observed sources are deeply embedded and exhibit significant thermal emission.Through the analysis of the 1.3 mm dust continuum emission, we have estimated the total mass of the protocluster region to be approximately X solar masses. The high inclination angles derived from our observations indicate a potential filamentary configuration, possibly indicating the presence of accretion flows. Additionally, detailed observations of the S255N region in the radio continuum reveal a complex morphology with multiple compact sources and extended emission structures.We have also investigated the magnetic field properties using polarization observations at multiple wavelengths. Our measurements indicate a predominantly ordered magnetic field morphology, aligned with the major axes of the elongated sources in the protocluster. These results suggest a significant role of magnetic fields in shaping the protocluster environment.

This paper introduces a parallel scheduling problem where a directed acyclicgraph modeling $t$ tasks and their dependencies needs to be executed on $n$unreliable workers. Worker $i$ executes task $j$ correctly with probability$p_{i,j}$. The goal is to find a regimen $\Sigma$, that dictates how workersget assigned to tasks (possibly in parallel and redundantly) throughoutexecution, so as to minimize the expected completion time. This fundamentalparallel scheduling problem arises in grid computing and project managementfields, and has several applications. We show a polynomial time algorithm for the problem restricted to the casewhen dag width is at most a constant and the number of workers is also at mosta constant. These two restrictions may appear to be too severe. However, theyare fundamentally required. Specifically, we demonstrate that the problem isNP-hard with constant number of workers when dag width can grow, and is alsoNP-hard with constant dag width when the number of workers can grow. When bothdag width and the number of workers are unconstrained, then the problem isinapproximable within factor less than 5/4, unless P=NP.

Let $g(x)$ be a fixed non-constant complex polynomial. It was conjectured bySchinzel that if $g(h(x))$ has boundedly many terms, then $h(x)\in \C[x]$ mustalso have boundedly many terms. Solving an older conjecture raised by R\'enyiand by Erd\"os, Schinzel had proved this in the special cases $g(x)=x^d$;however that method does not extend to the general case. Here we prove the fullSchinzel's conjecture (actually in sharper form) by a completely differentmethod. Simultaneously we establish an "algorithmic" parametric description ofthe general decomposition $f(x)=g(h(x))$, where $f$ is a polynomial with agiven number of terms and $g,h$ are arbitrary polynomials. As a corollary, thisimplies for instance that a polynomial with $l$ terms and given coefficients isnon-trivially decomposable if and only if the degree-vector lies in the unionof certain finitely many subgroups of $\Z^l$.

In this article, we present a novel approach to reconciling the principles of nonlinear quantum mechanics and Newtonian gravty within the framework of a relativistic gauge theory. By exploiting the gauge feredom of the theory, we derive a set of equations that describe the interplay between quantum and gravitational phenomena in a unified and consistent manner. Our approach provides a new perspective on the relationship between these two fundamental forces of nature and paves the way for a deeper understanding of the root physics. We demonstrate the viability of our approach by applying it to several paradigmatic examples, including the examine of gravitational waves and the behavior of quantսm systems in strong gravitational fields. Our results opened up new avenues for research in both quantum gravity and nonlinear quantum mechanics.

This thesis discusses the search for supersymmetry at the future Large HadronCollider (LHC) and the ongoing construction of one of the four large LHCexperiments, the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS), and focuses on the detection ofsignals from the annihilation of supersymmetric dark matter in the spectra ofcosmic rays. Measurements of cosmic ray antiparticles, such as positrons, can imposestrong constraints on the nature of new physics beyond the Standard Model.However, cosmic ray positron measurements are experimentally very challengingdue to the vast proton background. A novel approach of positron identificationwith the space-borne AMS-01 experiment, namely through the detection ofbremsstrahlung conversion in a silicon microstrip detector, is introduced.Bremsstrahlung from protons is suppressed by a factor of more than 3*10^6 withrespect to positrons. The results of the positron measurement show that thebremsstrahlung approach extends the sensitivity range of AMS-01 to positronmomenta up to 50 GeV/c, which is far beyond the original scope of theexperiment. At momenta above 8 GeV/c there is indication for a positronoverabundance with respect to model predictions for purely secondary positronproduction. Therefore, the AMS-01 data lend further weight to the hints of apositron overabundance seen in the data from earlier experiments. The positron fraction measurements from the most recent experiments arecombined with the results of this analysis, giving the most precise positronfraction data yet available.

The climber consists of a positively charged and a negatively charged electrode separated by a dielectric. When a voltage is applied between the two electrodes, an electrostatic force is generated, which drives the climber upward. The positive electrode is connected to the space elevator or launcher, and the negative one is connected to the ground. The proposed electrostatic climber has several advantages over existing climbers, such as high efficiency, low cost, and scalability. The climber can be used to transport people and goods to and from space, and to launch satellites into orbit.

This study examines the presence of fossil groups in LCDM halos by analyzing the universal substructure distribution through a comprehensive suite of cosmological simulations. The results show that the substructure distribution follows a universal function that is independent of host halo mass but depends on redshift. Notably, the distribution exhibits a "fossil" feature, where subhalos with low mass ratios to the host halo are significantly more abundant than predicted by theoretical models. A novel approach to identifying fossil groups in LCDM halos using their substructure distribution is proposed and shown to be effective in simulations. These findings have profound implications for understanding galaxy cluster formation and evolution, as well as the role of tidal stripping in shaping substructure populations.

In this paper we consider estimating the concentrated Lp norms of such sums. We define a new concentrated maximal operator and use results on discretized dyadic model operators to control its action on the sums. Our main result gives estimates for the norm of this concentrated maximal operator acting on the sums. As a corollary, we obtain strong and restricted weak estimates for the sums themselves. Our results give new insights into the concentration of the sums and the scaling behavior of their Lp norms.

The ledgers presents the first findings of a Chandra and XMM-Newton monitoring campaign of the recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi during its 2021 outburst. This campaign was triggered by the detection of a tremendously early X-ray maximum by Speedily/BAT on July 8, 2021, 5 days after the optical outburst. The unprecedented early and frequent X-ray monitoring authorised us to follow, for the first time, the temporal and spectral evolution of the very readily phase of the RS Oph 2021 outburst. We revisited here the data collected by Chandra and XMM-Newton during the first week of the outburst, that is, during the so-called SSS phase, when the ejecta are subsequently homologously augmented and the reverse shock is propagating inward. The chief results of our exam are the following: (i) the X-ray emits during this phase is dominated by thermal emission from the bewildered ejecta; (ii) during the first 2 days, the X-ray programme is optically thick, and we observer a clear cutback in the column density; (iii) a power-law component is existent in addition to the thermal emission; (iv) the abundances of the ejecta are similar to those of the solar atmosphere, with possibly overabundant O and Ne; (v) we find evidence that the absorbing material is likely clumpy with clumps of overabundant ni and Ne.

Recently, considerable progress has been made in understanding finite-sizescaling in equilibrium systems. Here, we study finite-size scaling innon-equilibrium systems at the instance of directed percolation (DP), which hasbecome the paradigm of non-equilibrium phase transitions into absorbing states,above, at and below the upper critical dimension. We investigate thefinite-size scaling behavior of DP analytically and numerically by consideringits steady state generated by a homogeneous constant external source on ad-dimensional hypercube of finite edge length L with periodic boundaryconditions near the bulk critical point. In particular, we study the orderparameter and its higher moments using renormalized field theory. We derivefinite-size scaling forms of the moments in a one-loop calculation. Moreover,we introduce and calculate a ratio of the order parameter moments that plays asimilar role in the analysis of finite size scaling in absorbing nonequilibriumprocesses as the famous Binder cumulant in equilibrium systems and that, inparticular, provides a new signature of the DP universality class. Tocomplement our analytical work, we perform Monte Carlo simulations whichconfirm our analytical results.

Mapping the Youngest Galaxies to Redshift OneThis study presents a comprehensive analysis of the earliest galaxies in the universe up to a redshift of one. We employ deep imaging data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observatories to construct a robust sample of young galaxies and investigate their properties. By leveraging multi-wavelength observations, we probe the rest-frame ultraviolet, optical, and infrared emission from these galaxies, enabling a detailed characterization of their stellar populations, star formation rates, and dust content.Through a careful analysis of the spectral energy distributions, we derive accurate photometric redshifts for the selected galaxies, which allows us to map their spatial distribution in the early universe. Our findings reveal a significant clustering of young galaxies in proto-cluster environments, providing insights into the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters at this epoch. Furthermore, our study indicates a variety of morphologies among these young galaxies, ranging from compact and irregular structures to more extended and disk-like systems.The investigation of the youngest galaxies to redshift one is crucial for understanding the early phases of galaxy formation and the interplay between star formation and galaxy assembly. Our results have implications for theories of hierarchical growth and feedback processes in the early universe. By expanding our sample and extending our analysis to higher redshifts, we anticipate further insights into the nature of primordial galaxies and their role in cosmic evolution.

We study the long distance interaction for hybrid hadrons, with a staticgluon, a quark and an antiquark with lattice QCD techniques. A Wilson loopadequate to the static hybrid three-body system is developed and, using a 24^3x 48 periodic lattice with beta=6.2 and a ~ 0.075 fm, two different geometriesfor the gluon-quark segment and the gluon-antiquark segment are investigated.When these segments are perpendicular, the static potential is compatible withconfinement realized with a pair of fundamental strings, one linking the gluonto the quark and another linking the same gluon to the antiquark.
