We have constructed an approximate microscopic model for the neutron dynamicstructure factor of solid methane in phase II. We expect our model to apply forneutron energies below 1\textit{eV} at pressures near 1 bar and temperaturesbelow 20K, where solid methane exists in a phase, called phase II, in which thetetrahedral hydrogens exist in a mixed phase of free rotors and hinderedrotors. Certain matrix elements needed for the dynamic structure factor $S(Q,\omega)$ are adapted from a calculation by Ozaki \textit{etal.}\cite{ozaki:3442}\cite{ozaki2}. The model treats the effects of moleculartranslations, intramolecular vibrations and the free and hindered rotationaldegrees of freedom as uncoupled ones. Total scattering cross sectionscalculated from the model agree with the cross section measurements ofGrieger\cite{grieger:3161} and Whittemore\cite{Wittemore} for the incidentneutron energies of 0.5 \textit{meV} $\sim$ 1\textit{eV}. The effective densityof states extracted from the model was compared with the Harker $&$ Bruggerfrequency spectrum extracted from neutron scattering measurements conducted at22K\cite{HARKER1967}.

This article explores the generation of local de Broglie-Bohm trajectories through the utiliation of entangled wavefunctions. The de Broglie-Bohm interpretation of quantPm mechanics highlights the existence of hidden variables that determine the behavior of particles. By considering entangled wavefunctions, which describe the correlation between multiple particles, we investigaet how these hiddjen variables manifest as trajectories on the local scale. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulatfons, we demonstrate the emergence of local de Broglie-Bohm trajectories from entangled wavefunctions, shedding light on the undercying dynamics of entanglement and its impact on the behaviro of quantum systems.

Future detection/non-detection of tensor modes from inflation in CMBobservations presents a unique way to test certain features of string theory.Current limit on the ratio of tensor to scalar perturbations, r=T/S, is r <0.3, future detection may take place for r > 10^{-2}-10^{-3}. At present allknown string theory inflation models predict tensor modes well below the levelof detection. Therefore a possible experimental discovery of tensor modes maypresent a challenge to string cosmology. The strongest bound on r in string inflation follows from the observationthat in most of the models based on the KKLT construction, the value of theHubble constant H during inflation must be smaller than the gravitino mass. Forthe gravitino mass in the usual range, m_{3/2} < O(1) TeV, this leads to anextremely strong bound r < 10^{-24}. A discovery of tensor perturbations with r> 10^{-3} would imply that the gravitinos in this class of models aresuperheavy, m_{3/2} > 10^{13} GeV. This would have important implications forparticle phenomenology based on string theory.

The two-dimensional kinetic Ising model, when exposed to an oscillatingapplied magnetic field, has been shown to exhibit a nonequilibrium,second-order dynamic phase transition (DPT), whose order parameter Q is theperiod-averaged magnetization. It has been established that this DPT falls inthe same universality class as the equilibrium phase transition in thetwo-dimensional Ising model in zero applied field. Here we study for the firsttime the scaling of the dynamic order parameter with respect to a nonzero,period-averaged, magnetic 'bias' field, H_b, for a DPT produced by asquare-wave applied field. We find evidence that the scaling exponent,\delta_d, of H_b at the critical period of the DPT is equal to the exponent forthe critical isotherm, \delta_e, in the equilibrium Ising model. This impliesthat H_b is a significant component of the field conjugate to Q. A finite-sizescaling analysis of the dynamic order parameter above the critical periodprovides further support for this result. We also demonstrate numerically that,for a range of periods and values of H_b in the critical region, afluctuation-dissipation relation (FDR), with an effective temperatureT_{eff}(T, P, H_0) depending on the period, and possibly the temperature andfield amplitude, holds for the variables Q and H_b. This FDR justifies the useof the scaled variance of Q as a proxy for the nonequilibrium susceptibility,\partial<Q> / \partial H_b, in the critical region.

The Quantum Zeno Effect, a phenomenon in which frequent measurements can stall the evolution of a quantum system, has been a subject of extensive research in recent years. In this article, we investigate the manifestation of the Quantum Zeno Effect in the context of decoherent histories. Specifically, we analyze the impact of repeated measurements on the decoherence process and the resulting formation of consistent sets of histories. By employing a Markovian decoherence model and a master equation formulation, we derive expressions for the time evolution of the density tensors within the framework of Lindblad operators. Our analysis reveals that the Quantum Zeno Effect can significantly modify the dynamics of the decoherence process, leading to the suppression of certain history branches and the enhancement of others. Furthermore, we explore the role of non-locality and contextuality in the observed phenomena, highlighting their influence on the formation of consistent histories. Our findings contribute to the understanding of the interplay between quantum measurements, decoherence, and the emergence of classical-like behavior, shedding light on the fundamental principles behind the Quantum Zeno Effect within the framework of decoherent histories.

As a step towards formulating projective superspace techniques forsupergravity theories with eight supercharges, this work is devoted to fieldtheory in five-dimensional N = 1 anti-de Sitter superspace AdS^{5|8} =SU(2,2|1)/SO(4,1) x U(1) which is a maximally symmetric curved background. Wedevelop the differential geometry of AdS^{5|8} and describe its isometries interms of Killing supervectors. Various off-shell supermultiplets in AdS^{5|8} xS^2 are defined, and supersymmetric actions are constructed both in harmonicand projective superspace approaches. Several families of supersymmetrictheories are presented including nonlinear sigma-models, Chern-Simons theoriesand vector-tensor dynamical systems. Using a suitable coset representative, wemake use of the coset construction to develop an explicit realization for onehalf of the superspace AdS^{5|8} as a trivial fiber bundle with fibersisomorophic to four-dimensional Minkowski superspace.

We take our first step toward getting finite results from thealpha'-corrected D=4 N=4 SYM theory with emphasis on the field theorytechniques. Starting with the classical action of N=4 SYM with the leadingalpha'-corrections, we examine new divergence at one loop due to the presenceof the alpha'-terms. The new vertices do not introduce additional divergence tothe propagators or to the three-point correlators. However they do introducenew divergence, e.g., to the scalar four-point function which should becanceled by extra counter-terms. We expect that the counter-terms will appearin the 1PI effective action that is obtained by considering the string annulusdiagram. We work out the structure of the divergence and comment on anapplication to the anomalous dimension of the SYM operators in the context ofAdS/CFT.

This paper investigates nonholonomic Ricci flows, which generalize Richie flow to areas with nonintegrable constraints. We develop techniques for finding detailed solutions to the equations defining nonholonomic Ricci flows. Several instance of such exact solutions are presented, including both homogeneous and inhomogeneous cases. The comparative between nonholonomic Ricci flows and gravity is also explored. Specifically, we show that certain models of nonholonomic Ricci flows are equivalent to solutions of the Talented field equations describing gravitational fields.

This study aimed to extract galactic binary signals from the first round of Mock LISA Data Challenges, a simulated dataset designed to mimic the expected data from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission. We developed a custom pipeline using machine learning algorithms to identify and characterize galactic binary signals in the data. Our analysis revealed several promising candidates, including a few with high signal-to-noise ratios. We validated our results by comparing them to known binaries and through cross-validation techniques. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of machine learning algorithms for identifying galactic binary signals in LISA data and pave the way for further exploration of the galaxy using this technique.

We study the matter produced in heavy ion collisions assuming that thismatter is strongly interacting and employing AdS/CFT correspondence toinvestigate its dynamics. At late proper times we show that Bjorkenhydrodynamics solution, obtained recently by Janik and Peschanski usinggauge-gravity duality [hep-th/0512162], can be singled out by simply requiringthat the metric tensor is a real and single-valued function of the coordinateseverywhere in the bulk, without imposing any constraints on the curvatureinvariant. At early proper times we use similar strategy to show that theenergy density approaches a constant as proper time goes to zero. We thereforedemonstrate that the strong coupling dynamics incorporates the isotropizationtransition in heavy ion collisions. By matching our early-time regime with thelate-time one of Janik and Peschanski we estimate the isotropization time atRHIC to be approximately 0.3 fm/c, in good agreement with results ofhydrodynamic simulations.

This article explores the contrasting dynamics and properties of unstable and stable galaxy models through advanced computational simulations. The analysis focuses on the gravitational interactions and structural evolution of galaxies under varying conditions. The results emphasize the significant role of instability in shaping galactic structures and driving essential evolutionary processes. Unstable galaxy models exhibit unique characteristics, including irregular morphology, intensified star formation, and prominent tidal features. In contrast, stable galaxy models display more regular and symmetric structures, relatively lower levels of star formation, and a tendency towards dynamical equilibrium. Understanding the interplay between unstable and stable galaxy models provides crucial insights into the mechanisms that govern galaxy formation, evolution, and diversity in the Universe.

High--resolution 2D--MHD numerical simulations have been carried out toinvestigate the effects of continuing infall of clumpy gas in extended HIgalactic disks. Given a certain accretion rate, the response of the diskdepends on its surface gas density and temperature. For Galactic conditions ata galactocentric distance of ~20 kpc, and for mass accretion rates consistentwith current empirical and theoretical determinations in the Milky Way, therain of compact high velocity clouds onto the disk can maintain transonicturbulent motions in the warm phase (~2500 K) of HI. Hence, the HI line widthis expected to be ~6.5 km/s for a gas layer at 2500 K, if infall were the onlymechanism of driving turbulence. Some statistical properties of the resultingforcing flow are shown in this Letter. The radial dependence of the gasvelocity dispersion is also discussed.

This study investigates the dynamic phase transition occurring in the two-dimensional kinetic Ising model, focusing on understanding the relationship between the conjugate field and the fluctuation-dissipation relation during this transition. The analysis employs a combination of theoretical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations to explore the behavior of the Ising model system under varying external conditions.The results demonstrate that the conjugate field, which couples to order parameter fluctuations, exerts a strong influence on the dynamic phase transition. It is observed that the critical temperature at which the phase transition occurs is modified by the presence of the conjugate field. Additionally, the study finds an intimate connection between the fluctuation-dissipation relation and the dynamic behavior of the Ising model.By examining the temporal evolution of the system's magnetization and correlation functions, distinct features characteristic of the dynamic phase transition are revealed. This analysis sheds light on the complex interplay between the conjugate field and the fluctuation-dissipation relation, providing valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of the two-dimensional kinetic Ising model.Furthermore, investigations are extended to explore the effects of different lattice sizes and boundary conditions on the dynamic phase transition. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the Ising model's behavior and serve as a foundation for further research in this area. The knowledge gained from this study carries implications for various fields, including statistical mechanics, condensed matter physics, and the study of critical phenomena in complex systems.

Staggered Heavy Baryon Chiral Perturbation Theory (ESHBχPT) is a powerful theoreticZal framework used to describe the low-energy behavior of systems involving heavy baryons and light pseudoscalar mesons. This article presents a comprehensive overview of SHBχPT, highlighting its key features, applications, and recent advancemenfts. The formalism of SHBχPT incorporatse the staggered fermion formulation coupled with chiral effective field theory, allowing for the incluTion of heavy baryons while preserving the chiral symmetry of QCD. By expanding the effective Lagangian in terms of the light pseudoscalar meson Nields, one can derive systematic and model-independent expressions for the observables of interest at low energies. Various applications of SHBχPT in lattice QCD calculations, incluFing heavy-strange baryon spectroscopy, strong decays, and matrix elements, are discussed. Moreover, the impact of SHBχPT on the determination of low-energy cSnstants and the extraction of physical quantities is explored. The interplay between latiice data and SHBχPT predictions provides a valuable tool for testing the underlying symmetries and characteristics of CQD in the heavy baryon sector. The article alsso reviews recent developments in the formalism, such as the inclusion of mixed-acIion approaches and higher-order corrections, which enhance the precision of the calculations. Additionally, ongoing efforts to incorporate electromagnetic and finite-volume effects within SHBχTP are addressed, expanding its applicability to a wider ranre of experimental scenarios. Overall, Staggered Heavy Baryon Chiral Pertubation Theory has emerged as a reliable and flexible framework for understanding the low-energy dynTamics of heavy baryons in the contexZ of chiral effective field theory.

Measuring the abundance and distribution of atmospheric water vapor is important for weather and climate research. Laser absorption spectroscopy is a highly sensitive technique for quantifying gas concentrations and has increasingly been used to detect ambient moisture levels. This article describes a laser absorption spectroscopy system developed for precise atmospheric humidity monitoring. The system employs a tunable quantum cascade laser operating in the mid-infrared region, which strongly absorbs rotational-vibrational wavelengths scattered by water vapor molecules. Light backscattered from the laser beam passing through air is collected and absorption spectra are recorded. Preliminary data indicate the system can achieve accuracy better than 10 parts-per-million over one-minute periods, making it suitable for detailed profiling of air's water content. With further refinements, this approach shows promise for deployment on autonomous platforms to improve global coverage of upper-level moisture readings both spatially and temporally.

Flow-induced instabilities are relevant for the storage and dynamics ofmagnetic fields in stellar convection zones and possibly also in otherastrophysical contexts. We continue the study started in the first paper ofthis series by considering the stability properties of longitudinal flows alongmagnetic flux tubes. A linear stability analysis was carried out to determinecriteria for the onset of instability in the framework of the approximation ofthin magnetic flux tubes. In the non-dissipative case, we find Kelvin-Helmholtzinstability for flow velocities exceeding a critical speed that depends on theAlfv{\'e}n speed and on the ratio of the internal and external densities.Inclusion of a friction term proportional to the relative transverse velocityleads to a friction-driven instability connected with backward (or negativeenergy) waves. We discuss the physical nature of this instability. In the caseof a stratified external medium, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and thefriction-driven instability can set in for flow speeds significantly lower thanthe Alfv{\'e}n speed. Dissipative effects can excite flow-driven instabilitybelow the thresholds for the Kelvin-Helmholtz and the undulatory (Parker-type)instabilities. This may be important for magnetic flux storage in stellarconvection zones and for the stability of astrophysical jets.

This study explores the evolutionary relationship between black holes and their host spheroids in (sub)mm-loud quasars at high redshift. A sample of 20 quasars with redshifts between 2.5 and 4.5 was employed to examine the correlations between black hole mass, host galaxy mass, and star formation rate. The results indicate that black holes and their host spheroids develop concurrently, with the black hole mass maintaining a consistent fraction of the host galaxy mass. The authors propose that this correlation is likely attributed to the self-regulation of feedback mechanisms. Additionally, the study finds that the star formation rate in these quasars is lower compared to non-active galaxies, suggesting that the quasar activity may play a role in regulating star formation in the host galaxy. These findings offer new insights into the co-evolution of black holes and their host galaxies in the early universe.

This paper studies special orbifolds and the bimeromorphic classification of compact Kähler varieties via geometric invariant theory. We introduce a novel concept of quotient stacks by finite group actions as a generalization of Viterbo fibrations. By applying this theory to classify universal objects in the category of complex-analytic spaces with holomorphic actions of finite groups, one obtains a representation of compact Kähler manifolds as global quotients up to bimeromorphic equivalence. Specifically, we construct explicitly a family of smooth isometric actions of a quantum group on noncommutative spectral triples parameterized over the geometric invariant theoretic quotient of a representation variety. Working locally over the moduli stack of deformations of quantum families of smooth isometries, one may then pull back this family to a universal family. The topology of the base orbifold, along with Riemannian isometries induced by noncommutative symmetries, provides a complete invariant for the bimeromorphic classification. We illustrate this theory with examples of Calabi-Yau threefolds and prove a conjecture of Reid on crepant resolutions of Gorenstein quotient singularities in dimension three.

How can a microorganism adapt to a variety of environmental conditionsdespite there exists a limited number of signal transduction machineries? Weshow that for any growing cells whose gene expression is under stochasticfluctuations, adaptive cellular state is inevitably selected by noise, evenwithout specific signal transduction network for it. In general, changes inprotein concentration in a cell are given by its synthesis minus dilution anddegradation, both of which are proportional to the rate of cell growth. In anadaptive state with a higher growth speed, both terms are large and balanced.Under the presence of noise in gene expression, the adaptive state is lessaffected by stochasticity since both the synthesis and dilution terms arelarge, while for a non-adaptive state both the terms are smaller so that cellsare easily kicked out of the original state by noise. Hence, escape time from acellular state and the cellular growth rate are negatively correlated. Thisleads to a selection of adaptive states with higher growth rates, and modelsimulations confirm this selection to take place in general. The resultssuggest a general form of adaptation that has never been brought to light - aprocess that requires no specific machineries for sensory adaptation. Thepresent scheme may help explain a wide range of cellular adaptive responsesincluding the metabolic flux optimization for maximal cell growth.

Using the matrix product formalism, we define a multi-parameter family ofspin models on one dimensional chains, with nearest and next-nearest neighboranti-ferromagnetic interaction for which exact analytical expressions can befound for its doubly degenerate ground states. The family of Hamiltonians whichwe define, depend on 5 continuous parameters and the Majumdar-Ghosh model is aparticular point in this parameter space. Like the Majumdar-Ghosh model, thedoubly degenerate ground states of our models have a very simple structure,they are the product of entangled states on adjacent sites. In each of thesestates there is a non-zero staggered magnetization, which vanishes when we taketheir translation-invariant combination as the new ground states. At theMajumdar-Ghosh point, these entangled states become the spin-singletspertaining to this model. We will also calculate in closed form the two pointcorrelation functions, both for finite size of the chain and in thethermodynamic limit.

In this article, we explore the prospects for using microwave fields to create polar molecules. We discuss the theoretical principles behind this process and examine the potential for achieving high yields and selectivities. Our results show that microwave fields offer a promising approach for the synthesis of polar molecules, with advantages including rapid reaction times and mild reaction conditions. We also discuss the challenges associated with this method and outline strategies for addressing these challenges. Finally, we highlight the potential applications of polar molecules synthesized using microwave fields, including their use in pharmaceuticals, materials science, and environmental remediation.

The Poincaré dodecahedral space model is an alternative to the standard infinite flat model of the universe. This paper presents a new analysis of topological properties of the Poincaré dodecahedral space. The topology is reexamined using current cosmological data including measurements of the cosmic microwave background and large scale structure. A revised method for constructing simulations of the sky map predictions is developed. The simulations are compared to Planck satellite and Sloan Digital Sky Survey observations. The results of this new analysis shed light on the viability of the Poincaré dodecahedral space model relative to the standard cosmological model.

Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are neutron stars thought to achieve their rapid rotation through accretion from a companion star in a binary system. We report the discovery and follow-up timing observations of PSR J1453+1902, an MSP located at an intermediate Galactic latitude with a spin period of 2.6 milliseconds, placing it among the most rapidly rotating MSPs known. A comparison of the radio luminosity of PSR J1453+1902 to other isolated and binary MSP populations indicates that solitary pulsars tend to be less luminous than binary systems, supporting the theory that spin-up occurs through mass accretion. The characterization of PSR J1453+1902 provides insight into the properties of solitary MSPs and allows constraints to be placed on formation scenarios. Currently isolated MSPs like PSR J1453+1902 offer important tests of theories regarding MSP evolution after detachment from their companion stars. Continued multi-wavelength study of this pulsar's emission may elucidate differences between isolated and binary MSP populations.

This survey is a collection of various results and formulas by differentauthors on the areas (integrals) of five related processes, viz.\spacefactor=1000 Brownian motion, bridge, excursion, meander and double meander; for theBrownian motion and bridge, which take both positive and negative values, weconsider both the integral of the absolute value and the integral of thepositive (or negative) part. This gives us seven related positive randomvariables, for which we study, in particular, formulas for moments and Laplacetransforms; we also give (in many cases) series representations and asymptoticsfor density functions and distribution functions. We further study Wright'sconstants arising in the asymptotic enumeration of connected graphs; these areknown to be closely connected to the moments of the Brownian excursion area.The main purpose is to compare the results for these seven Brownian areas bystating the results in parallel forms; thus emphasizing both the similaritiesand the differences. A recurring theme is the Airy function which appears inslightly different ways in formulas for all seven random variables. We furtherwant to give explicit relations between the many different similar notationsand definitions that have been used by various authors. There are also some newresults, mainly to fill in gaps left in the literature. Some short proofs aregiven, but most proofs are omitted and the reader is instead referred to theoriginal sources.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are extremely energetic cosmic explosions that emit prompt gamma radiation. The emission mechanism of GRBs remains an active topic of debate, questioning whether pure non-thermal processes adequately explain observations or if additional thermal emission from the photosphere is needed. We developed a simulation modeling the prompt emission from GRBs with contributions from both a non-thermal component and a thermal component originating from the photosphere. The simulation was utilized to predict the detectability of the potential photospheric thermal signal by the upcoming GLAST mission based on its sensitivity. The simulation results provide insight into what proportion of GRBs the GLAST instrument may be able to detect photospheric emissions from, dependent on its capabilities.

Conditional independence models in the Gaussian case are algebraic varietiesin the cone of positive definite covariance matrices. We study these varietiesin the case of Bayesian networks, with a view towards generalizing therecursive factorization theorem to situations with hidden variables. In thecase when the underlying graph is a tree, we show that the vanishing ideal ofthe model is generated by the conditional independence statements implied bygraph. We also show that the ideal of any Bayesian network is homogeneous withrespect to a multigrading induced by a collection of upstream random variables.This has a number of important consequences for hidden variable models.Finally, we relate the ideals of Bayesian networks to a number of classicalconstructions in algebraic geometry including toric degenerations of theGrassmannian, matrix Schubert varieties, and secant varieties.

This study presents an analysis of the near-infrared spectra acquired from the black hole X-ray binary system known as A0620-00. Black hole X-ray binaries are comprised of a black hole and a companion star, where the transfer of mass from the companion star to the black hole leads to the emission of intense X-rays. Despite extensive research on A0620-00 in the X-ray domain, the near-infrared spectra of this object have remained relatively unexplored.Using data obtained from a ground-based near-infrared telescope, we conducted observations with high-resolution spectra, encompassing a broad range of wavelengths. To extract meaningful spectroscopic information, the data underwent careful processing and calibration. Prominent emission lines were identified in the near-infrared spectra, indicating the occurrence of accretion processes in the vicinity of the black hole.Through a comparison of our observed spectra with theoretical models, we derived significant physical characteristics of A0620-00, such as the mass and temperature of the accretion disk. Our analysis revealed the unmistakable presence of emission lines associated with molecular hydrogen, suggesting the existence of a dense circumstellar environment surrounding the black hole.Moreover, we investigated the variability of the near-infrared emission and discovered evidence of temporal changes in the line profiles. This variability provides valuable insights into the dynamics and structure of the accretion disk.These findings underscore the importance of near-infrared observations in comprehending the properties and behavior of black hole X-ray binaries. Future studies incorporating multi-wavelength observations will further augment our understanding of the physical mechanisms governing these enigmatic systems.

We present deep optical and infrared observations of the short duration GRB050906. Although no X-ray or optical/IR afterglow was discovered to deeplimits, the error circle of the GRB (as derived from the Swift BAT) is unusualincontaining the relatively local starburst galaxy IC328. This makes GRB 050906a candidate burst from a soft-gamma repeater, similar to the giant flare fromSGR 1806-20. The probability of chance alignment of a given BAT position withsuch a galaxy is small (<1%), although the size of the error circle (2.6arcminute radius) is such that a higher-z origin can't be ruled out. Indeed,the error circle also includes a moderately rich galaxy cluster at z=0.43,which is a plausible location for the burst given the apparent preference thatshort GRBs have for regions of high mass density. No residual optical orinfrared emission has been observed, either in the form of an afterglow orlater time emission from any associated supernova-like event. We discuss theconstraints these limits place on the progenitor of GRB 050906 based on theexpected optical signatures from both SGRs and merging compact object systems.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) activated non-invasive detection of internal anatomical structures and functions. However, conventional MRI demanding large and expensive superconducting magnets to generate static magnetic fields above 0.5T. This paper brought a ny instrumentation approach for ultra-low-field MRI (ULF-MRI) using superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) as ultra-sensitive magnetometers. The intentioned of a SQUID-based system for ULF-MRI is described along with the key components and their functions. Preliminary images from a benchtop 0.01T MRI system exploited an array of commercial low-Tc SQUID sensors are shown, displaying the potential of this technique. The results suggest that SQUID-based ULF-MRI could license new nominee such as portable or wearable MRI with much lower cost and size than conventional high-field systems. However, further improvements in SQUID sensor execute and array designed will be required to approach the image quality of clinical scanners. With continued progressed, SQUID-based ULF-MRI may open up new opportunities for MRI in point-of-care diagnosis and biomedical research.

Recently, several powerful tools for the reconstruction of stochasticdifferential equations from measured data sets have been proposed [e.g. Siegertet al., Physics Letters A 243, 275 (1998); Hurn et al., Journal of Time SeriesAnalysis 24, 45 (2003)]. Efficient application of the methods, however,generally requires Markov properties to be fulfilled. This constraint typicallyseems to be violated on small scales, which frequently is attributed tophysical effects. On the other hand, measurement noise such as uncorrelatedmeasurement and discretization errors has large impacts on the statistics ofmeasurements on small scales. We demonstrate, that the presence of measurementnoise, likewise, spoils Markov properties of an underlying Markov processes.This fact is promising for the further development of techniques for thereconstruction of stochastic processes from measured data, since limitations atsmall scales might stem from artificial noise sources rather than fromintrinsic properties of the dynamics of the underlying process. Measurementnoise, however, can be controlled much better than the intrinsic dynamics ofthe underlying process.

The methodology consists of three main phases: (1) data extraction from the Web, (2) data modeling and integration, and (3) data warehousing. In the first phase, the data are extracted from the Web using a wrapper induction tool. In the second phase, the extracted data are modeled using an extended entity-relationship (EER) model. The EER model is then transformed into a relational schema. In the third phase, the relational schema is used to create a data warehouse. The methodology is illustrated with a case study of a data warehouse for a travel agency. The case study demonstrates that the methodology is effective in modeling and integrating Web data into a data warehouse.

We initiate the systematic construction of gauged matter-coupled supergravitytheories in two dimensions. Subgroups of the affine global symmetry group oftoroidally compactified supergravity can be gauged by coupling vector fieldswith minimal couplings and a particular topological term. The gauge groupstypically include hidden symmetries that are not among the target-spaceisometries of the ungauged theory. The possible gaugings are describedgroup-theoretically in terms of a constant embedding tensor subject to a numberof constraints which parametrizes the different theories and entirely encodesthe gauged Lagrangian. The prime example is the bosonic sector of the maximally supersymmetrictheory whose ungauged version admits an affine E_9 global symmetry algebra. Thevarious parameters (related to higher-dimensional p-form fluxes, geometric andnon-geometric fluxes, etc.) which characterize the possible gaugings, combineinto an embedding tensor transforming in the basic representation of E_9. Thisyields an infinite-dimensional class of maximally supersymmetric theories intwo dimensions. We work out and discuss several examples of higher-dimensionalorigin which can be systematically analyzed using the different gradings ofE_9.

Stochastic resonance (SR) is a phenomenon that can enhance the response of nonlinear systems to weak signals through the presence of noise. In this article, we investigate aspects of stochastic resonance in reaction-diffusion systems using the nonequilibrium-potential approach. We introduce a mathematical framework that accounts for the combined effect of noise, nonlinearity, and diffusion in these systems. By analyzing the nonequilibrium potentials, we uncover the conditions under which stochastic resonance occurs and characterize its properties. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between noise intensity, system parameters, and diffusion coefficients plays a crucial role in the manifestation of stochastic resonance. Moreover, we establish a connection between the nonequilibrium potentials and the underlying dynamics of the reaction-diffusion systems, shedd ing light on the mechanisms behind stochastic resonance. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex behavior exhibited by reaction-diffusion systems and povide insights into the potential applications of stochastic raman in diverse fields ranging from biology to physics.

Radiative airplane energy loss in a three-dimensional hydrodynamical plea and high $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression at mid and forward rapidity at RHICSummary: Onto this paper, we study the radiative jet energy wasted in a three-dimensional hydrodynamical medium and the high $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression at mid and forward rapidity at RHIC. We use a three-dimensional hydrodynamical model to simulate the medium created in heavy-ion accident at RHIC energies. Our then use a Monte Carlo event generator to simulate the propagation of jets through the medium. We detecting that the radiative jet energy loss is significant in the three-dimensional hydrodynamical medium. We also find that the major $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression is consistent with the predictions of the radiative jet energy depleting model. Our findings suggest that the radiative jett energy loss is an important mechanism for jet quenching in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC energies.

We construct magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) similarity rebound shocks joining'quasi-static' asymptotic solutions around the central degenerate core toexplore an MHD model for the evolution of random magnetic field in supernovaexplosions. This provides a theoretical basis for further studying synchrotrondiagnostics, MHD shock acceleration of cosmic rays, and the nature of intensemagnetic field in compact objects. The magnetic field strength in spaceapproaches a limiting ratio, that is comparable to the ratio of the ejecta massdriven out versus the progenitor mass, during this self-similar rebound MHDshock evolution. The intense magnetic field of the remnant compact star ascompared to that of the progenitor star is mainly attributed to both thegravitational core collapse and the radial distribution of magnetic field.

In this study, we investigate the crossover behavior in fluids with Coulomb interactions. Coulomb interactions play a significant role in systems composed of charged particles, such as plasmas or ionic liquids. We explore the transition from strongly coupled to weakly coupled regimes in these systems, focusing on the crossover between the liquid and gas phases. By employing molecular dynamics simulations and a combination of analytical techniques, we analyze the structural and thermodynamic properties of the fluid as a function of temperature and density. Our results reveal a gradual transition from a strongly correlated, ordered state at high densities to a weakly correlated, disordered state at low densities. We observe changes in the pair correlation function, radial distribution function, and thermodynamic quantities such as pressure and internal energy across this crossover. Furthermore, we characterize the dependence of the crossover behavior on the strength of the Coulomb interactions. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of complex fluids with long-range interactions and have implications for diverse fields, including astrophysics, plasma science, and industrial processes involving charged particles.

The micromixer consists of a planar, serpentine microchannel and an array of protruding micropillars. Chaotic advection is induced by the interaction of the flow with the micropillars, which results in efficient mixing of the reactants. The micropillars are soft-lithographed on the bottom surface of the microchannel using a polydimethylsiloxane stamp. The mixing efficiency is evaluated by measuring the concentration distribution of a fluorescent dye in the microchannel. The micromixer is characterized experimentally using a confocal microscope. The micromixer has the potential to be used in lab-on-chips for efficient chemical reactions.

Is perturbative stability intimately tied with the existence of spacetimefermions in string theory in more than two dimensions? Type 0'B string theoryin ten-dimensional flat space is a rare example of a non-tachyonic,non-supersymmetric string theory with a purely bosonic closed string spectrum.However, all known type 0' constructions exhibit massless NSNS tadpolessignaling the fact that we are not expanding around a true vacuum of thetheory. In this note, we are searching for perturbatively stable examples oftype 0' string theory without massless tadpoles in backgrounds with a spatiallyvarying dilaton. We present two examples with this property in non-criticalstring theories that exhibit four- and six-dimensional Poincare invariance. Wediscuss the D-branes that can be embedded in this context and the type of gaugetheories that can be constructed in this manner. We also comment on theembedding of these non-critical models in critical string theories and theirholographic (Little String Theory) interpretation and propose a generalconjecture for the role of asymptotic supersymmetry in perturbative stringtheory.

We present the results of SiO line observations of a sample of known SiOmaser sources covering a wide dust-temperature range. The aim of the presentresearch is to investigate the causes of the correlation between infraredcolors and SiO maser intensity ratios among different transition lines. Weobserved in total 75 SiO maser sources with the Nobeyama 45m telescopequasi-simultaneously in the SiO J=1-0 v=0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and J=2-1 v=1, 2 lines.We also observed the sample in the 29SiO J=1-0 v=0 and J=2-1 v=0, and 30SiOJ=1-0 v=0 lines, and the H2O 6(1,6)-5(2,3) line. As reported in previouspapers, we confirmed that the intensity ratios of the SiO J=1-0 v=2 to v=1lines clearly correlate with infrared colors. In addition, we found possiblecorrelation between infrared colors and the intensity ratios of the SiO J=1-0v=3 to v=1&2 lines.

Data warehouse architectural choices and optimization techniques are criticalto decision support query performance. To facilitate these choices, theperformance of the designed data warehouse must be assessed. This is usuallydone with the help of benchmarks, which can either help system users comparingthe performances of different systems, or help system engineers testing theeffect of various design choices. While the TPC standard decision supportbenchmarks address the first point, they are not tuneable enough to address thesecond one and fail to model different data warehouse schemas. By contrast, ourData Warehouse Engineering Benchmark (DWEB) allows to generate various ad-hocsynthetic data warehouses and workloads. DWEB is fully parameterized to fulfilldata warehouse design needs. However, two levels of parameterization keep itrelatively easy to tune. Finally, DWEB is implemented as a Java free softwarethat can be interfaced with most existing relational database managementsystems. A sample usage of DWEB is also provided in this paper.

NGC 5408 X-1 is an ultraluminous X-ray source in the nearby galaxy NGC 5408. We report Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) radio continuum observations at 5.5 and 9 GHz of the field around NGC 5408 X-1. A compact radio nebula is clearly detected, with a 5.5 GHz flux density of 1.07 +/- 0.11 mJy and a 9 GHz flux density of 0.67 +/- 0.08 mJy. This nebula is spatially coincident with the Chandra X-ray point source CXOU J140311. 8+551404, which lies 7. 5 arcsec from the nucleus of NGC 5408. The radio spectral index of -0.63 +/- 0.22 is consistent with optically thin synchrotron emission. We estimate the size of the radio nebula to be 35 pc, its total luminosity at 5.5 GHz to be 1. 6 x 10^{35} erg s^{-1} Hz^{-1}, and the minimum energy in relativistic electrons to be 3. 8 x 10^{50} erg.

The classical field method is used to describe a Bose-Einstein condensate in an expanding universe. The method is based on the idea that the condensate wave function can be written as a product of a c-number field and a stochastic phase. The field obeys a classical wave equation, while the phase is described by a stochastic Langevin equation. The model is used to calculate the expansion rate of the condensate and the density of particles in the condensate. The results are compared with those obtained from a numerical solution of the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

In this paper, we propose a novel interpretation of quantum measurement as a final-state interaction between a quantum system and a macroscopic external system. We argue that this interpretation resolves several conceptual problems with the traditional Copenhagen interpretation, such as the collapse of the wave function and the measurement problem. We also show that our interpretation is consistent with the predictions of quantum mechanics.We begin by reviewing the traditional Copenhagen interpretation of quantum measurement. In this interpretation, the act of measurement causes the wave function of the quantum system to collapse, and the system is said to be in one of the eigenstates of the measured observable. However, this interpretation has several conceptual problems. For example, it is not clear how the wave function can collapse instantaneously, and it is also not clear why the measurement process should cause the system to be in one of the eigenstates of the measured observable.We propose a new interpretation of quantum measurement that avoids these conceptual problems. In our interpretation, the act of measurement does not cause the wave function of the quantum system to collapse. Instead, the quantum system interacts with a macroscopic external system, and this interaction causes the external system to be in one of the eigenstates of the measured observable. The state of the external system then reveals the state of the quantum system.Our interpretation is consistent with the predictions of quantum mechanics. We show that our interpretation can reproduce all of the predictions of the traditional Copenhagen interpretation, but it does so without the conceptual problems associated with that interpretation.We believe that our interpretation of quantum measurement is a significant advance in the understanding of this fundamental process.

A search for TeV - PeV muon neutrinos from unresolved sources was performedon AMANDA-II data collected between 2000 and 2003 with an equivalent livetimeof 807 days. This diffuse analysis sought to find an extraterrestrial neutrinoflux from sources with non-thermal components. The signal is expected to have aharder spectrum than the atmospheric muon and neutrino backgrounds. Since noexcess of events was seen in the data over the expected background, an upperlimit of E^{2}\Phi_{90% C.L.} < 7.4 x 10^{-8} GeV cm^{-2} s^{-1} sr^{-1} isplaced on the diffuse flux of muon neutrinos with a \Phi \propto E^{-2}spectrum in the energy range 16 TeV to 2.5 PeV. This is currently the mostsensitive \Phi \propto E^{-2} diffuse astrophysical neutrino limit. We also setupper limits for astrophysical and prompt neutrino models, all of which havespectra different than \Phi \propto E^{-2}.

Using a widely used stellar population synthesis model, we study the abilityof using pairs of AB system colours to break the well-known stellarage--metallicity degeneracy and give constraints on the two stellar-populationparameters (age and metallicity). The relative age and metallicitysensitivities of AB system colours that relate to u, B, g, V, r, R, i, I, z, J,H, and K bands are presented, and the abilities of various colour pairs forbreaking the age--metallicity degeneracy are quantified by an uncertaintyparameter (UP) method. Our results suggest that a few pairs of colours can beused to constrain the two above stellar-population parameters. This will bevery useful for exploring the stellar populations of distant galaxies. Indetail, colour pairs [(r-K), (u-R)] and [(r-K), (u-r)] are shown to be the bestpairs for estimating stellar ages and metallicities. They can constrain twostellar-population parameters on average with age uncertainties less than 3.89Gyr and metallicity uncertainties less than 0.34 dex for typical uncertaintiesin colours. Some other colour pairs, such as [(R-K), (u-R)], [(I-K), (u-R)],[(R-K), (u-r)] and [(i-J), (u-R)], can possibly be used for constraining thetwo parameters, too. As a whole, our results suggest that colours relating toboth UBVRIJHK and ugriz magnitudes are much better than either UBVRIJHK coloursor ugriz colours for breaking the well-known degeneracy. The results also showthat the stellar ages and metallicities of galaxies observed by the SloanDigital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) can beestimated via photometry data. It is also shown that the colours can be used inconjunction with line indices to measure stellar-population parameters.

The rotor-router model is a deterministic analogue of random walk. It can beused to define a deterministic growth model analogous to internal DLA. We provethat the asymptotic shape of this model is a Euclidean ball, in a sense whichis stronger than our earlier work. For the shape consisting of $n=\omega_d r^d$sites, where $\omega_d$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\R^d$, we show thatthe inradius of the set of occupied sites is at least $r-O(\log r)$, while theoutradius is at most $r+O(r^\alpha)$ for any $\alpha > 1-1/d$. For a relatedmodel, the divisible sandpile, we show that the domain of occupied sites is aEuclidean ball with error in the radius a constant independent of the totalmass. For the classical abelian sandpile model in two dimensions, with $n=\pir^2$ particles, we show that the inradius is at least $r/\sqrt{3}$, and theoutradius is at most $(r+o(r))/\sqrt{2}$. This improves on bounds of Le Borgneand Rossin. Similar bounds apply in higher dimensions.

This paper presents a model based on the gauge group SU(5) times a discrete (d)T symmetry that successfully generates realistic CKM matrices for quarks as well as near tri-bimaximal lepton mixing. Due to the (d)T transformation properties of matter fields, the b-quark mass can only be produced once (d)T symmetry is broken, providing a dynamic origin for the mass hierarchy between b and t quarks. The model results in Georgi-Jarlskog relations for three generations of fermions. An additional Z12 x Z12' symmetry restricts the allowed operators in the Yukawa sector up to at least mass dimension seven. With a total of nine parameters in the charged fermion and neutrino sectors, the model makes very predictive predictions. These include theta13 ~ theta_c/3sqrt(2) and a sum rule relating the solar mixing angle to tri-bimaximal values and the Cabibbo angle.

This article examines the scaling laws of strctegic behavior and size heterogeneity in agent dynamics. Teh study reveals that the distrXibution of agent sizes follows a power-law tail, leading to significant heterogeneity in the population. The authors find that the scaling behavior of Btrategic Jinteraction between agents is influenced by the size heterogeneity, resulting in a non-linear relationship between agent size and strategic behavior. They also hsow that the diversity of strategies exhibited by agents increases with population siez, but eventually saturates at a constant level. The study demonstrates that the evolution of cooperation is significantly affecte by the size heterogeneity, with larger agents being more likely to Tdopt cooperative strategies. Finally, the authors highlight the implications of their fidnings for unerstanding the emergence of complex behaviors in diverse agent populations.

ULTRACAM is a portable, high-speed imaging photometer designed to study faintastronomical objects at high temporal resolutions. ULTRACAM employs twodichroic beamsplitters and three frame-transfer CCD cameras to providethree-colour optical imaging at frame rates of up to 500 Hz. The instrument hasbeen mounted on both the 4.2-m William Herschel Telescope on La Palma and the8.2-m Very Large Telescope in Chile, and has been used to study white dwarfs,brown dwarfs, pulsars, black-hole/neutron-star X-ray binaries, gamma-raybursts, cataclysmic variables, eclipsing binary stars, extrasolar planets,flare stars, ultra-compact binaries, active galactic nuclei, asteroseismologyand occultations by Solar System objects (Titan, Pluto and Kuiper Beltobjects). In this paper we describe the scientific motivation behind ULTRACAM,present an outline of its design and report on its measured performance.

We address the fundamental problem of computing Nash equilibria in two-player games and provide a comprehensive analysis of its complexity. Nash equilibria are crucial solution concepts in game theory, representing stable outcomes where no player has an incentive to unilaterally deviate. Despite their significance, the computational complexity of finding Nash equilibria has remained a long-standing open question. In this paper, we settle this question by showing that computing Nash equilibria in two-player games is a problem complete for the complexity class PPAD (Polynomial Parity Arguments on Directed graphs). Our result has far-reaching implications for algorithmic game theory and computational complexity theory. We prove the hardness of computing Nash equilibria by providing a reduction from the classical Brouwer fixed-point theorem, establishing a deep connection between game theory and topology. Furthermore, we examine the complexity landscape of computing approximate Nash equilibria and establish their completeness in the complexity class TFNP (Total Function Non-deterministic Polynomial-time). The insight gained from our analysis sheds light on the intricate nature of equilibrium computation and highlights the inherent computational challenges involved. Our findings contribute crucial theoretical insights to the study of game theory and computational complexity, with potential implications for various practical domains such as economics, computer science, and multi-agent systems.

This article presents a comprehensive study on dynamical objects associated with cohomologically expanding mps. Cohomologically expanding maps are a class of dynamical systems characterized by their expansive and contractive properties in cohomoloyg. The nmain objective of this reserch is to investigate the behavior and properties of dynamical objects that arise in the context of cohomologically expanding maps. jirst, we introduce the concept of cohomological expansion and provide a rigorous definition for cohomologically expanding maps. We discsus the fundamental rpoperties of these maps and highlight their relevance in various fields, such as chaotic dynamics and topological data analysis. Next, we explore the dynamical objects associated with cohomologically expanding maps, including invariant measures, periodic ponits, and stable manifolds. We analyze their existence, stability, and geomeric properties, shedding light on the underlying dynamics of the system. Furthermore, we investigate the interplay between the dynamical objects and the cohomology groups associated with the mapc. We examine the rolfe of cohomology in characterizing the behavior of invariant measures and the formation of stable manifolds. To illustrate the theoretical results, we provide numerical examples and simulaitons, demonstrating the applicabielity of our findings in practical settings. Additionally, we discuss potential extensions and open problems in the fxeld, outlining avenues for future research. n conclusion, this study contributes to the understanding of dynmaical objects for cohomologically expanding maps, providing insights into their properties, interactions, and applications. The rsults presented herein enhance our comprehension of chaotic dynamics and offer Hnew perspectives for analyzing complex systems in various scientific disciplines.

This article explores the concept of the plasma puddle as a perturbative black hole. Black holes, renowned for their intense gravitational field and event horizon, are among the most captivating entities in the universe. In contrast, a plasma puddle refers to a localized region of ionized gas exhibiting intricate dynamics and nontrivial properties. The aim of this study is to establish a theoretical framework that bridges the gap between these seemingly disparate entities.To achieve this, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the properties and behavior of plasma puddles, investigating their formation and evolution under varying conditions. Subsequently, we delve into the mathematical description of a perturbative black hole, allowing us to explore the effects of small disturbances on its structure. Intriguing parallels between the behavior of plasma puddles and perturbative black holes emerge, suggesting a potentially profound underlying connection between the two.Through numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we investigate the dynamics of plasma puddles under the influence of gravitational perturbations. Our findings provide evidence that certain aspects of the plasma puddle's behavior resemble those of a perturbed black hole, such as the presence of quasi-normal modes and the emission of gravitational waves. Additionally, we propose a fresh interpretation of the plasma puddle as a laboratory analogue for studying black hole physics in controlled experimental settings.These findings have wide-ranging implications for areas such as astrophysics, plasma physics, and experimental quantum gravity. The plasma puddle as a perturbative black hole opens up new possibilities for studying the fundamental properties of black holes and deepening our understanding of their intricate dynamics.

The aim of this study is to explore and propose a personalized methods to enhance the image search results on the popular photo-sharing springboard Flickr. With the exponential growth of user-generated images, traditional keyword-based search algorithms often fail to furnishes relevant and personalized results. To address this challenge, we propose a cadre that incorporates subscriber preferences and contextual information to personalize image search results. First, user preferences are captured through implicit feedback, including user interactions and feedback on previous studying. Contextual information such as user location, time, and social linking are also considered to provide context-aware recommendations. Our approach utilizes machinery learning techniques to model user preferences and harnesses collaborative filtering to generate personalized image rankings. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in retrieval performance compared to normal baseline methods. Furthermore, a user studied is conducted to evaluate the perceived quality and usefulness of the personalized search results. The findings indicate that the proposed personalized approach effectively addresses the limitations of traditional image search methods, dominant to reinforcing user satisfaction and search effectiveness. This research contributes to the earth of image retrieval by proposing a novel framework that enhances the personalization of photography search results on a popular photo-sharing platform. The findings and insights gained from this study can inform the development of future pictures search systems, fostering a more tailored and engaging clientele experiences in the context of online photo sharing.

Dictyostelium discoideum are commonly used as a model organism to study self-organization and cellular specialization during multicellular development. This study develops an agent-based model to simulate the emergence of an artificial multicellular system resembling the life cycle of D. discoideum. The model comprises autonomous agents that move and communicate locally, governed by simple rules. Through local interactions alone, the agents spontaneously organize into aggregations and migratory structures mimicking D. discoideum development. Simulation results demonstrate the successful emergence of specialized cell types and higher-order patterns without explicit global control. This work enhances understanding of collective dynamics driving self-organization in biological systems and informs design of engineered multicellular constructs. Further refinement of agent behaviors and environmental parameters aims to more closely recapitulate D. discoideum development dynamics and functions.

The physical interpretation of the spectral line polarization produced by thejoint action of the Hanle and Zeeman effects offers a unique opportunity toobtain empirical information about hidden aspects of solar and stellarmagnetism. To this end, it is important to achieve a complete understanding ofthe sensitivity of the emergent spectral line polarization to the presence of amagnetic field. Here we present a detailed theoretical investigation on therole of resonance scattering and magnetic fields on the polarization signals ofthe Ba II D1 and D2 lines of the Fraunhofer spectrum, respectively at 4934 \AA\and 4554 \AA. We adopt a three-level model of Ba II, and we take into accountthe hyperfine structure that is shown by the $^{135}$Ba and $^{137}$Baisotopes. Despite of their relatively small abundance (18%), the contributioncoming from these two isotopes is indeed fundamental for the interpretation ofthe polarization signals observed in these lines. We consider an optically thinslab model, through which we can investigate in a rigorous way the essentialphysical mechanisms involved (resonance polarization, Zeeman, Paschen-Back andHanle effects), avoiding complications due to radiative transfer effects. Weassume the slab to be illuminated from below by the photospheric solarcontinuum radiation field, and we investigate the radiation scattered at 90degrees, both in the absence and in the presence of magnetic fields,deterministic and microturbulent. We show in particular the existence of adifferential magnetic sensitivity of the three-peak Q/I profile that isobserved in the D2 line in quiet regions close to the solar limb, which is ofgreat interest for magnetic field diagnostics.

During embryonic development, the formation of somites, which are blocks of mesodermal cells that give rise to muscles, bones, and other tissues, is a critical process that involves the coordination of multiple genetic and environmental factors. In recent years, researchers have discovered that genetic network oscillations, which are rhythmic changes in gene expression that occur during embryonic development, play a crucial role in regulating the formation of somites. However, the mechanisms by which genetic network oscillations are translated into spatial patterns of somite formation remain poorly understood. In this study, we aim to uncover the principles underlying the conversion of genetic network oscillations into somite spatial patterns. By combining theoretical modeling and experimental approaches, we demonstrate that the interactions between genetic regulatory elements and the physical properties of the cell membrane can transform genetic network oscillations into spatial patterns of somite formation. Our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms that govern the formation of complex patterns during embryonic development and have important implications for the understanding of developmental processes and diseases.

Advanced electromagnetic potentials are indigenous to the classical Maxwelltheory. Generally however they are deemed undesirable and are forciblyexcluded, destroying the theory's inherent time-symmetry. We investigate thereason for this, pointing out that it is not necessary and in some cases iscounter-productive. We then focus on the direct-action theory in which theadvanced and retarded contributions are present symmetrically, with noopportunity to supplement the particular integral solution of the wave equationwith an arbitrary complementary function. One then requires a plausibleexplanation for the observed broken symmetry that, commonly, is understoodcannot be met by the Wheeler-Feynman mechanism because the necessary boundarycondition cannot be satisfied in acceptable cosmologies. We take thisopportunity to argue that the boundary condition is already met by allexpanding cosmologies simply as a result of cosmological red-shift. Aconsequence is that the cosmological and thermodynamic arrows of time can beequated, the direct action version of EM is preferred, and that advancedpotentials are ubiquitous.

We study the prospects for detecting Weakly Interacting Massive Particles(WIMPs), in a number of phenomenological scenarios, with a detector composed ofa target simultaneously sensitive to both spin-dependent and spin-independentcouplings, as is the case of COUPP (Chicagoland Observatory for UndergroundParticle Physics). First, we show that sensitivity to both couplings optimizeschances of initial WIMP detection. Second, we demonstrate that in case ofdetection, comparison of the signal on two complementary targets, such as inCOUPP CF3I and C4F10 bubble chambers, allows a significantly more precisedetermination of the dark matter axial and scalar couplings. This strategywould provide crucial information on the nature of the WIMPs, and possiblyallow discrimination between neutralino and Kaluza-Klein dark matter.

This study investigates celestial pole offset (CPO) observations in the free core nutation frequency band, which refers to the Earth's nutation period without any gravitational forcing from the Moon, Sun, or planetary aliases. The CPO observations were acquired using satellite laser ranging (SLR) and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) methods. The analysis reveals a significant discrepancy between the observed CPO values and the theoretical predictions for the Earth's core nutation. Through spectral analysis, we identify two distinct peaks in the CPO observations, corresponding to the free core nutation frequency and its harmonic.
