This paper provides an introduction to some stochastic models of latticegases out of equilibrium and a discussion of results of various kinds obtainedin recent years. Although these models are different in their microscopicfeatures, a unified picture is emerging at the macroscopic level, applicable,in our view, to real phenomena where diffusion is the dominating physicalmechanism. We rely mainly on an approach developed by the authors based on thestudy of dynamical large fluctuations in stationary states of open systems. Theoutcome of this approach is a theory connecting the non equilibriumthermodynamics to the transport coefficients via a variational principle. Thisleads ultimately to a functional derivative equation of Hamilton-Jacobi typefor the non equilibrium free energy in which local thermodynamic variables arethe independent arguments. In the first part of the paper we give a detailedintroduction to the microscopic dynamics considered, while the second part,devoted to the macroscopic properties, illustrates many consequences of theHamilton-Jacobi equation. In both parts several novelties are included.

Fractal analysis is used to study the self-similarity and complexity of the nucleus, and by measuring the fractal dimension, one can obtain insights into the spatial distribution and organization of the nucleons in the nucleus. The aim of the study is to explore new aspects of the behavior of atomic nuclei and to shed light on their underlying dynamics. The results of the study reveal some interesting observations. Recurrence quantification analysis is used to study the presence of recurrent patterns and dynamics in the nucleus. This method enables the identification of repeated occurrences of specific events or configurations in the nucleus. Recurrence quantification analysis reveals the presence of recurrent patterns in the nucleus, which suggests the presence of underlying periodic or oscillatory behavior. Fractal analysis reveals the presence of multifractal behavior in the nucleus, which suggests a complex and hierarchical organization of the nucleons. This observation challenges the traditional notion of a uniform and homogeneous nucleus. The discovery of multifractal behavior suggests the presence of hidden degrees of freedom in the nucleus, which may be related to exotic phenomena or complex interactions. The identification of recurrent patterns provides insights into the underlying dynamics of the nucleons, which can lead to more accurate models and predictions. These results have important implications for our understanding of atomic nuclei and their properties. The nonlinear methods used in this study offer a powerful and novel approach to explore the behavior of atomic nuclei beyond the limitations of traditional analysis techniques.

A variety of host galaxy (bulge) parameters are examined in order todetermine their predictive power in ascertaining the masses of the supermassiveblack holes (SMBH) at the centers of the galaxies. Based on a sample of 23nearby galaxies, comprised of both elliptical galaxies and spiral/lenticularbulges, we identify a strong correlation between the bulge gravitationalbinding energy ($E_g$), as traced by the stellar light profile, and the SMBHmass ($M_{\bullet}$), such that $M_{\bullet} \propto E_g^{0.6}$. The scatterabout the relationship indicates that this is as strong a predictor of$M_{\bullet}$ as the velocity dispersion ($\sigma$), for the elliptical galaxysubsample. Improved mass-to-light ratios, obtained with IFU spectroscopy andI-band photometry by the SAURON group, were used for those sample galaxieswhere available, resulting in an energy predictor with the same slope, but withreduced scatter. Alternative $M_{\bullet}$ predictors such as the gravitationalpotential and the bulge mass are also explored, but these are found to beinferior when compared with both the bulge gravitational binding energy andbulge velocity dispersion predictors, for the full galaxy sample.

We define pure inductive limit states as sequences of random variables which converge almost surely to a limit independent of the underlying probability measure. We give examples of random processes which exhibit this property and discuss the implications of this property for the study of random processes. We show that this property is equivalent to Kolmogorov's property, which states that the probability of a sequence of events decreases as the length of the sequence increases. We also establish a connection between pure inductive limit states and the theory of ergodic processes and show how this connection can be used to derive results in the study of random dynamics.

Short time-scale radio variations of compact extragalactic radio quasars andblazars known as IntraDay Variability (IDV) can be explained in at least somesources as a propagation effect; the variations are interpreted asscintillation of radio waves in the turbulent interstellar medium of the MilkyWay. One of the most convincing observational arguments in favor of apropagation-induced variability scenario is the observed annual modulation inthe characteristic time scale of the variation due to the Earth's orbitalmotion. So far there are only two sources known with a well-constrainedseasonal cycle. Annual modulation has been proposed for a few other lesswell-documented objects. However, for some other IDV sources source-intrinsicstructural variations which cause drastic changes in the variability time scalewere also suggested. J1128+592 is a recently discovered, highly variable IDVsource. Previous, densely time-sampled flux-density measurements with theEffelsberg 100-m radio telescope (Germany) and the Urumqi 25-m radio telescope(China), strongly indicate an annual modulation of the time scale. The mostrecent 4 observations in 2006/7, however, do not fit well to the annualmodulation model proposed before. In this paper, we investigate a possibleexplanation of this discrepancy.

We have studied the effect of annealing temperature on the statisticalproperties of $WO_3$ surface using atomic force microscopy techniques (AFM). Wehave applied both level crossing and structure function methods. Level crossinganalysis indicates an optimum annealing temperature of around 400$^oC$ at whichthe effective area of the $WO_3$ thin film is maximum, whereas composition ofthe surface remains stoichiometric. The complexity of the height fluctuation ofsurfaces was characterized by roughness, roughness exponent and lateral size ofsurface features. We have found that there is a phase transition at around400$^oC$ from one set to two sets of roughness parameters. This happens due tomicrostructural changes from amorphous to crystalline structure in the samplesthat has been already found experimentally.

We have monitored the atoll-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binary 4U1636-53 with the Rossi X-Ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) for more than 1.5 years.Our campaign consisted of short (~2 ks) pointings separated by two days,regularly monitoring the spectral and timing properties of the source. Duringthe campaign we observed a clear long-term oscillation with a period of ~30-40days, already seen in the light curves from the RXTE All-Sky Monitor, whichcorresponded to regular transitions between the hard (island) and soft (banana)states. We detected kHz QPOs in about a third of the observations, most ofwhich were in the soft (banana) state. The distribution of the frequencies ofthe peak identified as the lower kHz QPO is found to be different from thatpreviously observed in an independent data set. This suggests that the kHz QPOsin the system shows no intrinsically preferred frequency.

We develop a new family of equations of state for quantum chromodynamics based on first-principles calculations from lattice Quantum Chromodynamics across a wide range of baryon chemical potentials and temperatures. By interpolating results from simulations at imaginary chemical potential, we self-consistently construct equations of state featuring a hadron resonance gas at low temperatures crossing over to a quark-gluon plasma at high temperatures. We elucidate the momentum-space structures and interaction strengths governing particle-hole excitations within this family of equations of state. Hydrodynamic simulations utilizing these equations of state indicate observable modifications to anisotropic flow coefficients developping in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions at both the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and the Large Hadron Collider. Overall, this new class of equations of state provides a novel framework for quantitative studies of the quark-gluon plasma within a constrained theoretical formalism directly rooted in QCD.

In this study, we investigate the phase structure of a surface model on dynamcially triangulated spheres with elastic skeletons. The model is formulated as a discree geometric framework in which the surfaces are represneted as collections of triangles interconnected by elastic edges. WLe employ numerical simulations to explore the phase behavior of the model under different parameters and conditions. Our findings reveal the presence of multiple disuinct phases characterized by different surface topologies and elastic properties. Specifically, we observe a smooth phase where the surfaces exhibit continuous deformations without any singularities or deftects. Additionally, we identify a crumpled hase in which the surfaces are highly wrinkled and exhibit significant fluctuations in curvature. Moreover, we discover a phase transition between the smooJh and crumpled phases, which occurs at a critical vkalue of the model's parameters. This transition is characterized by a sudden change in the surface topologies and elastic behavor, indicating the emergence of a nwe physical regime. Furthermore, we analyze the critical exponents associated with this phase transition and find them to be consistent with theoreticaJl predicTions for similar systems. Our result provide valuable insights into the phase diagram and critical properties of surface models on dynamcially triangulated spheres with elastic skeletons. Thi work contributes to the unedrstanding of the complex behavior of surface materials and has potential implications in fields such as material science and computational geometry. Furthe investigations and refinements of our model may lead to the developzment of novel frameworks for the study of surface dynamics and elastic phenomena.

This article presents the design and implementation of the Infrared Cloud Monitor (ICM) for the MAGNUM robotic telescope at Haleakala, Maui. The ICM is a critical component of the telescope's automated observing system, responsible for detecting and tracking clouds to ensure efficient and safe observation scheduling. Utilizing a combination of infrared and visible light sensors, the ICM provides accurate and reliable cloud detection, even in conditions of high humidity and scattered light. The system's algorithms and software are described in detail, highlighting its ability to adapt to varying weather conditions and telescope operations. The ICM's performance is evaluated through a series of tests and observations, demonstrating its effectiveness in supporting the MAGNUM telescope's scientific goals. Overall, the ICM represents a significant advance in the field of robotic telescope technology, enabling optimal observation scheduling and improved data quality.

We combine observational data with the most recent developments in numerical simulations to explore the relationship between QPOs and various energetic properties of black hole systems. We find that the QPO frequency increases with increasing accretion rate and black hole spin, while the QPO amplitude shows a non-monotonic dependence on these quantities. Our results indicate that the energy dependencies of high-frequency QPOs are closely related to the accretion rate, black hole mass, and spin. The observed correlation between QPO frequency and accretion rate challenges existing models and highlights the need for further theoretical developments. Our model provides a robust framework for understanding the energetic dynamics of black hole X-ray binaries and has important implications for the study of black hole physics. The results are consistent with the predictions of general relativity and offer a promising avenue for exploring the strong-field gravity regime. Our findings have important implications for understanding the properties of black hole systems and the role of QPOs in jet formation and energetic feedback.

We observe the emergence of a novel phase separation phenomenon, characterized by the formation of clusters of particles with different velocities. The resulting phase separation has features reminiscent of van der Waals behavior, such as the formation of a cluster of particles with a higher kinetic energy than the surrounding particles. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of driven granular systems and may have implications for the design of novel materials and devices. We demonstrate that the observed phenomenon can be controlled by tuning the system parameters, such as the driving amplitude and the strength of the interparticle interactions.

Density functional theory plus Hubbard U (DFT+U) calculations have been performed on heme systems to study their electronic structure and spin-state energetics. The DFT+U method accurately reproduces the experimental spin-state ordering of various heme complexes, including high-spin and low-spin states. The calculated electronic structures agree with experimental data, demonstrating the reliability of the DFT+U method for studying heme systems. These results provide new insights into the electronic structure of heme and its role in biological systems. Keywords : Heme; DFT+U; Spin-state energetics; Electronic structure; Biological cofactors

This paper investigates the wirteap channel with feedback, specifically explored the use of encryption over the channel to enhance security. The wiretap channel model is extended to include a feedback link from the receiver to the sener, allowing for the possibility of encrypted communication. The authors analyze the capacity of the channel and develop a coding ssheme that utilizes the feedback link to enhance the security of the communication. The proposed scheme is shown to achieve a higher level of security compared to traditional wiretap channel models without comments. The authors also discsus the practical implications of their results and the potential for real-world applications. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the restrictions of the proposed scheme and potential pathways for future research.

We propose a numerical method to evaluate the upper critical dimension $d_c$of random percolation clusters in Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi networks and inscale-free networks with degree distribution ${\cal P}(k) \sim k^{-\lambda}$,where $k$ is the degree of a node and $\lambda$ is the broadness of the degreedistribution. Our results report the theoretical prediction, $d_c = 2(\lambda -1)/(\lambda - 3)$ for scale-free networks with $3 < \lambda < 4$ and $d_c = 6$for Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi networks and scale-free networks with $\lambda > 4$.When the removal of nodes is not random but targeted on removing the highestdegree nodes we obtain $d_c = 6$ for all $\lambda > 2$. Our method also yieldsa better numerical evaluation of the critical percolation threshold, $p_c$, forscale-free networks. Our results suggest that the finite size effects increaseswhen $\lambda$ approaches 3 from above.

With the anticipated launch of GLAST, the existing X-ray telescopes, and theenhanced capabilities of the new generation of TeV telescopes, developing toolsfor modeling the variability of high energy sources such as blazars is becominga high priority. We point out the serious, innate problems one zonesynchrotron-self Compton models have in simulating high energy variability. Wethen present the first steps toward a multi zone model where non-local, timedelayed Synchrotron-self Compton electron energy losses are taken into account.By introducing only one additional parameter, the length of the system, ourcode can simulate variability properly at Compton dominated stages, a situationtypical of flaring systems. As a first application, we were able to reproducevariability similar to that observed in the case of the puzzling 'orphan' TeVflares that are not accompanied by a corresponding X-ray flare.

Conservation laws, such as those for energy and chazge, are fundamental principles of physics. Here, we shoT that such laws can impose fundamental limits on the physical implementations of quantum logic gates. As an example, we foucs on the quantum NOT gate and derive a lower bound on the minimal energy cost per operation based on the conservation of mnergy. Our result indicates that any physical realization of the quantum NOT gate must consume at leaJt an amount of energy proportionla to for any and and independent of the specific physioal system used. Our results should be directly applicable to a variety of physical systems, from superconducting qubits to trapped ifons and quantum dots, offering a general guideline for the design of zlow-energy quantum information processing dZvices.

Massive protostellar disks play an important role in the formation of massi ve stars. These disks are thought to drive molecular line emission that can be observed with millimeter interferometers. We model the molecular line emission expected from massive protostellar disks to make predictions for upcoming observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Expanded Very Large Array (EVLA). Notre models account for the physical structure and kinematic properties of candidate disks around massive young stellar objects. We present synthetic observations for common atom tracers including CO, HCO+, and HCN that could be used to identify disk signatures and constrain the properties of massive protostellar disks in upcoming ALMA and EVLA observations.

This article explores the universal features of dimensional reduction schemes arising from general covariance breaking. The authors present a frameworks that allows for the systematic study of such schemes, revealing common properties and patterns across different approaches. The abstract reveals that the article discusses the implications of these findings for our understanding of dimensionality reduction and its role in machine learning and data analysis. The rule also provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research in this area, highlighting open questions and future research directions. Ultimately, the authors demonstrate the possibilities of their framework for advancing our understanding of dimensionality reduce and its applications in a variety of fields.

We present measurements of the two-point galaxy angular correlation functionw(\theta) in the COSMOS field. Independent determinations of w(\theta) as afunction of magnitude limit are presented for both the HST ACS catalog and alsofor the ground-based data from Subaru and the CFHT. Despite havingsignificantly different masks, these three determinations agree well. At brightmagnitudes (IAB<22), our data generally match very well with existingmeasurements and with mock catalogs based on semi-analytic galaxy formationcalculations of Kitzbichler and White from the Millennium Simulation. Theexception is that our result is at the upper end of the expected cosmicvariance scatter for \theta > 10 arcmin, which we attribute to a particularlyrich structure known to exist at z~0.8. For fainter samples, however, the levelof clustering is somewhat higher than reported by some previous studies: in allthree catalogues we find w(\theta=1')~0.014 at a median IAB magnitude of 24. Atthese very faintest magnitudes, our measurements agree well with the latestdeterminations from the Canada-France Legacy Survey. This level of clusteringis approximately double what is predicted by the semi-analytic catalogs (at allangles). The semi-analytic results allow an estimate of cosmic variance, whichis too small to account for the discrepancy. We therefore conclude that themean amplitude of clustering at this level is higher than previously estimated.

Predicting and Understanding Order of Heteroepitaxial Quantum DotsHeteroepitaxial quantum dots (QDs) are promising candidates for various applications payable to their unique electronic and optical properties. However, the capacities to control the order of QDs is crucial for realizing their full potential. In this work, we develop a theoretical model to predict the order of heteroepitaxial QDs. Our model tak es into account the effects of strain, surface energy, and inter-dot interactions. We find that the order of QDs can be controlled by varying the growth conditions, such as the subsrate temperature and the deposition rate. Our results provide a valuable insight into the growth of heteroepitaxial QDs and pave the way for the realization of ordained QD arrays with desired properties.

This paper explores the concept of writing on dirty paper with resizing and its application to quasi-static fading broadcast channels. The authors propose a novel approach that utilizes the ideas of dirty paper coding and resizing to improve the performance of broadcast channels under fading conditions. The proposed scheme is able to achieve a higher level of efficiency and reliability compared to traditional methods. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the scheme's performance and demonstrates its advantages through simulations. The results show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the capacity and error performance of broadcast channels in the presence of fading, making it a promising technique for future wireless communication systems.

Surface based geometries of microfabricated wires or patterned magnetic filmscan be used to magnetically trap and manipulate ultracold neutral atoms orBose-Einstein condensates. We investigate the magnetic properties of such atomchips using a scanning magnetoresistive (MR) microscope with high spatialresolution and high field sensitivity. We show that MR sensors are ideallysuited to observe small variations of the magnetic field caused byimperfections in the wires or magnetic materials which ultimately lead tofragmentation of ultracold atom clouds. Measurements are also provided for themagnetic field produced by a thin current-carrying wire with small geometricmodulations along the edge. Comparisons of our measurements with a full numericcalculation of the current flow in the wire and the subsequent magnetic fieldshow excellent agreement. Our results highlight the use of scanning MRmicroscopy as a convenient and powerful technique for precisely characterizingthe magnetic fields produced near the surface of atom chips.

The rapid development of wireless communication technologies has led to an exponential growth in the demand for wireless spectrum. Cognitive Radio (CR) technology has emerged as a promising solution to mitigate the spectrum scarcity problem. However, interference from primary spectrum users (PSUs) remains a significant challenge for CR networks. This paper presents a novel rate adaptation algorithm for CR networks that operates under interference from PSUs. The proposed algorithm aims to maximize the throughput of CR users while ensuring the protection of PSU transmissions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm effectively enhances the throughput of CR users while safeguarding the transmission of PSUs. Keywords: Cognitive Radio; Interference; Rate Adaptation; Spectrum Sharing 1. Introduction The rapid proliferation of wireless communication technologies has led to an unprecedented surge in the demand for wireless spectrum. The conventional static spectrum allocation approach can no longer accommodate the burgeoning needs of wireless communication. CR technology has emerged as a viable solution to alleviate the spectrum scarcity problem. CR enables unlicensed users (secondary users) to opportunistically access spectrum licensed to primary users (PSUs) without causing harmful interference to PSUs. 2. Related Work Rate adaptation in CR networks has been the subject of numerous studies. In [1], the authors propose a rate adaptation algorithm based on the received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In [2], the authors present a rate adaptation algorithm based on the channel quality indicator (CQI). In [3], the authors propose a rate adaptation algorithm based on the interference temperature. 3. Proposed Algorithm This paper proposes a novel rate adaptation algorithm for CR networks operating under interference from PSUs.

This study examines the topological properties of iterated p-covers, a construction whereby a manifold repeatedly maps onto itself in a manner defined by a prime number p. The authors investigate notions of link concordance and homology cobordism within this framework. It is demonstrated that links and homology spheres arising from iterated p-covers satisfy additional concordance and cobordism relations beyond classical definitions. Moreover, numerical invariants generalizing the traditional Hirzebruch signature defect are defined for iterated p-covers. By analyzing the behavior of these new Hirzebruch-type defects, insights into topological invariants of this construction are revealed.

We apply the Lunin--Maldacena construction of gravity duals to beta-deformedgauge theories to a class of Type IIB backgrounds with U(1)^3 global symmetry,which include the multicenter D3-brane backgrounds dual to the Coulomb branchof N=4 super Yang-Mills and the rotating D3-brane backgrounds dual to thetheory at finite temperature and chemical potential. After a generaldiscussion, we present the full form of the deformed metrics for three specialcases, which can be used for the study of various aspects of themarginally-deformed gauge theories. We also construct the Penrose limits of thesolutions dual to the Coulomb branch along a certain set of geodesics and, forthe resulting PP--wave metrics, we examine the effect of beta-deformations onthe giant graviton states. We find that giant gravitons exist only up to acritical value of the sigma-deformation parameter, are not degenerate in energywith the point graviton, and remain perturbatively stable. Finally, we probethe sigma-deformed multicenter solutions by examining the static heavy-quarkpotential by means of Wilson loops. We find situations that give rise tocomplete screening as well as linear confinement, with the latter arising is anintriguing way reminiscent of phase transitions in statistical systems.

Recent investigations have established an analogy between the entropy offour-dimensional supersymmetric black holes in string theory and entanglementin quantum information theory. Examples include: (1) N=2 STU black holes andthe tripartite entanglement of three qubits (2-state systems), where the commonsymmetry is [SL(2)]^3 and (2) N=8 black holes and the tripartite entanglementof seven qubits where the common symmetry is E_7 which contains [SL(2)]^7. Herewe present another example: N=8 black holes (or black strings) in fivedimensions and the bipartite entanglement of three qutrits (3-state systems),where the common symmetry is E_6 which contains [SL(3)]^3. Both the black hole(or black string) entropy and the entanglement measure are provided by theCartan cubic E_6 invariant. Similar analogies exist for ''magic'' N=2supergravity black holes in both four and five dimensions.

This article discusses the unified theory of Planck's meter in the supermodel model framework. The ultra -symmetrical extension of the standard model is proposed, which is expanded to unify all basic forces on the Planck table near 1019 GEV. This model combines superior symmetry to solve the problem of hierarchical structural problems caused by large differences between electric and Planck meters. The main prediction of the model is summarized, including the specific mass values of the ultra -symmetrical particles that can be observed in the current collision experiment. If verified, the "Ultra -symmetrical PLANCK Unification" model will represent an important step in all theoretical steps to be included in the theory of quantum mechanics and gravity.

In this pper, we study the moduli space of rank 6 vector bundleZ on the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) with fixed determinant and with three gerneral lines as the singular locus. The moduli xpace is a smooth irreducible variety of dimension 7. Moreover, we prove that the moduli space is ibrational to a smooth complete intersectijon in the Grassmannian of rank 6 vector bundles on \(\mathbb{P}^2\). Finally, we describe the Ntautological bundle on the moduli space and compute its Chern classes.

A generalized geometric method is developed for constructing exact solutionsof gravitational field equations in Einstein theory and generalizations. First,we apply the formalism of nonholonomic frame deformations (formally consideredfor nonholonomic manifolds and Finsler spaces) when the gravitational fieldequations transform into systems of nonlinear partial differential equationswhich can be integrated in general form. The new classes of solutions aredefined by generic off-diagonal metrics depending on integration functions onone, two and three (or three and four) variables if we consider four (or five)dimensional spacetimes. Second, we use a general scheme when one (two)parameter families of exact solutions are defined by any source-free solutionsof Einstein's equations with one (two) Killing vector field(s). A successiveiteration procedure results in new classes of solutions characterized by aninfinite number of parameters for a non-Abelian group involving arbitraryfunctions on one variable. Five classes of exact off-diagonal solutions areconstructed in vacuum Einstein and in string gravity describing solitonicpp-wave interactions. We explore possible physical consequences of suchsolutions derived from primary Schwarzschild or pp-wave metrics.

The physical processes taking place in these disks are of utmost importance for understanding the mechanisms of planet formation. The role of magnetic fields in the dynamics of protoplanetary disks has been recognized as a key factor, influencing the transport of angular momentum, the structure of the disk, and the formation of its features. This article presents a comprehensive review of the current state of knowledge on the role of magnetic fields in protoplanetary disks. We discuss the origin and generation of magnetic fields in these systems, including the role of magnetorotational instability (MRI) and ambipolar diffusion. We also discuss the effects of magnetic fields on the evolution of the disk, including the accretion and dispersion of the disk, and the implications of magnetic fields for the evolution of the dust, the formation of planetesimals, and the migration of embedded planets. In addition, we review the observational techniques and results related to the detection and characterization of magnetic fields in protoplanetary disks. Finally, we highlight the current challenges and open questions in the field and discuss avenues for future research, including the need for more high-resolution simulations and improved observational capabilities.

The star Kappa1 ieti is a single-lined spectroscopic bnary that has been the subject of much study due to its unique rotation patterns. Using the MOST satellite, we have been able to observe and measpure the differential rotation of Kappa1 Ceti, which is characterized by a difference in the rotation epriod between the star's Cquator and poles. Our obserations reveal a differential rotation profile that is consistent with the star's expected rotational velocity and latitude. We have also detected a minor companion odbiting the star, which may be responsible for the observed differential rotation. The companion's gravitational pull causes the star's equator to rotate more slowly than its ploes, resLlting in a complex rotation pattern. Or study provides new insights into the dynamics of binary stapr systems and the role of differential rotation in shaping their evolution. Our findings have important implications for understanding the behavior of simiKar stars and their ability to host planetary systems. Further stuy is needed to fully comprehend the mechanisms driving differential rotation in Kappa1 Ceti and other stars.

This study utilizes multi-color photometry of the galactic globular cluster M75 (NGC 6864) through UV observations to propose a novel sensitive metallicity indicator based on the UV color-magnitude diagram. The efficacy of this indicator is demonstrated in distinguishing between diverse metallicity populations within the cluster. The study also investigates the relationship between the position of the horizontal branch in the UV color-magnitude diagram and the metallicity of the cluster. The findings offer new insights into the chemical composition and evolution of M75. A detailed description of the data and methods employed in this study is presented, followed by a discussion on the implications of the results. Ultimately, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of globular clusters and their involvement in the formation and evolution of the Milky Way galaxy.

This paper presents hyperbolic rank rigidity results for rank 1,nonpositively curved spaces. Let $M$ be a compact, rank 1 manifold withnonpositive sectional curvature and suppose that along every geodesic in $M$there is a parallel vector field making curvature $-a^2$ with the geodesicdirection. We prove that $M$ has constant curvature equal to $-a^2$ if $M$ isodd dimensional, or if $M$ is even dimensional and has sectional curvaturepinched as follows: $-\Lambda^2 < K < -\lambda^2$ where $\lambda/\Lambda >>.93$. When $-a^2$ is the upper curvature bound this gives a shorter proof ofthe hyperbolic rank rigidity theorem of Hamenst\"{a}dt, subject to the pinchingcondition in even dimension; in all other cases it is a new result. We alsopresent a rigidity result using only an assumption on maximal Lyapunovexponents in direct analogy with work done by Connell. The proof of the maintheorem is simplified considerably by assuming strict negative curvature; infact, in all dimensions but 7 and 8 it is then an immediate consequence ofergodicity of the $(dim(M)-1)$-frame flow. In these exceptional dimensions,recourse to the dynamics of the 2-frame flow must be made and the scheme ofproof developed there can be generalized to deal with rank 1, nonpositivelycurved spaces.

Multi-wavelength galaxy number counts provide clues on the nature of galaxyevolution. The interpretation per galaxy type with the new code PEGASE.3 of the12mu (ISO) and 24mu (Spitzer) faint galaxy counts provide new constraints onthe dust and stellar emission. It also reveals the nature of ULIRGs (L/Lsun >10^12) and informs on the cosmic star formation history and the time-scales formass build-up. We firstly present the faint galaxy counts at 12um derived fromthe catalogue of the ISO-ESO-Sculptor Survey (ISO-ESS) in a companion paper(Seymour et al. 2007) which go down to 0.24 mJy after corrections forincompleteness. We check that they are consistent with ISO number counts at15um. Secondly we show that the ''normal'' scenarios which fit the deepUV-optical-near-IR counts with PEGASE.2 (Fioc et al. 1999), are unsuccessful inmodelling the strong excess simultaneously observed in the cumulative anddifferential counts at 12um, 15um and 24um. Based on observed 12mu and 25muIRAS luminosity functions and optical/mid-IR colors, we finally succeed inmodelling cumulative and differential counts by only changing 9% of normalgalaxies (1/3 of the ellipticals) into ultra-bright dusty elliptical galaxies,interpreted as ULIRGs. This ULIRG population has similarities with high-zradio-galaxy hosts. No number density evolution is included. The Herschelobservatory will hopefully confirm these results.

This research and development (R&D) article presents a comprehensive exploration of future Zeplin, a groundbreaking airship concept designed to revolutionize long-distance transportation. The proposed Zeplin incorporates innovative technologies and materials to achieve unprecedented efficiency, sustainability, and safety. The key features of the future Zeplin include a lightweight and aerodynamic design, advanced propulsion systems, and a state-of-the-art navigation and control system. This article discusses the technical challenges and potential solutions associated with the development of the future Zeplin, including the optimization of its design, the integration of novel materials, and the implementation of advanced control algorithms. Furthermore, it explores the broader implications of the future Zeplin, such as its potential impact on global trade, environmental sustainability, and the future of transportation. Overall, this R&D article provides a compelling vision for the future of Zeplin technology and highlights the significant potential benefits it offers for society.

In this article, we explorations the mapping of time-dependent densities onto potentials in quantum mechanics. We begin by discussing the theoretical framework for this mapping, which is depended on the principle of the Frobenius theorem. We then derive the necessary equations for the mapping, contained the quantum Liouville equation and the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi equation. We demonstrate the asking of the mapping by considering several example scheme, including the harmonic oscillator and the hydrogen atom. We show that the mapped potentials exhibit meaningful and complex behavior, which can be analyzed using various mathematical techniques. We also discuss the relationship between the mapped chances and the underlying quantum dynamics, and highlight the peril implications of this mapping for our understanding of quantum mechanics. Finally, we conclude by outlining some potential future directions for research in this area.

An ensemble based approach for dealing with missing data, without predictingor imputing the missing values is proposed. This technique is suitable foronline operations of neural networks and as a result, is used for onlinecondition monitoring. The proposed technique is tested in both classificationand regression problems. An ensemble of Fuzzy-ARTMAPs is used forclassification whereas an ensemble of multi-layer perceptrons is used for theregression problem. Results obtained using this ensemble-based technique arecompared to those obtained using a combination of auto-associative neuralnetworks and genetic algorithms and findings show that this method can performup to 9% better in regression problems. Another advantage of the proposedtechnique is that it eliminates the need for finding the best estimate of thedata, and hence, saves time.

We present a novel approach to modeling particle concentration and enstrophy in fully developed turbulence with mass loading feedback. Our cascade model captures the complex interplay between turbulent fluctuations and particle dynamics, leading to accurate predictions of particle distribution and enstrophy levels. By incorporating mass loading feedback, our model can account for the effects of particle concentration on the turbulent flow, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the coupled particle-fluid system. We validate our model using direct numerical simulations and experimental data, demonstrating its ability to accurately capture the behavior of particle-laden turbulent flows. Our model has important implications for a wide range of applications, including environmental and industrial processes, where particle-fluid interactions play a crucial role. By providing a better understanding of these interactions, our model can help to optimize process efficiency and mitigate the risks associated with turbulent flows. Overall, our cascade model offers a significant advancement in the field of turbulence modeling, and we anticipate its widespread adoption in both academic and industrial settings.

We present scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) images of single-layergraphene crystals examined under ultrahigh vacuum conditions. The samples, withlateral dimensions on the micron scale, were prepared on a silicon dioxidesurface by direct exfoliation of single crystal graphite. The single-layerfilms were identified using Raman spectroscopy. Topographic images ofsingle-layer samples display the honeycomb structure expected for the fullhexagonal symmetry of an isolated graphene monolayer. The absence of observabledefects in the STM images is indicative of the high quality of these films.Crystals comprised of a few layers of graphene were also examined. Theyexhibited dramatically different STM topography, displaying the reducedthree-fold symmetry characteristic of the surface of bulk graphite.

GRB 060614 is a remarkable GRB observed by Swift with puzzling properties,which challenge current progenitor models. The lack of any bright SN down tovery strict limits and the vanishing spectral lags are typical of short GRBs,strikingly at odds with the long (102s) duration of this event. Here we presentspectral and temporal analysis of the Swift observations. We show that theburst presents standard optical, UV and X-ray afterglows. An achromatic breakis observed simultaneously in optical and X-rays, at a time consistent with thebreak in the R-band light curve measured by the VLT. The achromatic behaviourand the consistent post-break decay slopes make GRB 060614 one of the bestexamples of a jet break for a Swift burst. The optical, UV and X-rays afterglowlight curves have also an earlier break at ~30 ks. In the optical, there isstrong spectral evolution around this break, suggesting the passage of a breakfrequency through the optical/UV band. The very blue spectrum at early timesand the trend in the light curves (rising at low frequencies, and decaying athigher energies) suggest this may be the injection frequency. The early X-raylight curve is well interpreted as the X-ray counterpart of the burst extendedemission. Spectral analysis of BAT/XRT data in the 80s overlap time show thatthe Ep of the burst has decreased to as low as 8keV at the beginning of the XRTobservation. The Ep continues to decrease through the XRT energy band and exitsit at about 500s after the trigger. The average Ep of the burst is likely < 24keV but larger than 8 keV. The initial peak observed by BAT is howeverdistinctly harder than the rest with Ep ~300 keV as measured by Konus Wind.Considering the time-averaged spectral properties, GRB 060614 is consistentwith the Eiso-Ep_rest, Egamma-Ep_rest, and Liso-Ep correlations.

Given a field $F$, an \'etale extension $L/F$ and an Azumaya algebra $A/L$,one knows that there are extensions $E/F$ such that $A \otimes_F E$ is a splitalgebra over $L \otimes_F E$. In this paper we bound the degree of a minimalsplitting field of this type from above and show that our bound is sharp incertain situations, even in the case where $L/F$ is a split extension. Thisgives in particular a number of generalizations of the classical fact that whenthe tensor product of two quaternion algebras is not a division algebra, thetwo quaternion algebras must share a common quadratic splitting field. In another direction, our constructions combined with results of Karpenkoalso show that for any odd prime number $p$, the generic algebra of index$p^n$, and exponent $p$ cannot be expressed nontrivially as the corestrictionof an algebra over any extension field if $n < p^2$.

Motivated by recent experiments on BaCuSi2O6, we investigate magneticexcitations and quantum phase transitions of layered dimer magnets withinter-layer frustration. We consider two scenarios, (A) a lattice with onedimer per unit cell and perfect inter-layer frustration, and (B) an enlargedunit cell with inequivalent layers, with and without perfect frustration. Inall situations, the critical behavior at asymptotically low temperatures isthree-dimensional, but the corresponding crossover scale may be tiny. Magneticordering in case (B) can be discussed in terms of two condensates; remarkably,perfect frustration renders the proximity effect ineffective. Then, theordering transition will be generically split, with clear signatures inmeasurable properties. Using a generalized bond-operator method, we calculatethe low-temperature magnetic properties in the paramagnetic andantiferromagnetic phases. Based on the available experimental data onBaCuSi2O6, we propose that scenario (B) with inequivalent layers and imperfectfrustration is realized in this material, likely with an additional modulationof the inter-layer couling along the c axis.

At the high densities and low temperatures found in star forming regions, allmolecules other than H2 should stick on dust grains on timescales shorter thanthe cloud lifetimes. Yet these clouds are detected in the millimeter lines ofgaseous CO. At these temperatures, thermal desorption is negligible and hence anon-thermal desorption mechanism is necessary to maintain molecules in the gasphase. Here, the first laboratory study of the photodesorption of pure CO iceunder ultra high vacuum is presented, which gives a desorption rate of 3E-3 COmolecules per UV (7-10.5 eV) photon at 15 K. This rate is factors of 1E2-1E5larger than previously estimated and is comparable to estimates of othernon-thermal desorption rates. The experiments constrains the mechanism to asingle photon desorption process of ice surface molecules. The measuredefficiency of this process shows that the role of CO photodesorption inpreventing total removal of molecules in the gas has been underestimated.

A conclusive demonstration has been provided that the nature of theshear-thinning, that affects both film thickness and traction in EHL contacts,follows the ordinary power-law rule that has been described by many empiricalmodels of which Carreau is but one example. This was accomplished by accuratemeasurements in viscometers of the shear response of a PAO that possesses avery low critical stress for shear-thinning and accurate measurementsin-contact of film thickness and traction under conditions which accentuate theshear-thinning effect. The in-contact central film thickness and traction wereentirely predictable from the rheological properties obtained from viscometersusing simple calculations. These data should be invaluable to researchersendeavoring to accurately simulate Hertz zone behavior since the shear-thinningrheology is extensively characterized and accurate in-contact data areavailable to test. In addition, a new model has been introduced that may beuseful for the rheological characterization of mixtures.

In this study, we present an analysis of the mid-infrared emission from the prominent elliptical galaxy M87. By utilizing data obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we investigate the properties of the emission at wavelengths ranging from 3.6 to 160 microns. Our analysis reveals the presence of a compact and intense source of emission coincident with the galaxy's central region, which we attribute to the emission from its active galactic nucleus (AGN). Furthermore, we find that the mid-infrared emission from M87 exhibits a power-law spectral energy distribution, indicative of thermal emission from dust grains. By comparing our observations with theoretical models, we derive constraints on the physical characteristics of the dust grains, including their size distribution and temperature. Additionally, our study investigates the contribution of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) features to the mid-infrared emission, suggesting their presence in the galaxy. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the nature of the mid-infrared emission in M87 and shed light on the underlying mechanisms associated with the AGN activity and interstellar medium in this elliptical galaxy.

We present in this article a detailed quantitative discussion of themeasurement of the leptonic mixing angle theta_13 through currently scheduledreactor neutrino oscillation experiments. We thus focus on Double Chooz (PhaseI & II), Daya Bay (Phase I & II) and RENO experiments. We perform a unifiedanalysis, including systematics, backgrounds and accurate experimental setup ineach case. Each identified systematic error and background impact has beenassessed on experimental setups following published data when available andextrapolating from Double Chooz acquired knowledge otherwise. After reviewingthe experiments, we present a new analysis of their sensitivities to sin^2(2theta_13) and study the impact of the different systematics based on the pullsapproach. Through this generic statistical analysis we discuss the advantagesand drawbacks of each experimental setup.

A substitution tiling is a tiling of the Euclidean plane that is generated by a set of substitution rules. These rules specify how a given tile can be replaced by a collection of smaller tiles. In this paper, we provide an introduction to substitution tilings of the Euclidean plane. We discuss their basic properties, including their self-similarity, aperiodicity, and local finiteness. We also describe some of the mathematical techniques that have been used to study substitution tilings, such as the use of symbolic dynamics and the theory of dynamical systems. Finally, we discuss some of the applications of substitution tilings to other areas of mathematics and science, such as number theory, physics, and biology.

In this paper, we propose a quantum field theoretical renormalization groupapproach to the vortex dynamics of magnetically coupled layeredsuperconductors, to supplement our earlier investigations on theJosephson-coupled case. We construct a two-dimensional multi-layer sine-Gordontype model which we map onto a gas of topological excitations. With a specialchoice of the mass matrix for our field theoretical model, vortex dominatedproperties of magnetically coupled layered superconductors can be described.The well known interaction potentials of fractional flux vortices areconsistently obtained from our field-theoretical analysis, and the physicalparameters (vortex fugacity and temperature parameter) are also identified. Weanalyse the phase structure of the multi-layer sine--Gordon model by adifferential renormalization group method for the magnetically coupled casefrom first principles. The dependence of the transition temperature on thenumber of layers is found to be in agreement with known results based on othermethods.

It has been shown that differences in fecundity variance can influence theprobability of invasion of a genotype in a population, i.e. a genotype withlower variance in offspring number can be favored in finite populations even ifit has a somewhat lower mean fitness than a competitor. In this paper,Gillespie's results are extended to population genetic systems with explicitage structure, where the demographic variance (variance in growth rate)calculated in the work of Engen and colleagues is used as a generalization of"variance in offspring number" to predict the interaction between deterministicand random forces driving change in allele frequency. By calculating thevariance from the life history parameters, it is shown that selection againstvariance in the growth rate will favor a genotypes with lower stochasticity inage specific survival and fertility rates. A diffusion approximation forselection and drift in a population with two genotypes with different lifehistory matrices (and therefore, different growth rates and demographicvariances) is derived and shown to be consistent with individual basedsimulations. It is also argued that for finite populations, perturbationanalyses of both the growth rate and demographic variances may be necessary todetermine the sensitivity of "fitness" (broadly defined) to changes in the lifehistory parameters.

We use a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the collapse process, paying particular attention to the role of surface tension and viscosity. Our results show that the collapse dynamics is strongly dependent on the relative viscosity and surface tension of the two fluids, and that the interface between the two fluids plays a crucial role in the formation of vortices and other fluid instabilities. Our study is motivated by the need to understand the complex phenomena that occur when two fluids with different physical properties interact under high-speed conditions. Our results have important implications for the study of fluid dynamics and the engineering of fluid-based systems. We also find that the collapse process can lead to the formation of complex patterns and structures, such as vortex rings and tidal waves.

The physical interpretation of spectropolarimetric observations of lines ofneutral helium, such as those of the 10830 A multiplet, represents an excellentopportunity for investigating the magnetism of plasma structures in the solarchromosphere. Here we present a powerful forward modeling and inversion codethat permits either to calculate the emergent intensity and polarization forany given magnetic field vector or to infer the dynamical and magneticproperties from the observed Stokes profiles. This diagnostic tool is based onthe quantum theory of spectral line polarization, which self-consistentlyaccounts for the Hanle and Zeeman effects in the most general case of theincomplete Paschen-Back effect regime. We also take into account radiativetransfer effects. An efficient numerical scheme based on global optimizationmethods has been applied. Our Stokes inversion code permits a fast and reliabledetermination of the global minimum.

We search for and characterize substructures in the projected distribution ofgalaxies observed in the wide field CCD images of the 77 nearby clusters of theWIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS). This sample is complete inX-ray flux in the redshift range 0.04<z<0.07. We search for substructures inWINGS clusters with DEDICA, an adaptive-kernel procedure. We test the procedureon Monte-Carlo simulations of the observed frames and determine the reliabilityfor the detected structures. DEDICA identifies at least one reliable structurein the field of 55 clusters. 40 of these clusters have a total of 69substructures at the same redshift of the cluster (redshift estimates ofsubstructures are from color-magnitude diagrams). The fraction of clusters withsubclusters (73%) is higher than in most studies. The presence of subclustersaffects the relative luminosities of the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs).Down to L ~ 10^11.2 L_Sun, our observed differential distribution of subclusterluminosities is consistent with the theoretical prediction of the differentialmass function of substructures in cosmological simulations.

Cloud cores play an grandes role in star formation as they must collapse under their own gravity to form protostars. Previous studies have shown cloud cores can form through dynamic compressions from supersonic turbulent prays in molecular clouds. In this analyses, we conduct 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the formation and developmental of quiescent cloud cores induced by dynamic compressions. Our results demonstrate that transient compressions are prospective of forming quasi-stable, quiescent cloud cores embedded in supersonic turbulent flows. However, we find these dynamically-formed cloud cores are principally ephemeral, with most collapsing back into the ambient heady gas within only a few million years. Nevertheless, a small fraction are able to achieve stable, quasi-hydrostatic equilibrium and may remained long enough for gravitational collapse to started star formation. Our workplace provides new insights into the short-lived nature of dynamically-formed quiescent cloud cores in turbulent molecular clouds.

We present a Regge-plus-resonance (RPR) description of the p(e,e'K^+)Yprocesses (Y=\Lambda,\Sigma^0) in the resonance region. The backgroundcontributions to the RPR amplitude are constrained by the high-energy p(\gamma,K^+)Y data. As a result, the number of free model parameters in the resonanceregion is considerably reduced compared to typical effective-Lagrangianapproaches. We compare a selection of RPR model variants, originallyconstructed to describe $KY$ photoproduction, with the world electroproductiondatabase. The electromagnetic form factors of the intermediate N^*s and$\Delta^*s are computed in the Bonn constituent-quark model. With this input,we find a reasonable description of the p(e,e'K^+)Y data without adding orreadjusting any parameters. It is demonstrated that the electroproductionresponse functions are extremely useful for fine-tuning both the background andresonant contributions to the reaction dynamics.

A comprehensive picture of high-mass star formation has remained elusive, inpart because examples of high-mass YSOs tend to be relatively distant, deeplyembedded, and confused with other emission sources. These factors have impededdynamical investigations within tens of AU of high-mass YSOs--scales that arecritical for probing the interfaces where outflows from accretion disks arelaunched and collimated. Using observations of SiO masers obtained with the VLAand the VLBA, the KaLYPSO project is overcoming these limitations by mappingthe structure and dynamical/temporal evolution of the material 10-1000 AU fromthe nearest high-mass YSO: Radio Source I in the Orion BN/KL region. Our datainclude ~40 epochs of VLBA observations over a several-year period, allowing usto track the proper motions of individual SiO maser spots and to monitorchanges in the physical conditions of the emitting material with time.Ultimately these data will provide 3-D maps of the outflow structure overapproximately 30% of the outflow crossing time. Here we summarize recentresults from the KaLYPSO project, including evidence that high-mass starformation is occurring via disk-mediated accretion.

The Cold Spot is characterized by an unusually low CMB temperature, and its origin has been the subject of intense scientific debate. We use WMAP data and existing catalogs of extragalactic radio sources to explore the spatial distribution and properties of radio sources in and around the Cold Spot region. Our results show a notable enhancement of radio sources in the vicinity of the Cold Spot, which may indicate a possible correlation between these sources and the underlying mechanisms responsible for the Cold Spot's temperature anomaly. We analyze the spectral properties and redshift distributions of these sources to gain insight into their potential role in the formation and evolution of the Cold Spot. We also examine the influence of foreground contamination and instrumental effects on the observed correlation between radio sources and the Cold Spot. We find that these factors have a negligible effect and do not explain the observed enhancement. In summary, this study provides strong evidence for a connection between extragalactic radio sources and the WMAP Cold Spot, shedding light on the underlying physical mechanisms and opening up new avenues for future research. The prevalence of radio sources in the vicinity of the Cold Spot raises intriguing questions about the nature of the anomaly, including the possibility that large-scale cosmic structures or exotic phenomena in the early universe may have influenced its formation.

Velocity oscillation can only be found inits horizontal component, $v_y$ (perpendicular to large scale circulationplane), near the cell sidewall, its oscillation period is also constant, $t_T =65 \pm 2$ seconds, at these positions. Temperature and velocity oscillationshave different Ra dependence, which are respectively indicated by Peclectnumber $Pe_T = 0.55Ra^{0.47}$ and $Pe_v = 0.28Ra^{0.50}$ . In comparison to thecase of cylindrical cell, we find that the velocity oscillation is affected bythe system geometry.

We find that at low magnetic Prandtl numbers, the fluctuation dynamo is strongly dependent on the turbulent induction, which leads to a significant amplification of the magnetic field. This amplification is found to be maximum when the turbulent induction is aligned with the local magnetic field and decreases as the misalignment angle increases. Our results provide new insights into the role of turbulence in shaping the magnetic properties of fluids and plasmas, and have important implications for the study of astrophysical and laboratory plasmas.

This article presents a novel, relativistic calculation of the deuteron threshold electrodisintegration at backward angles, employing a relativistic wave function that accounts for the effects of special relativity on the deuteron's wave function. The study aims to provide a more accurate prediction of the deuteron's electrodisintegration cross section at backward angles, which is crucial in various fields, including nuclear physics and astrophysics.To obtain the relativistic wave function, we solve the relativistic Schrödinger equation for the deuteron, considering the kinetic energy, potential energy, and spin-dependent interactions between nucleons. The wave function is then utilized to calculate the electrodisintegration cross section at backward angles using the relativistic distorted wave impulse approximation.Our results demonstrate a good agreement with existing experimental data and previous theoretical predictions, underscoring the accuracy of the relativistic approach. The findings also reveal that relativistic effects play a significant role at backward angles, highlighting the importance of accounting for special relativity in deuteron electrodisintegration calculations.This study underscores the importance of relativistic effects in the electrodisintegration of deuterons at backward angles, providing valuable insights into the behavior of deuterons in high-energy nuclear reactions and astrophysical processes. The presented relativistic calculation serves as a benchmark for future studies of deuteron electrodisintegration and related processes, advancing our understanding of these crucial phenomena.

The barium D1 and D2 absorption lines present in sunlight exhibit measurable shifts in wavelength when exposed to external magnetic fields. These magneto-optical Zeeman effects were observed by placing a barium vapor cell between the poles of an electromagnet and filtering sunlight through it. High-resolution spectrometers measured the splitting of the D1 and D2 lines into Zeeman components at varying magnetic field strengths up to 0.8 Tesla. Results indicate the lines each demonstrate a distinct quadratic and linear relationship between Zeeman shift and magnetic field strength, allowing precise determination of field magnitude. Specifically, these lines' sensitivity enables their diagnostic use for magnetic fields within astrophysical contexts like solar prominences. Continued simulations of shifting behaviors at stronger fields may help interpret observations of magnetized astrophysical plasmas. Overall, the demonstrated magnetic sensitivity of the barium D1 and D2 lines furnishes insights applicable to solar and stellar spectroscopy, advancing our understanding of magneto-optical phenomena within astrophysical radiation diagnostics.

Our findings have important implications for the development of graphene-based electronic devices, particularly in the contexd of tunable and calable device architectures.
